gee-hye-lee.why_it_matters: A contemporary Korean pianist active in the German jazz scene and transnational ensembles.

evidence.claim: Norwegian Academy of Music lists Lysne as professor of jazz and improvised music.
Its biography lists composition and conducting for NDR Big Band and Geir Lysne Listening Ensemble.

geir-lysne.limitations: Faculty biography covers professional experience without all album dates.
geir-lysne.summary: Norwegian saxophonist and arranger Geir Lysne leads and composes for large jazz ensembles. His conducting includes the NDR Big Band and Geir Lysne Listening Ensemble.
geir-lysne.why_it_matters: Documents Nordic jazz big-band arranging and composition.

evidence.claim: His official biography names the solo album Quiet Now and earlier Acoustic Romance.
It credits his Jobim arrangements on Someone to Light Up My Life and performing with Paul Desmond.

gene-bertoncini.limitations: Short artist-level account only; do not infer unlisted session or ensemble personnel.
gene-bertoncini.summary: American jazz guitarist Gene Bertoncini blends classical guitar touch with jazz improvisation, leading solo recordings and arranging Jobim songs.
gene-bertoncini.why_it_matters: Adds a documented performer or composer and a specific musical contribution to the catalog.

evidence.claim: Gifford joined the Orange Blossoms in 1929; that group became the Casa Loma Orchestra.
Gifford stopped playing regularly in late 1933 and led one Victor recording session in 1935.

gene-gifford.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
gene-gifford.summary: Arranger-guitarist Gene Gifford joined the Orange Blossoms in 1929 and gave the renamed Casa Loma Orchestra its distinctive early swing charts.
gene-gifford.why_it_matters: His arrangements helped define pre-Goodman big-band swing.

evidence.claim: International Archives for the Jazz Organ credits the 1964 Organ Out Loud sessions to Gene Ludwig on organ, Jerry Byrd on guitar and Randy Gelispie on drums.
The organ archive's discography dates Sonny Stitt's Night Letter session to October 1969 and credits Gene Ludwig on organ alongside Pat Martino and Randy Gelispie.

gene-ludwig.limitations: International Archives for the Jazz Organ is a specialist compiled discography; its credited sessions are not independent original tape-box confirmations.
gene-ludwig.summary: Hammond organist Gene Ludwig recorded Organ Out Loud in 1964 with Jerry Byrd and Randy Gelispie, then joined Sonny Stitt's 1969 Night Letter session.
gene-ludwig.why_it_matters: A specialist jazz-organ discography lists exact players, instruments, albums and recording dates for Ludwig's organ-combo history.

evidence.claim: Perla switched to upright bass in 1964 after studying piano at Berklee.
He played with Elvin Jones, Sarah Vaughan and Sonny Rollins.
Stone Alliance formed with Steve Grossman and Don Alias and recorded ten albums.

gene-perla.limitations: Artist biography supplies broad career details without complete session discography.
gene-perla.summary: Bassist Gene Perla switched from piano to upright bass in 1964 and played with Elvin Jones and Sarah Vaughan. He founded Stone Alliance with Steve Grossman and Don Alias.
gene-perla.why_it_matters: Perla bridges acoustic jazz, electric groups and self-produced releases.

evidence.claim: Gene Rodgers recorded solo piano sides Was It A Lie and Three Minutes Of Blues in October 1936, matrices S-128 and S-129, Vocalion 527.
Rodgers is listed on piano for Coleman Hawkins Body And Soul, New York October 11, 1939, matrix 042936-1.
Rodgers played piano with the Coleman Hawkins All-Star Octet on Bouncing With Bean on January 3, 1940, matrix 046159-1.

gene-rodgers.limitations: Historical personnel is reconstructed from Rust, whose publisher warns of errors; no unlisted piano solos should be attributed.
gene-rodgers.summary: Gene Rodgers recorded solo piano for Vocalion in 1936 and accompanied Coleman Hawkins on landmark sessions in 1939-40.
gene-rodgers.why_it_matters: Original matrix identifiers document both a solo piano session and sideman recordings.

evidence.claim: Gene Roland joined Stan Kenton's orchestra in 1944 as a fifth trumpeter and arranger.
Roland arranged Kenton's hit Tampico and contributed 65 arrangements to Woody Herman in 1956-1958.

gene-roland.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
gene-roland.summary: Trumpeter, trombonist and arranger Gene Roland joined Stan Kenton in 1944, arranged Tampico in 1945 and later wrote extensively for Woody Herman.
gene-roland.why_it_matters: His orchestral writing links swing arranging to experimental postwar big bands.

evidence.claim: Concord identifies Gene Taylor as bassist in the Cedar Walton and Roy Brooks rhythm section of Blue Mitchell's The Cup Bearers.
Concord names Gene Taylor alongside Junior Cook, Blue Mitchell, Ronnie Mathews, Dolo Coker and Roy Brooks on Junior's Cookin'.
Concord includes Gene Taylor among players on Eddie Jefferson's vocalese recording Come Along With Me alongside Barry Harris and Bill Hardman.

gene-taylor.limitations: The retrospective Plays for Lovers is compiled from multiple sessions and is not used to attribute every track to Taylor.
gene-taylor.summary: Jazz bassist Gene Taylor played with Cedar Walton and Roy Brooks on Blue Mitchell's The Cup Bearers and appeared on Junior Cook's Junior's Cookin'.
gene-taylor.why_it_matters: The original Jazzland/Riverside reissues document two distinct, personnel-identified jazz ensemble recordings.

evidence.claim: Edition Records specifically credits Geoffrey Keezer with piano on track 1 of Tim Garland's Songs to the North Sky.
The label states that the track 1 piano was recorded at SpraguerLand Recording Studio in California; the double album was released June 2, 2014.

geoffrey-keezer.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
geoffrey-keezer.summary: American pianist Geoffrey Keezer contributes the opening track's piano part to Tim Garland's Songs to the North Sky, released by Edition in June 2014.
geoffrey-keezer.why_it_matters: His piano is part of a cross-Atlantic jazz-and-strings collaboration.

evidence.claim: ACT dates the live Mingus centenary performance at the Berlin Philharmonie Kammermusiksaal to April 13, 2022.
ACT credits Breinschmid with arrangements of Jelly Roll (track 1) and Boogie Stop Shuffle (track 4).

georg-breinschmid.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
georg-breinschmid.summary: Austrian bassist Georg Breinschmid co-led the 2022 Berlin Philharmonic Mingus centenary concert and arranged Jelly Roll and Boogie Stop Shuffle.
georg-breinschmid.why_it_matters: Connects orchestral virtuosity, Viennese musical idioms and modern improvised bass.

evidence.claim: In the original Caprice Records interview Georg Riedel states that he and Rune Ofwerman's trio won the 1950 AT-jazzen competition.
Riedel's original interview says he participated in a Lars Gullin recording during March 1953 and went on tour with Gullin's newly formed quintet that summer.
The Caprice interview identifies Georg Riedel as a bassist with Arne Domnerus's orchestra at Stockholm's Nalen venue during his conservatory studies.

georg-riedel.limitations: Interview recollections are preserved as the musician's testimony rather than exact dates for every undocumented session.
georg-riedel.summary: Swedish jazz bassist Georg Riedel played with Lars Gullin's 1953 quintet after winning a 1950 Swedish jazz contest in Rune Ofwerman's trio.
georg-riedel.why_it_matters: The original Caprice Svensk Jazzhistoria interview is Riedel's first-person account of the bands, recordings and Swedish postwar jazz community.

evidence.claim: His official biography dates his musical directorship of the Jazz Orchestra Rhineland-Palatinate to 1980-1997.
The same artist biography names him initiator of Cologne's JazzHausMusik label.

georg-ruby.limitations: Artist-level historical synopsis; specific session credits restricted to cited primary material.
georg-ruby.summary: German pianist, composer and bandleader Georg Ruby founded jazz education initiatives in Cologne and directed regional youth orchestras.
georg-ruby.why_it_matters: Documents concrete genre, performance and recording contributions to a diverse jazz catalog.

evidence.claim: Fresh Sound's Boss: Bossa Nova reissue credits George Bohanon on trombone with Kirk Lightsey on piano, Joe Messina on guitar and Cecil McBee on bass.
The original Workshop Jazz Boss: Bossa Nova LP was recorded in Detroit in 1962, as specified by the label's historical reissue notes.
The Boss: Bossa Nova label tracklist credits George Bohanon as composer of El Rio, Conmigo and Simpatica.

george-bohanon.limitations: This source supports Bohanon's 1962 Detroit studio quartet, not assumptions about his later Motown and Hollywood session instrumentation.
george-bohanon.summary: Detroit trombonist George Bohanon led the 1962 Boss: Bossa Nova session with Kirk Lightsey, Joe Messina and Cecil McBee.
george-bohanon.why_it_matters: The original Workshop Jazz LP reissue gives the recording year, personnel and composition credits for a specific early-career jazz quartet.

evidence.claim: Blue Note says Braith developed a one-handed stritch and soprano saxophone method.
Blue Note identifies Two Souls in One, Soul Stream and Extension as his label albums.

george-braith.limitations: Label retrospective; avoid inferring exact players on unlisted tracks.
george-braith.summary: Multi-reedist George Braith devised a two-saxophone technique and recorded Two Souls in One, Soul Stream and Extension for Blue Note.
george-braith.why_it_matters: Illustrates experimental multiple-horn playing in 1960s soul jazz.

evidence.claim: The National Jazz Archive dates his professional start on piano in a Glasgow cinema to 1932.
The archive documents his Ambrose band trombone tenure from 1937 to 1939.

george-chisholm.limitations: Short artist-level account only; do not infer unlisted session or ensemble personnel.
george-chisholm.summary: Scottish jazz trombonist George Chisholm played with the Ambrose dance band and became a leading figure in Britain's swing and broadcast scene.
george-chisholm.why_it_matters: Adds a documented performer or composer and a specific musical contribution to the catalog.

evidence.claim: MPS Records documents George Duke recording two projects beginning April 1971, originally issued together in 1973 as The Inner Source, with bassist John Heard and drummer Dick Berk on its Solus portion.
Concord/Heads Up announced Duke's DreamWeaver for July 16, 2013, listing Stanley Clarke, Christian McBride, Lalah Hathaway and other named contributing musicians.
The Recording Academy lists Stanley Clarke and George Duke's The Clarke/Duke Project as a 1982 Grammy nominee for R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals, not a winner.

identity_resolution.method: MPS's artist-specific original releases matched against Concord Heads Up label personnel and the Recording Academy's named performer credits.
identity_resolution.note: All four separate musician-authority sites describe a keyboardist named George Duke whose 1971 fusion recordings, later Heads Up catalog, Clarke/Duke collaborations and lifetime career form the same performing person. The original seed identifies the American keyboardist born in 1946 and deceased in 2013. Several database MBID candidates remain in conflict, but their identifiers were not treated as historical evidence or arbitrarily selected.

george-duke.limitations: The 1971 MPS session was issued as a two-LP set in 1973; these are different events. Duke's 1982 Clarke/Duke Project was Grammy-nominated, not a winner. Heads Up label's collective album personnel are not asserted to appear on every song. MusicBrainz identity ambiguity is preserved.
george-duke.summary: Jazz-fusion keyboardist George Duke recorded The Inner Source for MPS in 1971 and released DreamWeaver on Heads Up in 2013 with Stanley Clarke and Christian McBride.
george-duke.why_it_matters: An original fusion-label discography and Duke's later record label independently establish named musician credits, the recording/reissue timeline and a later collaborative ensemble.

evidence.claim: Fremeaux identifies George E. Lee as tenor saxophonist and leader on Meritt Stomp, original Meritt 2206, recorded in Kansas City in 1927.
The Meritt Stomp session personnel include Sam Utterbach on trumpet, Thurston Maupins on trombone, Clarence Taylor on saxophone and Jesse Stone on piano.
Fremeaux documents Lee's 1929 Brunswick recordings and identifies Paseo Street and Ruff Scufflin' as performances by his expanded orchestra.

george-e-lee.limitations: The original Meritt recordings have poor sound quality. The 1927 and 1929 ensembles differ, and individual saxophone solos cannot be attributed without further evidence.
george-e-lee.summary: Kansas City saxophonist and bandleader George E. Lee led the Novelty Singing Orchestra on Meritt recordings in 1927 and Brunswick sides in 1929.
george-e-lee.why_it_matters: Historical Fremeaux recording documentation identifies Lee as tenor saxophonist and leader, with original Meritt and Brunswick record references.

evidence.claim: Delmark says Freeman played with Gene Ammons from 1969 until 1974.
The label lists his leader records Birth Sign (1972) and Man and Woman (1974).

george-freeman.limitations: Artist-level historical synopsis; specific session credits restricted to cited primary material.
george-freeman.summary: Chicago jazz guitarist George Freeman drew on blues and soul, working with Gene Ammons and releasing jazz albums under his own name.
george-freeman.why_it_matters: Documents concrete genre, performance and recording contributions to a diverse jazz catalog.

evidence.claim: Melodiya credits Georgy Garanian as a performer on Melodiya Ensemble Plays Duke Ellington, recorded and released in 1977 under catalog MEL CO 1175.
That 1977 album identifies Garanian in its credits for Take the A Train and Cotton Tail, while listing the performing ensemble separately.
Melodiya's Concert in Bombay catalog MEL CO 1119 lists Garanian as a performer and dates the original concert recording to 1980, distinct from its 2022 release.
Melodiya's All That Jazz reissue credits the Georgy Garanian Sextet on Ballad and the Georgy Garanian Quartet on Terem-Teremok; its 2004 date is a reissue year.

george-garanian.limitations: Melodiya gives the 1977 Ellington tribute recording and issue year; the 1980 Bombay concert was released digitally in 2022. Collective ensemble credits do not establish an individual saxophone solo on each track.
george-garanian.summary: Soviet jazz saxophonist Georgy Garanian led his own quartet and sextet and recorded with the Melodiya Ensemble in 1977 and 1980.
george-garanian.why_it_matters: The original Melodiya catalogue separately credits Garanian as a performer and arranger on jazz projects and identifies his named smaller ensembles.

evidence.claim: Storyville credits George Girard on trumpet and vocals in George Girard and His New Orleans Five with Bob Havens, Harry Shields, Bob Discon, Emile Christian and Paul Edwards.
Storyville identifies Girard's New Orleans Five recordings at the Parisian Room on July 1, 1956 for tracks 8-9 and July 15, 1956 for tracks 10-13.
Storyville credits Girard on trumpet in Dixieland All Stars with Santo Pecora, Raymond Burke and Lester Bouchon for a New Orleans Municipal Auditorium concert on September 19, 1954.

george-girard.limitations: Storyville's digital release dates in 2008 are anthology issue years. The original recordings described on those releases are from 1954 and 1956, and their personnel vary.
george-girard.summary: New Orleans trumpeter and vocalist George Girard led a five-piece group recorded at the Parisian Room in July 1956 and played a 1954 jazz concert.
george-girard.why_it_matters: Original Storyville tape documentation identifies Girard's trumpet and vocal credits, his sidemen and specific performances separated by two years.

evidence.claim: Handy arranged for Boyd Raeburn's orchestra in 1944-1946.
Norman Granz commissioned Handy's composition The Bloos, recorded in 1946.

george-handy.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
george-handy.summary: Pianist-arranger George Handy worked with Boyd Raeburn in 1944-1946, wrote Tonsillectomy and Dalvatore Sally, and recorded his commissioned work The Bloos in 1946.
george-handy.why_it_matters: His dissonant big-band writing anticipated later orchestral jazz experiments.

evidence.claim: Felsted reissue notes credit tenor saxophonist George Kelly on Rex Stewart's Rendezvous with Rex tracks 1, 3 and 5.
The Kelly and Rex Stewart septet with trombonist George Stevenson and reed player Haywood Henry recorded in New York City on January 28, 1958.
The Felsted session notes name Willie The Lion Smith at the piano on Rex Stewart's tracks 1 and 3, while Dick Cary replaced him on track 5, all alongside saxophonist Kelly.

george-kelly.limitations: The credit concerns Rex Stewart's January 28 septet tracks only. Kelly is not credited on the separate January 31 sextet; no other Kelly with the same name is inferred.
george-kelly.summary: Tenor saxophonist George Kelly played with Rex Stewart's orchestra on the original 1958 Felsted recording Rendezvous with Rex in New York.
george-kelly.why_it_matters: Named original studio credits and track numbers establish a specific tenor role, ensemble membership and historical album.

evidence.claim: George Lewis developed 'Voyager' (1987) as a real-time computer improviser playing with human musicians.
George Lewis joined the AACM in 1971

george-lewis.limitations: Source-specific music facts; not a complete discography.
george-lewis.summary: Trombonist and AACM composer George Lewis created 'Voyager' (1987), an interactive computer-improvisation system that plays alongside human jazz musicians.
george-lewis.why_it_matters: Pioneer of jazz human-computer improvisation and experimental AACM aesthetics

evidence.claim: Masso worked with Jimmy Dorsey in 1948 and continued teaching until 1973.
He toured with Benny Goodman's sextet in 1973 and led sessions for Famous Door and Dreamstreet in 1978-83.

george-masso.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
george-masso.summary: Trombonist George Masso toured with Benny Goodman's sextet in 1973 after years of teaching and later led recording sessions for Famous Door and Dreamstreet.
george-masso.why_it_matters: A versatile trombone voice linking late-swing repertory with later jazz festivals.

evidence.claim: The Definitive Records reissue identifies George Matthews as a trombonist in Ella Fitzgerald and Her Famous Orchestra's 1940 NBC broadcasts.
Original Felsted personnel place George Matthews beside Dicky Wells, Vic Dickenson and Benny Morton on a four-trombone New York session dated February 3, 1958.
The same Felsted sessionography documents Matthews in another Dicky Wells four-trombone recording with pianist Skip Hall and guitarist Kenny Burrell dated April 21, 1959.

george-matthews.limitations: The 1940 Fitzgerald broadcasts and 1958-1959 Felsted sessions are unrelated projects. No unsupported personal dates or saxophone attribution are used.
george-matthews.summary: Trombonist George Matthews recorded with Ella Fitzgerald's orchestra in 1940 and with Dicky Wells's four-trombone groups in 1958 and 1959.
george-matthews.why_it_matters: Original broadcaster and Felsted session credits document this trombonist in separate, precisely dated jazz lineups.

evidence.claim: Robert's discography includes albums with Kenny Barron, Clark Terry and Phil Woods.
New Life quartet personnel are Dado Moroni, Peter Washington and Jeff Hamilton.
He was named Officer of the French Order of Arts and Letters in 2008.

george-robert.limitations: Estate-maintained site reports discography and lineup; broad acclaim omitted.
george-robert.summary: Swiss alto saxophonist George Robert recorded with Kenny Barron, Clark Terry and Phil Woods. His quartet album New Life features Dado Moroni, Peter Washington and Jeff Hamilton.
george-robert.why_it_matters: His quartet and international collaborations connect European alto saxophone jazz with American players.

evidence.claim: George Russell published his Lydian Chromatic Concept in 1953, expanding the harmonic language of modal jazz.
His 1956 Jazz Workshop sextet included pianist Bill Evans and trumpeter Art Farmer.

george-russell.limitations: Research is source-specific; credits denote actual documented roles, not an exhaustive discography.
george-russell.summary: Composer George Russell's 1953 Lydian Chromatic Concept helped open modal jazz; his 1956 'Jazz Workshop' featured Bill Evans and Art Farmer.
george-russell.why_it_matters: Pioneer of modal theory and advanced small-group composition.

evidence.claim: Concord artist biography says Shearing moved to the United States in 1947 and formed a quintet in 1949 to record September in the Rain for MGM.
The NEA interview with bassist and manager John Levy names Chuck Wayne, Marjorie Hyams, Denzil Best and himself as the original Shearing Quintet lineup.

george-shearing.limitations: The group had changing personnel after its original lineup; John Levy first played with a different Shearing group before its formal quintet sessions.
george-shearing.summary: Pianist George Shearing formed his quintet in 1949 and recorded September in the Rain for MGM; the group included bassist John Levy.
george-shearing.why_it_matters: A label biography and a participant interview anchor the sound of Shearing original American quintet without conflating later personnel.

evidence.claim: Jazz Lines Publications attributes Frank Sinatra's Let It Snow arrangement JLP-9889 to Siravo.
The same publisher attributes Tony Bennett's Who Can I Turn To arrangement JLP-6267 to Siravo.

george-siravo.limitations: Published arrangements distinguish arranger from later score preparation; no personnel inferred.
george-siravo.summary: American big-band arranger George Siravo wrote charts for recordings by Frank Sinatra and Tony Bennett after work with swing orchestras.
george-siravo.why_it_matters: Identifies surviving publisher-issued studio arrangements and their featured singers.

evidence.claim: Horace Parlan's Us Three (Blue Note BLP 4037) was recorded April 20, 1960 at Van Gelder Studio with George Tucker on bass and Al Harewood on drums.
The July 14, 1960 Speakin' My Piece (Blue Note BLP 4043) quintet session credits Tucker on bass with Tommy and Stanley Turrentine, Parlan and Harewood.

george-tucker.limitations: Specific original session and track credits; not a complete discography.
george-tucker.summary: Bassist George Tucker recorded Horace Parlan's Us Three at Van Gelder Studio on April 20, 1960 and Speakin' My Piece with Tommy and Stanley Turrentine that July.
george-tucker.why_it_matters: His documented Blue Note session credits identify the bassist's role in Horace Parlan's hard-bop trio and quintet.

evidence.claim: Wallington was in Dizzy Gillespie's 1943-1944 group on 52nd Street.
His New York groups in 1954-1960 included Donald Byrd and Jackie McLean.

george-wallington.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
george-wallington.summary: Bop pianist George Wallington played in Dizzy Gillespie's 1943-44 combo, wrote Lemon Drop and Godchild, and later led bands featuring Donald Byrd and Jackie McLean.
george-wallington.why_it_matters: He linked bebop's first New York combos to hard-bop apprenticeships.

evidence.claim: The National Jazz Archive says Webb's Dixielanders played the Red Barn at Barnehurst from the early 1940s.
An original Swingtime broadcast script lists Webb's Dixielanders as performers of traditional New Orleans jazz.

george-webb.limitations: National Jazz Archive photographs and an original programme script support ensemble context, but not specific commercial recording credits.
george-webb.summary: British pianist George Webb led the Dixielanders during the early New Orleans jazz revival, playing at the Red Barn and on 1940s radio.
george-webb.why_it_matters: Documents early British traditional jazz performance and radio history.

evidence.claim: Wettling played drums with Artie Shaw's 1936 band and Bunny Berigan in 1937.
His 1938 trio recordings included Bud Freeman and Jess Stacy; he later worked on Eddie Condon broadcasts.

george-wettling.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
george-wettling.summary: Chicago jazz drummer George Wettling worked in Artie Shaw's 1936 orchestra and led 1938 trio sessions with Bud Freeman and Jess Stacy before joining Eddie Condon.
george-wettling.why_it_matters: His responsive drumming became central to classic Chicago-style jazz ensembles.

evidence.claim: RCA Victor LPM-1301 Rhythm Was His Business credits George Williams as arranger and director of the Jimmie Lunceford tribute orchestra.
The reissue documents a New York session on April 23, 1956 with Hank Jones, Charlie Shavers, Conte Candoli and Milt Hinton.
The track listing credits Harlem Express to George Williams and documents Hollywood sessions on April 24-25, 1956.

george-williams.limitations: The reissue combines New York and Hollywood sessions. Williams is credited as arranger and director, not an instrumental performer.
george-williams.summary: Jazz arranger George Williams directed Rhythm Was His Business, a 1956 RCA Victor tribute to Jimmie Lunceford featuring Hank Jones and Charlie Shavers.
george-williams.why_it_matters: The RCA Victor sessionography identifies Williams as arranger and director and documents his composition Harlem Express.

evidence.claim: Blue Note issued Gerald Clayton Bells On Sand in 2022.
Gerald Clayton's 'Bells On Sand' (2022) includes Charles Lloyd, John Clayton and Justin Brown among its guests.

gerald-clayton.limitations: Research is source-specific; credits denote actual documented roles, not an exhaustive discography.
gerald-clayton.summary: Pianist Gerald Clayton released 'Bells On Sand' on Blue Note in 2022, featuring saxophonist Charles Lloyd and guest players John Clayton and Justin Brown.
gerald-clayton.why_it_matters: Modern piano-led composition with selected guest instrumental voices.

evidence.claim: Northern Spy issued Black Host album in 2013
Personnel includes Darius Jones, Cooper-Moore and Brandon Seabrook

gerald-cleaver.limitations: Source-specific musical details, not a complete discography.
gerald-cleaver.summary: Drummer Gerald Cleaver led the free-jazz quintet Black Host on 'Life in the Sugar Candle Mines' (2013) with Darius Jones, Cooper-Moore and Brandon Seabrook.
gerald-cleaver.why_it_matters: New York free-jazz group improvisation, merging layered rhythms and noise

evidence.claim: Wiggins toured with the big bands of Louis Armstrong and Benny Carter in 1943.
Wiggins toured with singer Lena Horne during 1950-1951.

gerald-wiggins.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
gerald-wiggins.summary: Pianist Gerald Wiggins toured with Louis Armstrong and Benny Carter in 1943, accompanied Lena Horne in 1950-51 and led a longstanding trio with Andy Simpkins and Paul Humphrey.
gerald-wiggins.why_it_matters: His understated swing anchored both vocal accompaniment and small-group jazz.

evidence.claim: Wilson took Sy Oliver's position with Jimmie Lunceford in 1939.
Wilson formed a big band in late 1944 that included Melba Liston.

gerald-wilson.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
gerald-wilson.summary: Arranger Gerald Wilson joined Jimmie Lunceford in 1939 and formed his own big band in 1944 with trombonist Melba Liston; his Pacific Jazz albums displayed innovative harmonies.
gerald-wilson.why_it_matters: His orchestration transformed swing-era big-band writing.

evidence.claim: ACT's original artist profile says Presencer entered the Charlie Watts Tentet at eighteen.
ACT's own release catalog lists Presencer's Chasing Reality and What's Nu? Music Beyond.

gerard-presencer.limitations: ACT artist-page facts; avoid its potentially dated teaching-post description.
gerard-presencer.summary: British jazz trumpeter Gerard Presencer joined Charlie Watts's Tentet at eighteen and recorded Chasing Reality and What's Nu? for ACT.
gerard-presencer.why_it_matters: Preserves documented jazz recording or instrumental context for this named performer.

evidence.claim: Bethel Woods Center for the Arts identifies percussionist Gerardo Velez as a member of Jimi Hendrix's Gypsy Sun and Rainbows ensemble at Woodstock.
Spyro Gyra's official Access All Areas credits Gerardo Velez on percussion for performances recorded live in Florida on November 17-19, 1983.
Spyro Gyra's Access All Areas credits Gerardo Velez and Jorge D'Alto as composers of Latin Streets and lists congas and timbales among Velez's instruments.

gerardo-velez.limitations: Bethel Woods directly corroborates his Woodstock percussion role; the official Spyro Gyra album documents only the specific 1983 live sessions.
gerardo-velez.summary: Percussionist Gerardo Velez played at Woodstock with Jimi Hendrix in 1969 and later recorded Latin percussion with jazz-fusion group Spyro Gyra.
gerardo-velez.why_it_matters: Artist account and original band album credit separately confirm rock history and a documented 1983 fusion concert with specific instruments.

evidence.claim: Oahspe recorded November 22 and 25 1978
Auricle Records released Oahspe January 15 1979

gerry-hemingway.limitations: Source-specific musical details, not a complete discography.
gerry-hemingway.summary: Drummer Gerry Hemingway formed BassDrumBone with Ray Anderson and Mark Helias; their trio recorded 'Oahspe' in November 1978 (released 1979).
gerry-hemingway.why_it_matters: Unusual trombone-bass-drums trio focused on collective rhythmic free improvisation

evidence.claim: Eastman School of Music documents that Gerry Niewood earned a music education bachelor's degree with a saxophone emphasis in 1970.

Eastman confirms that Niewood joined a 2007 recreation of Chuck Mangione's 1970 Friends and Love concert with the Rochester Philharmonic.

gerry-niewood.limitations: The Eastman memorial concerns career relationships and an actual concert, not a track-by-track discography.
gerry-niewood.summary: Multi-reed jazz player Gerry Niewood spent nearly fourteen years with Chuck Mangione's group and took part in a 2007 Friends and Love reunion concert.
gerry-niewood.why_it_matters: His own conservatory records the band's long collaboration, reed instruments and reunion performance.

evidence.claim: The Revolution Will Be Jazz features songs associated with Gil Scott-Heron.
Milestones applies Giacomo Gates's vocals to the music of Miles Davis.
His 2022 album YOU was released by Savant.

giacomo-gates.limitations: Artist biography supplies named projects; radio rankings are omitted.
giacomo-gates.summary: Vocalist Giacomo Gates released The Revolution Will Be Jazz, interpreting Gil Scott-Heron, and Milestones, a Miles Davis songbook. His album YOU appeared in 2022.
giacomo-gates.why_it_matters: His lyric-centered albums reinterpret instrument-led jazz and politically engaged songs.

evidence.claim: The duo's Deconstructing Monk in Africa lists Giancarlo Schiaffini on trombone and Sergio Armaroli on chromatic balafon, drums, mbira and percussion.
The album's credits specify recording on May 11-12, 2019 at Il Pollaio in Ronco Biellese, with a 2021 Dodicilune publication date.

giancarlo-schiaffini.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
giancarlo-schiaffini.summary: Italian trombonist Giancarlo Schiaffini recorded Deconstructing Monk in Africa with percussionist Sergio Armaroli in 2019 for a 2021 Dodicilune release.
giancarlo-schiaffini.why_it_matters: Italian free improvisation joins Monk's blues language with African percussion and electronics.

evidence.claim: The Saint Louis archive dates Basso's Lunet recording to March 17, 1982 at Fontana Studio 7 in Milan.
It identifies Klaus Koenig on piano, Isla Eckinger on bass and Peter Schmidlin on drums in that quartet.

gianni-basso.limitations: Only claims recorded in the cited artist, label, institution or original archive are included; crossovers are not classified exclusively as jazz.
gianni-basso.summary: Italian tenor saxophonist Gianni Basso led a European quartet with pianist Klaus Koenig and later recorded standards in Bari.
gianni-basso.why_it_matters: Documents specific recordings, ensembles or performance roles and their place in jazz or adjacent genres.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Gianni Coscia on accordion and Gianluigi Trovesi on piccolo and alto clarinets for Round About Weill.
Round About Weill was recorded in July 2004 at Radio Studio DRS in Zurich and originally released March 7, 2005.

gianni-coscia.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
gianni-coscia.summary: Accordionist Gianni Coscia recorded Round About Weill with clarinetist Gianluigi Trovesi in Zurich in July 2004; ECM released the duo album in March 2005.
gianni-coscia.why_it_matters: Coscia brought Italian folk, jazz and theatre music into an improvising clarinet-accordion dialogue.

evidence.claim: Intakt Records lists Gianni Gebbia on saxophones with Heiner Goebbels on prepared grand piano, Camille Emaille on percussion and Cecile Lartigau on ondes Martenot.
The Mayfield was recorded during a residence at La Muse en Circuit in Paris in January 2022 and published as Intakt Recording 426 in 2024.

gianni-gebbia.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
gianni-gebbia.summary: Sicilian saxophonist Gianni Gebbia joined The Mayfield with Heiner Goebbels, Camille Emaille and other improvisers for a Paris session recorded in January 2022.
gianni-gebbia.why_it_matters: His saxophone joins prepared piano, electronics and ondes Martenot in a contemporary collective approach.

evidence.claim: Mad About Records attributes composition, bandleading, piano and original liner notes of Jazz Fantasia to Gideon Nxumalo.
The reissue credits Kippie Moeketsi and Dudu Pukwana on alto saxophones, Martin Mgijima on bass and Makaya Ntshoko on drums.
Mad About Records states that Jazz Fantasia was recorded live at Wits University Great Hall in Johannesburg in September 1962.

gideon-nxumalo.limitations: The current digital release date is 2019, while the original recording dates to September 1962; the two should never be conflated.
gideon-nxumalo.summary: South African pianist and composer Gideon Nxumalo recorded Jazz Fantasia live in Johannesburg in 1962 with Kippie Moeketsi, Dudu Pukwana and Makaya Ntshoko.
gideon-nxumalo.why_it_matters: The licensed historical reissue gives named original instrumental credits, concert venue, composition and recording history.

Jazz Lab Quintet featured trumpeter Donald Byrd

gigi-gryce.limitations: Source-specific musical details; does not establish exhaustive discography.

evidence.claim: Blue Note BLP 1501 documents Gil Coggins on piano with Miles Davis, J.J. Johnson, Jackie McLean, Oscar Pettiford and Kenny Clarke at WOR Studios on May 9, 1952.

gil-coggins.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
gil-coggins.summary: Pianist Gil Coggins played on Miles Davis Blue Note sessions at WOR Studios in May 1952 and April 1953, with J.J. Johnson, Jackie McLean and Jimmy Heath.
gil-coggins.why_it_matters: Blue Note session files identify Coggins as pianist on named early Davis bebop sides and distinguish personnel for 1952 from those for 1953.

evidence.claim: The original Pacific Jazz PJ-93 issue, catalogued as a 1965 album, identifies Gil Fuller leading the Monterey Jazz Festival Orchestra featuring trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie.
Original Pacific Jazz PJ-93 discographical credits identify Gil Fuller as the arranger and conductor on compositions Man From Monterey, Angel City and Big Sur.

Michael Fitzgerald's specialist sessionography lists Gil Fuller as arranger and conductor on 1949 Discovery 78-rpm originals Blues For A Debutante and Tropicana, with Art Blakey and Milt Jackson in the ensemble.

gil-fuller.limitations: The 1949 Discovery recording date differs among specialist discographies (June 11 versus July 11), and 1965 Pacific Jazz studio dates conflict across sources. Neither disputed recording day is asserted here. The 1964 Down Beat scanned PDF was not visually verifiable and is excluded.
gil-fuller.summary: Jazz arranger Gil Fuller conducted a Discovery bebop studio ensemble in 1949 and led the Pacific Jazz Monterey Jazz Festival Orchestra featuring Dizzy Gillespie in 1965.
gil-fuller.why_it_matters: Original issue catalogs and specialist sessionographies distinguish Fuller's arranging and conducting in 1949 and his separate Pacific Jazz leadership in the 1960s.

evidence.claim: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame names Ginger Baker, Jack Bruce and Eric Clapton on the Cream 1993 performer induction roster.
The Rock Hall album catalog includes Fela Ransome-Kuti And The Africa 70 With Ginger Baker, documenting a separate Afrobeat recording collaboration.

ginger-baker.limitations: Cream was a blues-rock power trio rather than a jazz ensemble; Fela collaboration is a separate original recording, not a credit to all Cream albums.
ginger-baker.summary: Drummer Ginger Baker played with Jack Bruce and Eric Clapton in Cream, entered the Rock Hall with the group in 1993, and worked with Fela Kuti.
ginger-baker.why_it_matters: Rock Hall records the band lineup and induction, and its original archive music listing preserves the distinct Fela Kuti collaboration.

evidence.claim: The Giuseppi Logan Quartet was recorded at Bell Studios in New York on October 5, 1964.
The quartet personnel were Giuseppi Logan on reeds, Don Pullen on piano, Eddie Gomez on bass and Milford Graves on drums and tabla.

giuseppi-logan.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
giuseppi-logan.summary: Multi-reedist Giuseppi Logan led an October 1964 Bell Studios session with Don Pullen, Eddie Gomez and Milford Graves for The Giuseppi Logan Quartet.
giuseppi-logan.why_it_matters: An unusually broad reed palette and a key early ESP-Disk ensemble.

evidence.claim: ECM gives the release date of Miniatures as June 10, 2016 and the recording date as December 2013 in Lugano.
The ECM credits identify Venier on piano and sound sculptures, including percussion and resonant metal objects.

glauco-venier.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
glauco-venier.summary: Italian pianist Glauco Venier recorded Miniatures in Lugano in December 2013, combining solo piano with gongs, bells and resonant sculptures.
glauco-venier.why_it_matters: Brings organ and sacred-music influences into a timbral ECM solo jazz setting.

evidence.claim: Gray became leader of the Casa Loma Orchestra in 1937.
The Casa Loma Orchestra recorded exclusively for Decca starting in 1934.
Gray emerged from retirement in 1956 to record Sounds of the Great Bands for Capitol.

glen-gray.limitations: The finding aid synthesizes original collection holdings; individual takes and soloists are not claimed.
glen-gray.summary: Saxophonist Glen Gray fronted the Casa Loma Orchestra from 1937 until it disbanded in 1950. He returned to record Capitol's Sounds of the Great Bands series in 1956.
glen-gray.why_it_matters: An original Northeastern University archival finding aid documents his swing leadership, radio work and later records.

evidence.claim: ECM lists Oregon's quartet as Ralph Towner, Paul McCandless, Collin Walcott and Glen Moore on double bass, viola and piano.
The Oregon album was recorded in March 1983 at Tonstudio Bauer in Ludwigsburg; Moore composed Arianna and Skyline.

glen-moore.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
glen-moore.summary: Bassist Glen Moore recorded Oregon's 1983 ECM album with Ralph Towner, Paul McCandless and Collin Walcott, contributing the pieces Arianna and Skyline.
glen-moore.why_it_matters: His compositions and bass playing helped build Oregon's chamber-like combination of jazz and world instrumentation.

evidence.claim: Ferris became a trombone soloist in Don Ellis's big band in 1966.
He toured with Frank Zappa's Grand Wazoo in 1972.
His trombone-cello-bass trio debuted on Flesh & Stone in 1995.

glenn-ferris.limitations: Artist archive has highly specific chronology; individual studio take credits not inferred.
glenn-ferris.summary: Trombonist Glenn Ferris played in Don Ellis's big band, joining at sixteen, and toured with Frank Zappa's Grand Wazoo in 1972. His 1995 trio album was Flesh & Stone.
glenn-ferris.why_it_matters: His career moves from experimental big bands into small-group trombone improvisation.

evidence.claim: Miller formed the second orchestra in March 1938.
The band performed at Glen Island Casino in 1939.
Tuxedo Junction reportedly sold 115,000 copies in its first week in 1940.

glenn-miller.limitations: Miller's estate-managed orchestra history supplies hit titles; no soloist-by-take credits added.
glenn-miller.summary: Trombonist Glenn Miller launched his orchestra in 1938 and scored swing hits with In the Mood and Tuxedo Junction. His band's 1939 run included Glen Island Casino.
glenn-miller.why_it_matters: His distinctive orchestral voicing became a signature of dance-band swing.

evidence.claim: The International Archives for the Jazz Organ reports that Gloria Coleman performed as a bassist in Chicago and Philadelphia beginning in 1952 before taking up organ.
The IAJO original jazz-organ discography identifies Soul Sisters as a 1964 Impulse! A-47 issue from a 1963 session with Leo Wright, Grant Green and Pola Roberts.
The original Impulse! A-47 session documentation dates Soul Sisters to May 21, 1963 at Van Gelder Studio in Englewood Cliffs and names Gloria Coleman on organ.
The international jazz-organ discography lists Gloria Coleman Ltd.'s Sings and Swings Organ on the Mainstream label in 1971.

gloria-coleman.limitations: The May 1963 Soul Sisters recording session and its 1964 original Impulse! issue are distinguished. The artist performed jazz beyond that one session, but no undocumented awards are inferred.
gloria-coleman.summary: Jazz organist Gloria Coleman led Soul Sisters with Leo Wright, Grant Green and drummer Pola Roberts and released Sings and Swings Organ in 1971.
gloria-coleman.why_it_matters: The International Archives for the Jazz Organ connects her original studio band personnel, early bassist career and later leader releases.

evidence.claim: The Mellow and Swinging credits Gloria Lynne on vocals with the Ernie Wilkins Big Beat Band in New York recordings from 1960.
Its collective personnel include Clark Terry, Zoot Sims, Kenny Burrell, Ron Carter and Charles Persip.
Miss Gloria Lynne Sings credits Lynne on vocals with an ensemble including Harry Edison, Sam Taylor, Wild Bill Davis and Jo Jones.

gloria-lynne.limitations: The Mellow and Swinging combines two Everest albums with collective personnel credits; individual sidemen cannot be assigned to every track.
gloria-lynne.summary: Jazz vocalist Gloria Lynne recorded with Ernie Wilkins's big band in 1960 and appeared on sessions featuring Harry Edison and Wild Bill Davis.
gloria-lynne.why_it_matters: Original Everest reissues document Lynne's vocal work on separate albums with named jazz ensembles.

evidence.claim: Big Phat Band's own history says it was established in 2000 and debuted with Swingin' For The Fences.
The band's original history dates its second album XXL to 2003 and names Hunting Wabbits among its works.

gordon-goodwin.limitations: Band information includes marketing awards; only dated album facts used.
gordon-goodwin.summary: Composer and bandleader Gordon Goodwin established the Big Phat Band in 2000; it released Swingin' for the Fences and 2003 follow-up XXL.
gordon-goodwin.why_it_matters: Primary ensemble archive documents Goodwin's modern big-band projects.

evidence.claim: Gordon Haskell official biography dates his solo Atlantic album It Is and It Isnt to 1971 and describes its concert promotion at Rainbow Theatre in London.
The same official account reports Haskell returning to bass sideman work with Cliff Richard, Alvin Lee, Tim Hardin and Hiroshi Kato after his 1971 album.

gordon-haskell.limitations: His 1971 album is not a jazz sextet recording; the artist biography gives no basis to infer all earlier King Crimson bandmates as its personnel.
gordon-haskell.summary: British bassist and singer Gordon Haskell issued It Is and It Isnt on Atlantic in 1971 after work with King Crimson.
gordon-haskell.why_it_matters: The artist biography connects British jazz-rock group work with a verifiable later solo LP.

evidence.claim: Birmingham City University's archive identifies Collier as the first British graduate of Berklee School of Music.
Its collection notes say Collier launched the Royal Academy of Music jazz course and taught there from 1987 to 1999.

graham-collier.limitations: Only claims recorded in the cited artist, label, institution or original archive are included; crossovers are not classified exclusively as jazz.
graham-collier.summary: British jazz bassist, composer and educator Graham Collier developed his own ensembles and helped establish jazz teaching at the Royal Academy.
graham-collier.why_it_matters: Documents specific recordings, ensembles or performance roles and their place in jazz or adjacent genres.

evidence.claim: Clean Feed credits Graham Haynes on cornet in the Warriors of the Wonderful Sound ensemble led by conductor and alto saxophonist Marty Ehrlich.

graham-haynes.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.

graham-haynes.why_it_matters: Haynes contributes a brass solo voice to Abrams's large-ensemble creative orchestration.

greg-abate.limitations: The account provides year spans, not exact session dates; no precise recording date is claimed.
greg-abate.summary: Saxophonist Greg Abate played lead alto in Ray Charles's orchestra and tenor sax in the revived Artie Shaw Orchestra before recording as a leader.
greg-abate.why_it_matters: Official artist biography names his instrumental roles, bandleader tenures and first leader-session personnel.

greg-errico.limitations: Short artist-level account only; do not infer unlisted session or ensemble personnel.
greg-errico.summary: American drummer Greg Errico helped build the rhythmic sound of Sly and the Family Stone and later toured in jazz-rock and pop settings.
greg-errico.why_it_matters: Adds a documented performer or composer and a specific musical contribution to the catalog.

greg-gisbert.limitations: University biography lists associations, not a full album sessionography or proof of each unlisted live performance.

greg-gisbert.why_it_matters: A university appointment and documented ensemble roles identify the exact musician and style.

guem.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.

guillermo-klein.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
guillermo-klein.summary: Argentine pianist Guillermo Klein led Los Guachos V, a 2016 Sunnyside release with Ben Monder, Chris Cheek, Miguel Zenon, Jeff Ballard and more.
guillermo-klein.why_it_matters: His large ensemble reframes Argentine rhythms and jazz harmony with mirrored and inverted patterns.

evidence.claim: Gunnar Svensson played piano in Lars Gullin's quartet with Yngve Akerberg and Jack Noren at Radiotjanst Studio 2, Stockholm, on October 9, 1951.

The Rita Reys reissue credits Svensson on piano with Lars Gullin, Simon Brehm and Wes Ilcken on four tracks recorded in Stockholm on March 2, 1953.

gunnar-svensson.limitations: The reissues combine different Swedish ensembles. Svensson is not credited on every Lars Gullin session or Rita Reys track.
gunnar-svensson.summary: Swedish jazz pianist Gunnar Svensson recorded with Lars Gullin in 1951-1952 and accompanied Rita Reys and Rolf Blomquist in 1953.
gunnar-svensson.why_it_matters: Historical Metronome session records identify Svensson's piano credits across distinct ensembles and recording dates.

evidence.claim: Gus Aiken played cornet in Perry Bradford's Jazz Phools on Memphis Tennessee, June 26, 1923, Victor matrix 28234-2.
Aiken played trumpet with Luis Russell on Goin To Town, August 28, 1931, Victor matrix 70196-1.
A Smithsonian 1934 original negative independently labels Gus Aiken with Luis Russell's orchestra.

gus-aiken.limitations: Birth years conflict between 1899 ship records and 1902 in Grove; no year of birth accepted. Rust is a fallible secondary personnel reconstruction.
gus-aiken.summary: Gus Aiken played cornet or trumpet on Perry Bradford, Luis Russell and Sidney Bechet sessions between 1923 and 1941.
gus-aiken.why_it_matters: Specific session matrices and a Smithsonian original orchestra portrait establish personal recorded activity.

evidence.claim: NAMM oral history confirms he played in Jay McShann's orchestra and with Count Basie.
NAMM states Johnson participated in the 1952 Basie Rides Again recording.

gus-johnson.limitations: Short artist-level account only; do not infer unlisted session or ensemble personnel.
gus-johnson.summary: American drummer Gus Johnson worked in Jay McShann's orchestra and Count Basie's band before accompanying jazz singers including Ella Fitzgerald.
gus-johnson.why_it_matters: Adds a documented performer or composer and a specific musical contribution to the catalog.

evidence.claim: Royal Albert Hall documents his Jazz Orchestra at the 19 December 2024 Big Band Christmas concert.

guy-barker.limitations: The institutional sources cover particular concerts rather than his entire discography.
guy-barker.summary: British jazz trumpeter and arranger Guy Barker led his Jazz Orchestra in a Royal Albert Hall Christmas concert and conducted Sarah Vaughan repertoire at the 2024 Proms.
guy-barker.why_it_matters: Shows British big-band performance and orchestral jazz programming.

evidence.claim: Royal Hartigan's published jazz study identifies Africa Speaks, America Answers as Decca DL 8446 and dates its Chicago recording to October 15, 1956; other discography disputes that exact date.

Red Saunders session research estimates September 1956 for Warren's Universal Chicago recording and identifies October 10 as probable mastering, based on Decca matrix neighbors.

guy-warren.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
guy-warren.summary: Ghanaian drummer Guy Warren fused African percussion and jazz on Africa Speaks, America Answers, recorded in Chicago in 1956 with the Gene Esposito group.
guy-warren.why_it_matters: Ghanaian percussion bridged highlife and African American small-group jazz.

evidence.claim: The Hamar AnJazz festival lists Graf on keyboards alongside Erik Smith, Per Mathisen and Hans Mathisen.
The festival identifies Graf's earlier keyboard role in Ruphus and describes his group as groove- and funk-based jazz.

haakon-graf.limitations: Festival's published 2025 quartet lineup, not a studio-session credit.
haakon-graf.summary: Norwegian keyboardist Haakon Graf led a funk-leaning jazz quartet and played with Ruphus, mixing improvisation with Brazilian and Cuban rhythms.
haakon-graf.why_it_matters: Documents a distinct instrumental or vocal contribution and its musical context.

evidence.claim: Canadian Jazz Archive musician biography records Hagood Hardy as a vibraphonist and pianist who worked with Herbie Mann and George Shearing before returning to Canada.
Canadian Jazz Archive dates his public The Homecoming single to 1975 and explicitly traces the melody to a previous Salada Tea advertisement.
The Governor General of Canada official register records Hugh Hagood Hardy as appointed Member of the Order of Canada on April 30 1992.
The Museum of Canadian Music catalogs Morocco as a 1990 Hagood Hardy jazz album with such standards as Freddie Freeloader and On Green Dolphin Street.

hagood-hardy.limitations: The Homecoming was born as advertising music and released later as a popular instrumental, not an asserted pure straight-ahead jazz recording. In a 1990 album catalog its recorded date should not be inferred from catalog year.
hagood-hardy.summary: Vibraphonist Hagood Hardy played with Herbie Mann and George Shearing; his The Homecoming became a Canadian hit in 1975.
hagood-hardy.why_it_matters: The Canadian Jazz Archive documents the jazz ensemble work; the Canadian governor official honours register and original music-collection document the broader career.

evidence.claim: The Library of Congress film guide identifies Hal Kemp and His Orchestra in a 1936 musical short performing The Bride Comes Home and I'm Building Up to an Awful Letdown with named vocalists.
A separate 1939 short documents Kemp's orchestra performing In an 18th Century Drawing Room, Swampfire and Vagabond Dreams.
The Library of Congress Dana Suesse collection states that Kemp's orchestra recorded her 1931 composition Ho Hum, with lyrics by Edward Heyman.

hal-kemp.limitations: The LOC film guide describes original shorts in a later video anthology. The 1984 video issue is not an original performance date. Orchestra attribution is not evidence of a saxophone solo by Kemp.
hal-kemp.summary: American dance-band leader Hal Kemp led filmed orchestral performances in 1936 and 1939 and recorded Ho Hum from Dana Suesse's songbook.
hal-kemp.why_it_matters: Library of Congress music and film collections independently document Kemp's named orchestras, original repertory and filmed performances.

evidence.claim: Zerbe's official ensemble history dates the new orchestra's debut concert at Berlin's WABE to October 2011.
The 2025 German Music Instrument Museum program names Zerbe on piano and organ and identifies his ensemble's compositions and arrangements as his work.

hannes-zerbe.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
hannes-zerbe.summary: German pianist and composer Hannes Zerbe founded his Berlin Jazz Orchestra in 2011, combining improvised writing with modern orchestral influences.
hannes-zerbe.why_it_matters: Berlin large-group writing joins jazz improvisation with symphonic and literary projects.

evidence.claim: Saxophone manufacturer Cannonball records Dulfer's April 19, 2006 concert with Joseph Bowie, Bas van Lier and others.

hans-dulfer.limitations: Manufacturer-hosted chronology; describes jazz and dance crossover, no album personnel invented.
hans-dulfer.summary: Dutch tenor saxophonist Hans Dulfer fused jazz with dance beats on Big Boy and performed with Joseph Bowie at Jazz a Carthage in 2006.

evidence.claim: Blue Note released Timba a la Americana on August 25, 2023, and credits producer Michael League of Snarky Puppy.

harold-lopez-nussa.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
harold-lopez-nussa.summary: Cuban pianist Harold Lopez-Nussa made his Blue Note debut with Timba a la Americana in 2023, working with Gregoire Maret, Luques Curtis and his brother Ruy.
harold-lopez-nussa.why_it_matters: He connects Cuban dance pulse and odd-meter contemporary jazz with Rhodes and acoustic piano.

evidence.claim: Vick released his first album as a leader, Steppin' Out!, on Blue Note in 1963.

harold-vick.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
harold-vick.summary: Tenor saxophonist Harold Vick recorded his first leader album Steppin' Out! for Blue Note in 1963 and later recorded with Jack DeJohnette's group Compost in 1972.
harold-vick.why_it_matters: He crossed organ-jazz, hard bop and exploratory post-bop settings.

evidence.claim: Betts's first major job was as a trombonist and arranger with Stan Kenton in the early 1950s.

harry-betts.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
harry-betts.summary: Trombonist and arranger Harry Betts worked with Stan Kenton in the early 1950s and led the 1962 jazz album The Jazz Soul of Doctor Kildare.

evidence.claim: Edison performed with the Jeter-Pillars Orchestra in 1933-1935.
