marcus-rojas.limitations: Bard's faculty biography lacks dates for the performances and no solo record claims are assumed.
marcus-rojas.summary: Tuba player Marcus Rojas has performed in ensembles led by Lionel Hampton and David Byrne. He has premiered music by LaMonte Young and Gunther Schuller.
marcus-rojas.why_it_matters: Bard Conservatory documents his work across improvised music, orchestras and stage productions.

evidence.claim: Strickland's official site credits him on tenor saxophone, bass clarinet and programming for Plateaus.
The artist names Keith Brown on piano, Ben Williams on bass and E.J. Strickland on drums for Plateaus.

marcus-strickland.limitations: Only claims recorded in the cited artist, label, institution or original archive are included; crossovers are not classified exclusively as jazz.
marcus-strickland.summary: American saxophonist Marcus Strickland blends contemporary jazz improvisation with production, leading projects including Twi-Life.
marcus-strickland.why_it_matters: Documents specific recordings, ensembles or performance roles and their place in jazz or adjacent genres.

evidence.claim: Hyams played vibraphone with Woody Herman's First Herd in 1944-1945.
Hyams led a trio in 1945-1948 and was an original member of George Shearing's quintet in 1949-1950.

margie-hyams.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
margie-hyams.summary: Vibraphonist Margie Hyams played with Woody Herman's First Herd in 1944-45, led a trio in 1945-48 and joined George Shearing's original quintet in 1949.
margie-hyams.why_it_matters: A woman instrumentalist at the center of swing-to-bop changes.

evidence.claim: ECM lists Il Pergolese as released October 25, 2013 by Maria Pia De Vito, Francois Couturier, Anja Lechner and Michele Rabbia.
ECM states that De Vito translated the Stabat Mater text into Neapolitan and that Couturier arranged the materials for improvisation.

maria-pia-de-vito.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
maria-pia-de-vito.summary: Neapolitan vocalist Maria Pia De Vito translated Pergolesi's Stabat Mater into Neapolitan for Il Pergolese, an ECM quartet recording issued in 2013.
maria-pia-de-vito.why_it_matters: Transforms Baroque Neapolitan material through jazz improvisation and electronic textures.

evidence.claim: Scott's 1977 solo single was a cover of God Only Knows.
Her debut Dreams of Tomorrow was released on Atco/Atlantic.
Her 2022 The Landscape release was on Blue Canoe Records.

marilyn-scott.limitations: Artist's biography lists general collaborators but does not attribute them to unlisted tracks.
marilyn-scott.summary: Singer Marilyn Scott recorded Dreams of Tomorrow for Atco after a 1977 solo single of God Only Knows. Her later collaborations include Bob Mintzer and Terri Lyne Carrington.
marilyn-scott.why_it_matters: Her discography crosses soul, Brazilian music and vocal jazz.

evidence.claim: The band's own Full Blast page dates its recording at The Loft in Cologne to February 6, 2006 and its release to June 6, 2006.
The album credits Peter Brotzmann on saxophones and tarogato, Marino Pliakas on bass, and Michael Wertmuller on drums.

marino-pliakas.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
marino-pliakas.summary: Swiss electric bassist Marino Pliakas recorded Full Blast with Peter Brotzmann and Michael Wertmuller in Cologne in February 2006.
marino-pliakas.why_it_matters: His forceful electric-bass improvisation anchors a leading European free-jazz power trio.

evidence.claim: Clean Feed names Pavone on double bass, Dave Ballou on trumpet, Tony Malaby on saxophones, Oscar Noriega on clarinets, Peter McEachern on trombone and Mike Sarin on drums.
Pavone composed all music on Vertical, Dave Ballou arranged it and the ensemble recorded June 16, 2016 at Systems Two in Brooklyn.

mario-pavone.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mario-pavone.summary: Double bassist Mario Pavone led the horn-rich Vertical sextet with Dave Ballou, Tony Malaby, Oscar Noriega, Peter McEachern and Mike Sarin in Brooklyn.
mario-pavone.why_it_matters: Pavone's percussive bass writing supports a dense, dynamically arranged avant-bop horn ensemble.

evidence.claim: Leo Records dates the Italian Instabile Festival performance to December 1997 at Teatro Verdi in Pisa; the archive appeared March 6, 2026.
The release credits Schiano on soprano and alto saxophones and voice, alongside bassist Bruno Tommaso and trombonist Sebi Tramontana.

mario-schiano.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mario-schiano.summary: Italian alto and soprano saxophonist Mario Schiano played and sang with the Italian Instabile Orchestra in its December 1997 Pisa festival recording.
mario-schiano.why_it_matters: A free-jazz pioneer contributed reeds and voice to Italian collective improvisation.

evidence.claim: The National Jazz Archive states that singer Marion Montgomery performed with Johnny Dankworth's band in 1965 and met pianist Laurie Holloway.
The Jazz Archive biography says Montgomery performed regularly at Ronnie Scott's in the 1970s and toured with pianist Richard Rodney Bennett.
The archive hosts a 1988 Marion Montgomery interview conducted by journalist Les Tomkins.

marion-montgomery.limitations: The archive documents performance venues and career intersections, not the personnel of every club or television appearance.
marion-montgomery.summary: American-born jazz singer Marion Montgomery settled in Britain, worked with Johnny Dankworth in 1965 and later performed at Ronnie Scott's and on television.
marion-montgomery.why_it_matters: National Jazz Archive preserves a first-person interview and explicit jazz performance chronology.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Charig on cornet with Elton Dean, Keith Tippett, Louis Moholo and Marcio Mattos.
Charig shares composition credit on Out Of Bounds; the album was recorded February 1980 and released May 1, 1980.

mark-charig.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mark-charig.summary: Cornetist Mark Charig recorded Boundaries with Elton Dean, Keith Tippett, Louis Moholo and Marcio Mattos in Ludwigsburg in February 1980.
mark-charig.why_it_matters: His cornet is a distinctive part of British free jazz ensemble improvisation.

evidence.claim: Clean Feed released Nourishments in 2013
Album led by bassist Mark Dresser

mark-dresser.limitations: Source-specific musical details, not a complete discography.
mark-dresser.summary: Bassist Mark Dresser led the 2013 quintet album 'Nourishments', bringing extended double-bass techniques into tightly composed free improvisation.
mark-dresser.why_it_matters: Instrumental innovations and composed structures in contemporary free jazz

evidence.claim: Ancient and Future Airs credits Mark Helias on double bass, Paul Dunmall on tenor saxophone and bagpipes, Tony Malaby on saxophones and Kevin Norton on drums and vibraphone.
Clean Feed says Dunmall recorded Ancient and Future Airs with Helias, Malaby and Norton the day after his 2008 Vision Festival performance.

mark-helias.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mark-helias.summary: Bassist Mark Helias joined Paul Dunmall, Tony Malaby and Kevin Norton on Ancient and Future Airs, an improvising quartet recorded after the 2008 Vision Festival.
mark-helias.why_it_matters: His independent bass line balances open improvisation with a strong blues and swing pulse.

evidence.claim: ECM's Rubisa Patrol credits Mark Isham on trumpet, flugelhorn and soprano saxophone beside Art Lande, Bill Douglass and Glenn Cronkhite, recorded in Oslo in May 1976.
ECM's 1987 We Begin documents Isham on trumpet, piccolo trumpet and synthesizer in a duo with pianist Art Lande, recorded January 1987 in Oslo.
ECM credits Isham on trumpet, piccolo trumpet and synthesizer for David Torn's Cloud About Mercury, recorded in March 1986 with Tony Levin and Bill Bruford.

mark-isham.limitations: ECM's 1994 CD reissue of Rubisa Patrol carries a different reissue date from the original 1976 LP; the underlying studio date is May 1976.
mark-isham.summary: Trumpeter Mark Isham recorded with Art Lande's Rubisa Patrol in Oslo in 1976 and later collaborated with Lande on the 1987 ECM duo album We Begin.
mark-isham.why_it_matters: Original ECM release entries provide instrumentation, compositions, recording years and two different configurations.

evidence.claim: Mark Lockheart's Shapeshifter credits him on saxophones and bass clarinet with Huw V Williams on double bass and Jay Davis on drums.
The album was released March 6, 2026; tracks 1, 2, 7 and 9 were composed by Lockheart, and the recordings were made at Lightship Studio in London.

mark-lockheart.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mark-lockheart.summary: British saxophonist Mark Lockheart released Shapeshifter in 2026 with bassist Huw V Williams and drummer Jay Davis, combining improvised jazz and ambient textures.
mark-lockheart.why_it_matters: The trio connects acoustic jazz improvisation with electronic texture and broader rock and folk influences.

evidence.claim: NMC lists Nightingale's jazz trombone work with Ray Brown, Clark Terry and Scott Hamilton.
Nightingale wrote big-band charts in National Youth Jazz Orchestra.
NMC says his compositions have been featured by BBC Big Band and international trombone festivals.

mark-nightingale.limitations: NMC biography is general and omits dates of individual sessions.
mark-nightingale.summary: British jazz trombonist Mark Nightingale worked with Ray Brown and Clark Terry and wrote for National Youth Jazz Orchestra. He later composed features for BBC Big Band.
mark-nightingale.why_it_matters: NMC's composer catalogue documents both jazz performance and original ensemble arrangements.

evidence.claim: Manhattan School of Music identifies Shim as a jazz tenor saxophone faculty member.
Its biography says he toured with Betty Carter in 1995 and made three albums for Blue Note.

mark-shim.limitations: Institutional biography; avoid inferring precise instrumentation on individual tracks.
mark-shim.summary: Jamaican-born tenor saxophonist Mark Shim toured with Betty Carter and Elvin Jones and released three Blue Note albums, including Turbulent Flow.
mark-shim.why_it_matters: Connects Betty Carter's ensembles, Elvin Jones and late-1990s Blue Note jazz.

evidence.claim: Milestone's Sunny Days, Starry Nights identifies Mark Soskin among Sonny Rollins's band, recorded January 1984.
Milestone's G-Man documents Soskin in Rollins's quartet on the August 16, 1986 recording.
Craft's original master-tape reissue history credits Soskin on keyboards for Roger Glenn's 1977 Reachin'.

mark-soskin.limitations: Personnel credits establish participation in named albums, without assigning him to every track on multi-session anthologies.
mark-soskin.summary: Keyboardist Mark Soskin recorded with Sonny Rollins in 1984, 1986 and 1991, and played keyboards on Roger Glenn's 1977 jazz-funk album Reachin'.
mark-soskin.why_it_matters: The original Milestone recording catalog and Craft master-tape notes identify his role across both acoustic and electric jazz.

evidence.claim: The trio concert was recorded at Lviv's Jam Factory Art Center on April 28, 2024 and released on June 25, 2025.
Tokar is credited on bass, Mockunas on three saxophones and Mikalkenas on drums and piano; all three share composition credit.

mark-tokar.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mark-tokar.summary: Ukrainian bassist Mark Tokar joined Lithuanian saxophonist Liudas Mockunas and drummer Arnas Mikalkenas for a live Lviv trio performance in April 2024.
mark-tokar.why_it_matters: Documents wartime Ukrainian free improvisation and collaboration with Lithuania.

evidence.claim: Jazz.com documents Whitecage's work with Perry Robinson's clarinet project Licorice Factory in the 1980s.
Its account dates performances by Whitecage's Glass House Ensemble to 1988-1997.

mark-whitecage.limitations: Specialist jazz encyclopedia appears partly autobiographical; label-level recordings not independently checked.
mark-whitecage.summary: Reed player Mark Whitecage worked with Perry Robinson's Licorice Factory and built sound sculptures for his Glass House Ensemble, active from 1988 to 1997.
mark-whitecage.why_it_matters: Shows experimental jazz saxophone alongside instrument-building and free improvisation.

evidence.claim: Marlon Jordan's official musician biography identifies him as a trumpeter and names his Columbia albums For You Only, Learson's Return and The Undaunted.
The musician's own page credits Marlon's Mode as an Arabesque-label album released in 1997.
AllMusic identifies Jordan on trumpet and as primary artist of his 1988 Columbia debut For You Only.

marlon-jordan.limitations: The artist website contains an apparent typo '1998 to 1992' for Columbia chronology; the first year is not accepted without independent verification.
marlon-jordan.summary: New Orleans jazz trumpeter Marlon Jordan recorded the Columbia albums For You Only, Learson's Return and The Undaunted before Marlon's Mode.
marlon-jordan.why_it_matters: Jordan's own recorded history and published musician credits establish real jazz albums, avoiding conflation with other performers of the same surname.

evidence.claim: The archive places Morris in the 1944 film Jammin' the Blues.
His Columbia Play The Thing recording featured Buddy Tate and Matthew Gee.
He accompanied Coleman Hawkins in 1940-1941.

marlowe-morris.limitations: International Archives for the Jazz Organ is specialist archival compilation; label session details not all original.
marlowe-morris.summary: Jazz organist Marlowe Morris appeared in Jammin' the Blues in 1944 and later led organ trios. He recorded with tenor saxophonist Buddy Tate and trombonist Matthew Gee.
marlowe-morris.why_it_matters: An early organ specialist appears in archival organ discographies and a filmed jazz performance.

evidence.claim: Rutgers' Institute of Jazz Studies Count Basie family papers name Marshal Royal as the orchestra's deputy music director, alto saxophonist and clarinetist in mid-1952.
The Rutgers finding aid documents Royal in Basie's reed section alongside Paul Quinichette, Eddie Lockjaw Davis, Ernie Wilkins and Charlie Fowlkes.
The Royal Albert Hall archival authority record identifies Marshal Royal as a clarinetist and lead alto saxophonist who remained with the Basie band until 1970.

marshal-royal.limitations: The archive documents a 1952 orchestra role and duties, not every later Basie session or Royal solo credit.
marshal-royal.summary: Clarinetist and lead alto saxophonist Marshal Royal became Count Basie's deputy musical director in the 1952 big-band lineup, shaping its reed sound.
marshal-royal.why_it_matters: The Institute of Jazz Studies archival finding aid specifically preserves Royal's position in Basie's reconstructed ensemble.

evidence.claim: Jimmy Owens says Brown organized an International Youth Band in 1958.
Owens describes Brown starting the Newport Youth Band in 1959.
BnF catalogs a 1959 Newport performance by Brown's youth band.

marshall-brown.limitations: NEA interview is first-person Jimmy Owens testimony; 1959 release separately checked in the BnF record.
marshall-brown.summary: Trombonist Marshall Brown led the Newport Youth Band. A 1959 Newport performance under his direction was issued on Coral, and he mentored young players including Jimmy Owens.
marshall-brown.why_it_matters: Band-building and coaching gave young jazz musicians early professional experience.

evidence.claim: The official Marshall Gilkes biography dates his WDR Big Band membership 2010 to 2014 and the resulting Koln recording to 2015.
His official biography dates Always Forward to 2018 and Cyclic Journey, an eight-brass-plus-jazz-combo suite, to 2022.

marshall-gilkes.limitations: The 2015 and 2018 years refer to albums, whereas his WDR membership covered 2010 to 2014; no track-specific solo assumption is made.
marshall-gilkes.summary: Trombonist Marshall Gilkes wrote and soloed with WDR Big Band on Koln (2015) and Always Forward (2018), then made Cyclic Journey in 2022.
marshall-gilkes.why_it_matters: An original bandleader account establishes composition and ensemble roles across two WDR albums and a subsequent brass suite.

evidence.claim: Jackpot's master-tape reissue notes date Martin Denny's Latin Village to 1964 and identify its mix of samba, bossa nova and Latin jazz.
The Latin Village reissue tracklist includes Corcovado, On Green Dolphin Street and The Girl From Ipanema.
The Exotica Vol. III reissue identifies Harvey Ragsdale on bass, Julius Wechter on vibraphone and Augie Colon on percussion in Denny's group.

martin-denny.limitations: Latin Village's track list documents arrangements and repertoire, not an invention of bossa nova by Denny; the archival reissue credits apply to specified albums.
martin-denny.summary: Exotica pianist Martin Denny released the Latin-inspired Latin Village in 1964 and worked with percussionist Augie Colon and vibraphonist Julius Wechter.
martin-denny.why_it_matters: Master-tape reissue notes document Denny's shift toward Latin repertoire and identify his ensemble personnel on a separate album.

evidence.claim: Songs for Quintet credits France on drums, Wheeler on flugelhorn, Sulzmann on tenor sax, Parricelli on guitar and Laurence on bass.
The December 2013 Abbey Road session became Kenny Wheeler's final album recording.

martin-france.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
martin-france.summary: Drummer Martin France joined Kenny Wheeler for Songs for Quintet, recorded in December 2013 at Abbey Road with Stan Sulzmann, John Parricelli and Chris Laurence.
martin-france.why_it_matters: His nuanced rhythmic backing shapes Wheeler's final ensemble studio session.

evidence.claim: The 2013 premiere of Streams featured clarinetist Matthias Mueller and trombonist David Taylor.
The 2009 premiere of pulsar_2 used voice, flute, piano and spatial electronics.
His 2013 album STREAMS included concertos Mouvements, Waves and Streams.

martin-schlumpf.limitations: Compositions are crossover concert works rather than conventional jazz albums.
martin-schlumpf.summary: Swiss composer Martin Schlumpf played jazz double bass in his youth. His 2013 concerto Streams features clarinet, bass trombone and 17 instruments.
martin-schlumpf.why_it_matters: His writing merges contemporary composition, jazz improvisation and electronics.

evidence.claim: The trio website dates the SKIP Records album PAX to August 1, 2025 and names Cruisin' and A Promise among its tracks.
The official member credits name Martin Tingvall on piano and compositions, Omar Rodriguez Calvo on double bass, and Jurgen Spiegel on drums.

martin-tingvall.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
martin-tingvall.summary: Swedish pianist Martin Tingvall released PAX with Cuban bassist Omar Rodriguez Calvo and German drummer Jurgen Spiegel on SKIP Records in August 2025.
martin-tingvall.why_it_matters: Modern European piano jazz with a Cuban bass voice and strongly melodic originals.

evidence.claim: The official rights-authorized Jeanne Lee Conspiracy reissue credits Marty Cook on trombone at the 1974 New York recording with Sam Rivers, Gunter Hampel and Steve McCall.
Finland's National Library catalog lists Marty Cook on trombone with Jim Pepper on tenor, Essiet Essiet on bass and John Betsch on drums for the Enja album Nightwork (ENJA5033).
The same national library catalog documents separate Nightwork recording dates October 9, 1986 and January 12, 1987, rather than inferring those dates from the album's printed issue year.

marty-cook.limitations: Conspiracy was recorded in 1974, originally released in 1975 and reissued in 2021. The Finnish library lists the Nightwork release as 1986 despite identifying a January 1987 session; release-date discrepancy is left unresolved.
marty-cook.summary: Free-jazz trombonist Marty Cook performed on Jeanne Lee's 1974 Conspiracy and co-led the 1986-87 Nightwork sessions with Jim Pepper.
marty-cook.why_it_matters: The rights-authorized Jeanne Lee original-recording reissue and a national library's original Enja release catalog establish two distinct projects and exact roles.

evidence.claim: Clean Feed credits Marty Ehrlich on alto saxophone, clarinet, bass clarinet and wooden flutes, with John Hebert on bass and Nasheet Waits on drums.
Trio Exaltation features eight new Ehrlich compositions and one Andrew Hill work, Dusk, and was recorded at Namouche Studios in Lisbon.

marty-ehrlich.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
marty-ehrlich.summary: Multi-reedist Marty Ehrlich led Trio Exaltation with bassist John Hebert and drummer Nasheet Waits, presenting eight new originals and Andrew Hill's Dusk.
marty-ehrlich.why_it_matters: His arrangements connect the Andrew Hill legacy to contemporary freely improvised small-group jazz.

evidence.claim: Jan Evensmo's jazz archive documents Marty Marsala on trumpet in Joe Marsala and His Chicagoans for Variety's April 21, 1937 New York session.
The same independent sessionography credits Marty Marsala in a four-title Vocalion recording session on March 16, 1938 with Buddy Rich on drums.
It records Marty Marsala's trumpet participation in Joe Marsala's August 18, 1939 America Dances radio broadcast with Bud Freeman and Dave Tough.

marty-marsala.limitations: The document is specialist reconstructed jazz sessionography rather than a label's current site; source names Joe Marsala as the leader, and does not imply Marty was leading.
marty-marsala.summary: Trumpeter Marty Marsala worked with clarinetist Joe Marsala on 1937 Variety and 1938 Vocalion sessions and on a 1939 America Dances broadcast.
marty-marsala.why_it_matters: The independently compiled archival session log gives specific recording locations, dates, instrumentation and original labels.

evidence.claim: The official Bill Evans biography names Marty Morell as trio drummer alongside Bill Evans and Eddie Gomez for 1968 to 1974.
Canadian Jazz Archive states Morell began recording and touring with the Evans Trio in 1968 for seven years, later settling in Toronto.

marty-morell.limitations: His late-Evans trio run is different from Paul Motian original LaFaro trio, and the band-tenure does not imply every Evans recording from 1968 to 1975.
marty-morell.summary: Drummer Marty Morell joined the Bill Evans Trio in 1968 and toured and recorded with Evans and bassist Eddie Gomez through 1975.
marty-morell.why_it_matters: Official Evans and Canadian jazz archive biographies establish the trio lineup and its post-LaFaro era with precise tenure.

evidence.claim: Napoleon joined Chico Marx's orchestra at age twenty.
He played in the Big Four with Buddy Rich, Chubby Jackson and Charlie Ventura.
He joined Louis Armstrong's All Stars in 1952.

marty-napoleon.limitations: Retrospective union obituary; some widely repeated Armstrong recording claims avoided.
marty-napoleon.summary: Pianist Marty Napoleon joined Chico Marx's orchestra at twenty and played in the Big Four with Buddy Rich and Charlie Ventura. He joined Louis Armstrong's All Stars in 1952.
marty-napoleon.why_it_matters: A union obituary documents his path through swing and Armstrong's small-group jazz.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Marvin Smitty Smith on drums, Steve Coleman on alto sax, Kevin Eubanks on guitar and Dave Holland on double bass for Extensions.
Extensions was recorded at Power Station, New York in September 1989 and originally released September 1, 1990.

marvin-smith.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
marvin-smith.summary: Drummer Marvin Smitty Smith recorded Dave Holland Quartet's Extensions at Power Station, New York, in September 1989 with Steve Coleman and Kevin Eubanks.
marvin-smith.why_it_matters: His drums shaped Holland's saxophone-and-guitar quartet drive.

evidence.claim: McCall was Charlie Barnet's vocalist in 1939-1940.
She returned to Woody Herman for the First Herd in 1946 and Second Herd from 1947 to 1950.

mary-ann-mccall.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mary-ann-mccall.summary: Vocalist Mary Ann McCall sang with Charlie Barnet in 1939-40 and Woody Herman's First and Second Herds, then recorded leader sessions for Columbia and Discovery.
mary-ann-mccall.why_it_matters: Her career illustrates how big-band vocalists navigated swing and bebop.

evidence.claim: Mode Records credits Mary Oliver as violin, viola and Hardanger fiddle performer and names her work with Instant Composers Pool and Han Bennink.
Mode identifies Oliver's 1996 world premiere of Brian Ferneyhough's incipits for solo viola and ensemble.
The original New Music Co-op concert profile states she added Hardanger fiddle during her 1993-94 Schloss Solitude residency and lists her improvisations with Joelle Leandre.

mary-oliver.limitations: Mode Records describes classical premieres and free improvisation together; the summary does not class all of her compositions as jazz.
mary-oliver.summary: Improvising violinist Mary Oliver played with the Instant Composers Pool and premiered contemporary works for violin, viola and Hardanger fiddle.
mary-oliver.why_it_matters: The artist's original record-label biography and an early concert-presenter profile document specific premieres, instrumental range and ensemble work.

evidence.claim: Archeophone's remastering history credits Mary Stafford with the first released Royal Garden Blues with Charlie Johnson's Orchestra and a separate Crazy Blues performance in early 1921.
Archeophone documents Stafford's return to the studio in September 1921 for Arkansas Blues and Blind Man Blues, after the earlier full-band recordings.
The label distinguishes Stafford's final two Pathe-Actuelle recordings around March 1926, Ain't Got Nobody to Grind My Coffee in the Morning and Take Your Finger Off It.

mary-stafford.limitations: The 2008 Archeophone edition is a restoration, not a 1921 recording. Historic reports of birth or death year vary; none is asserted. Charlie Johnson led Stafford's backing orchestra rather than composing every title. A Smithsonian PDF liner reference has not been visually page-checked; it is excluded from accepted evidence.
mary-stafford.summary: Blues vocalist Mary Stafford recorded Royal Garden Blues and Crazy Blues with Charlie Johnson's band in 1921, then cut her final sides in 1926.
mary-stafford.why_it_matters: Archeophone's original archival restoration gives distinct 1921 and 1926 recordings, named accompanists, and separate studio phases; Folkways' primary label scholarship corroborates the Columbia sessions.

evidence.claim: The ESP-Disk session listing identifies Marzette Watts on tenor and soprano saxophone and bass clarinet for his 1966 And Company recordings.
The ESP original-matrix session reconstruction documents Watts on tenor and soprano saxophones and bass clarinet with Byard Lancaster, Sonny Sharrock and Henry Grimes on And Company.
The musician's original interview in The Wire describes his later Savoy ensemble recording after the ESP session and recounts his own move into sound engineering.

marzette-watts.limitations: Original ESP session date is December 1966 but 1968 is the cataloged issue year; an eyewitness interview gives a different day than sessionography, so no exact day appears in the summary. His Savoy record is mentioned as a second project, not given an unsupported exact issue date.
marzette-watts.summary: Saxophonist Marzette Watts recorded the 1966 ESP-Disk And Company session with Sonny Sharrock and Clifford Thornton and later recorded for Savoy.
marzette-watts.why_it_matters: The original ESP-Disk inventory identifies his album, the specialist original matrix catalog specifies individual instruments and tracks, and a primary interview documents later work.

evidence.claim: Masha Bijlsma's authored biography states that she formed the Masha Bijlsma Band near the end of 1990.
Her original catalogue lists Lopin' as a 2003 Lion Jazz album and the Abbey Lincoln tribute For Love of Abbey in 2010.
Bijlsma's official site identifies Benny Bailey, Tony Lakatos and Bart van Lier among the guest horn players in her jazz band projects.

identity_resolution.note: The singer's own biography and dated record catalogue identify the exact Dutch jazz vocalist, while original Jazzfest Gronau archives independently list the Masha Bijlsma Band among its 1992 performing acts. No nonreciprocal MusicBrainz identifier is used to supply a biography.

masha-bijlsma.limitations: The source is the singer's own archival website. There is no reciprocal identity crosslink in the local metadata, so primary artist identity is documented explicitly.
masha-bijlsma.summary: Dutch jazz singer Masha Bijlsma founded her band in 1990 and recorded Lopin' in 2003 with trumpeters Jarmo Hoogendijk and Ruud Breuls.
masha-bijlsma.why_it_matters: The singer's original band history, named guest credits and detailed year-by-year album catalogue establish her individual musical work.

evidence.claim: The Saint Louis jazz archive identifies Urbani's first solo Horo recording with Calvin Hill and Nestor Astarita.
The archived 1975 interview places Urbani with Enrico Rava for a Palermo concert and mentions Mario Schiano's Sud.

massimo-urbani.limitations: Claims anchored to the archived contemporary interview and institutional introduction.
massimo-urbani.summary: Italian alto saxophonist Massimo Urbani recorded for Horo and performed with Mario Schiano and Enrico Rava in the 1970s Roman jazz scene.
massimo-urbani.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: ECM says Maneri began to favor viola after borrowing one at its 1998 Badenweiler festival.
The label lists his 2011 recorded duo performance with Lucian Ban at the Culture Palace in Targu Mures.

mat-maneri.limitations: Only claims recorded in the cited artist, label, institution or original archive are included; crossovers are not classified exclusively as jazz.
mat-maneri.summary: American violinist and violist Mat Maneri pursued jazz improvisation on strings, recording with his father Joe Maneri and with pianist Lucian Ban.
mat-maneri.why_it_matters: Documents specific recordings, ensembles or performance roles and their place in jazz or adjacent genres.

evidence.claim: Mathews learned music during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands and was inspired by Joe Mooney on radio.
His 1956 discography includes The Modern Art of Jazz by Mat Mathews and Accordion Solos.

mat-mathews.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mat-mathews.summary: Dutch jazz accordionist Mat Mathews pursued bebop-oriented playing after hearing Joe Mooney on radio and recorded The Modern Art of Jazz in 1956.
mat-mathews.why_it_matters: His work made an unusual instrument viable in modern jazz ensembles.

evidence.claim: Matana Roberts recorded the first 'Coin Coin' chapter live in a Montreal studio on July 9, 2010.
Constellation released the 2011 recording with Matana Roberts on reeds and voice.

matana-roberts.limitations: Research is source-specific; credits denote actual documented roles, not an exhaustive discography.
matana-roberts.summary: Alto saxophonist Matana Roberts recorded 'Coin Coin Chapter One' live in a Montreal studio in July 2010; the 2011 release blends voice and improvisation.
matana-roberts.why_it_matters: Multi-voice experimental jazz and ancestral narrative compositions.

evidence.claim: ECM lists Matthew Garrison on electric bass and electronics with drummer Jack DeJohnette and saxophonist Ravi Coltrane on In Movement.
ECM documents the recording in October 2015 at Avatar Studios, New York, produced by Manfred Eicher.
Garrison's official artist biography describes his study with Jack DeJohnette and Dave Holland after returning to the United States in 1988.

matt-garrison.limitations: Artist biography describes broad collaborations without individual session detail; summary confines itself to ECM's documented trio.
matt-garrison.summary: Electric bassist Matthew Garrison recorded In Movement with Jack DeJohnette and Ravi Coltrane, using electronic loops in addition to his bass lines.
matt-garrison.why_it_matters: ECM's original release credits and the musician's self-authored chronology establish a specific trio, session, and earlier studies.

evidence.claim: His biography says he released Love Story independently in 2003.
He served as a guitarist and musical director for singer Catherine Russell.

matt-munisteri.limitations: His site is self-authored; avoid subjective critical judgments.
matt-munisteri.summary: Brooklyn guitarist and songwriter Matt Munisteri connects early jazz guitar and American roots music. He worked with Catherine Russell and recorded Love Story.
matt-munisteri.why_it_matters: Shows how prewar jazz repertoire overlaps American folk and song traditions.

evidence.claim: Broede's original First Album: Harmonica Tunes release identifies tenor saxophonist Wolfgang Engstfeld, vibraphonist Christoph Eidens, bassist Volker Heinze and drummer Felix Astor alongside his harmonica.
The artist identifies Reinhard Kobialka as recording and mixing engineer in Cologne and says his 1999 debut led to an Hohner harmonica endorsement.
Broede's 2023 Introducing the Duo release with Rolf Langhans explicitly dates its recording to 2021 at two locations in Berlin and Duesseldorf.
His official career history identifies the Instinct to Play quartet recorded in Berlin in 2011 with Claudio Puntin, Oliver Potratz and Alex Huber.

matthias-broede.limitations: First Album: Harmonica Tunes bears a 1999 release date; original studio day is not given. Introducing the Duo was recorded in 2021 but released in 2023. Do not treat cover-song composer credits as Broede's compositions.
matthias-broede.summary: German harmonica player Matthias Broede recorded a 1999 jazz quintet debut and later worked in a 2021 duo with pianist Rolf Langhans.
matthias-broede.why_it_matters: Two original artist-operated album releases identify distinct recording personnel and projects, while the musician's own biography locates his later Berlin quartet.

evidence.claim: LOFT Cologne documents Schubert on tenor sax with pianist Simon Nabatov, bassist Mark Dresser and drummer Tom Rainey for the 1994 Enja album Blue and Grey Suite.
The LOFT recording archive separately credits tenor saxophonist Matthias Schubert and pianist Simon Nabatov on Descriptions, issued on Leo Records in December 2013.
The official Roder-Griener trio site identifies Schubert on tenor sax on the August 25, 2021 live recording IL BIS at Sowieso, Berlin, with Jan Roder and Michael Griener.

matthias-schubert.limitations: LOFT's archival index labels album release years; it does not necessarily state session days. Schubert's 2021 concert should not be confused with the 2013 duo album.
matthias-schubert.summary: German tenor saxophonist Matthias Schubert led a 1994 quartet on Blue and Grey Suite and recorded the 2013 duo Descriptions with Simon Nabatov.
matthias-schubert.why_it_matters: The originating LOFT Cologne recording archive supplies separate dated releases and specific ensemble personnel; the performers' concert archive independently names a 2021 trio.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Matthieu Michel on flugelhorn alongside Elina Duni on voice, Rob Luft on guitar and Fred Thomas on piano and drums.
Lost Ships was recorded in February 2020 at Studios La Buissonne, Pernes les Fontaines, and released November 13, 2020.

matthieu-michel.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
matthieu-michel.summary: Swiss flugelhornist Matthieu Michel recorded Elina Duni's Lost Ships in February 2020 with Rob Luft and Fred Thomas, blending folk songs and jazz ballads.
matthieu-michel.why_it_matters: His flugelhorn offers a quiet melodic countervoice to Duni's singing and Luft's guitar.

evidence.claim: Smithsonian Folkways credits Matty Malneck on violin in Frank Trumbauer and His Orchestra's Mississippi Mud, alongside Bix Beiderbecke, Bing Crosby and Min Leibrook.
The Library of Congress moving-image finding aid documents Matty Malneck and His Orchestra as a 1940 Vitaphone motion-picture item, copyright registration MP 10461.

matty-malneck.limitations: The Folkways 1953 anthology date is a reissue year, not the original recording date. The Library of Congress preserves a film copyright description, not proof that the film's score was recorded in 1940.
matty-malneck.summary: Jazz violinist Matty Malneck played on Frank Trumbauer's Mississippi Mud with Bix Beiderbecke and led an orchestra filmed by Vitaphone in 1940.
matty-malneck.why_it_matters: Smithsonian's original personnel credits and the Library of Congress' 1940 Vitaphone registration establish a recorded instrumental role and a distinct orchestra-leading event.

evidence.claim: Universal Music records his 1955 album Paris Jazz.
The label biography identifies Vander as a long-time accompanist of Claude Nougaro and lists Nougaro tributes.

maurice-vander.limitations: Label biography; does not verify individual recording personnel.
maurice-vander.summary: French jazz pianist Maurice Vander recorded Paris Jazz in 1955 and later became closely associated with singer Claude Nougaro as accompanist.
maurice-vander.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: Ibanez's artist biography identifies Frankl as the first German guitarist in the European Jazz Orchestra.
The manufacturer credits Frankl with founding the Max Frankl Academy and publishing guitar books.

max-frankl.limitations: Manufacturer's artist biography; independent from recording personnel.
max-frankl.summary: German jazz guitarist Max Frankl played in the European Jazz Orchestra and developed guitar education materials and the Max Frankl Academy.
max-frankl.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: Flory formed his own New York band in 1954 and moved to the West Coast in 1956.
Flory co-founded Supersax with Buddy Clark in 1972; its debut won a Grammy in 1973.

med-flory.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
med-flory.summary: Saxophonist-arranger Med Flory founded a New York band in 1954, moved west in 1956 and co-founded Supersax in 1972 to play Charlie Parker solos as ensemble parts.
med-flory.why_it_matters: He transformed improvised Parker solos into arranged saxophone-section music.

evidence.claim: Melba Liston arranged for many Randy Weston albums from Little Niles (1959) through Khepera (1998).
Liston joined Dizzy Gillespie's bebop big band in 1950 and formed an all-woman quintet in 1958.

melba-liston.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
melba-liston.summary: Trombonist-arranger Melba Liston shaped Randy Weston's 'Little Niles' (1959) and later 'Khepera' (1998), expanding jazz orchestration.
melba-liston.why_it_matters: An important composer-arranger whose scores supported African-rooted jazz and expanded the creative role of women in jazz.

evidence.claim: Her artist discography lists Worrisome Heart on Verve in 2007.
It identifies Entre eux deux featuring Philippe Powell on Decca in 2022.

melody-gardot.limitations: Genre label is contextual; official discography alone does not establish jazz arrangements.
melody-gardot.summary: Singer-songwriter Melody Gardot recorded Worrisome Heart and My One and Only Thrill for Verve, later releasing Sunset in the Blue and Entre eux deux on Decca.
melody-gardot.why_it_matters: Documents jazz-influenced vocal pop with a verified album chronology.

evidence.claim: About Time Records credits Melvin Gibbs on electric bass for Eye on You with Billy Bang, Byard Lancaster, Charles Brackeen, Vernon Reid and Bern Nix.
The recording took place February 16-17, 1980 at Sound Ideas in New York; all music was composed and arranged by leader Ronald Shannon Jackson.

melvin-gibbs.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
melvin-gibbs.summary: Electric bassist Melvin Gibbs joined Ronald Shannon Jackson's Decoding Society on Eye on You, recorded February 1980 with Billy Bang, Bern Nix and Vernon Reid.
melvin-gibbs.why_it_matters: His electric bass is a driving part of the Decoding Society's dense harmolodic ensemble.

evidence.claim: Concord identifies Rhyne as the Hammond B-3 organist reunited with Wes Montgomery on Boss Guitar.
Boss Guitar's label history identifies Jimmy Cobb on drums in that Montgomery and Rhyne organ trio.
Concord includes Rhyne among the credited musicians on the Riverside anthology The Best Of Wes Montgomery.

melvin-rhyne.limitations: The Best Of Wes Montgomery aggregates multiple ensembles and should not imply Rhyne plays every selection.
melvin-rhyne.summary: Hammond organist Melvin Rhyne recorded with guitarist Wes Montgomery on Boss Guitar and in Montgomery's Indianapolis organ-trio repertoire.
melvin-rhyne.why_it_matters: Riverside's label notes establish the organ trio, Rhyne's return to Montgomery's group and the specific Boss Guitar recording.

evidence.claim: Bear Family's Boogie My Blues Away documents 44 Capitol masters and recordings from Moore's 1952-1958 label career, including previously unissued tracks.
The label's retrospective track list features House Of Blue Lights, Big Bug Boogie, Red Light and Flyright Boogie under Merrill Moore's name.
Bear Family's historical notes describe Capitol producer Ken Nelson hearing Moore's San Diego club band and offering a recording contract.

merrill-moore.limitations: Moore's music crosses jazz, country and early rock; historical credits do not justify labeling every track as jazz. Bear Family notes disagree on exact birth day and death day; neither is used.
merrill-moore.summary: Boogie pianist Merrill Moore recorded for Capitol between 1952 and 1958 and led a small California club band blending swing, country and blues.
merrill-moore.why_it_matters: Bear Family's retrospective reissue reconstructs Capitol masters and specific original track titles, with rare previously unissued sessions.

evidence.claim: Smithsonian Folkways credits Merritt Brunies on cornet and Harry Brunies on trombone for Masculine Women! Feminine Men! by the Friar's Inn Orchestra.
The Louisiana Historical Association documents Brunies's relocation from New Orleans through Los Angeles to Chicago, where he played at the Friars Inn.
The Louisiana Historical Association identifies seven Brunies records on the Okeh and Autograph labels and his subsequent return to the Gulf Coast.

merritt-brunies.limitations: Original 1924-25 recordings must be distinguished from Smithsonian's 1977 anthology issue; exact release chronology not inferred from reissue.
merritt-brunies.summary: Cornetist Merritt Brunies led the Friar's Inn Orchestra in Chicago, recording for Autograph and Okeh and appearing on Masculine Women! Feminine Men!.
merritt-brunies.why_it_matters: Smithsonian original performer credits and the Louisiana Historical Association's biographical archive establish both ensemble activity and record-label history.

evidence.claim: The Smithsonian Folkways edition credits Mezzrow on Sister Kate.
The same catalog credits him with Art Hodes on Jazz Me Blues.
He also appears on The Blues with Pops Foster and Pee Wee Russell.

mezz-mezzrow.limitations: Source verifies distinct recording credits, not an extended biographical chronology.
mezz-mezzrow.summary: Clarinetist Mezz Mezzrow appears on Folkways' Jazz at Town Hall with James P. Johnson and Baby Dodds on Sister Kate and with Art Hodes and others on Jazz Me Blues.
mezz-mezzrow.why_it_matters: Original album credits preserve his appearances within the early jazz revival.

evidence.claim: Recording engineer Marc Urselli states that he recorded SKM, featuring Michael Bisio, Stephen Gauci and Kris Davis, in 2008 at EastSide Sound.
Clean Feed's archival review identifies SKM as a drummerless trio with Stephen Gauci on tenor saxophone, Kris Davis on piano and Bisio on double bass.

michael-bisio.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
michael-bisio.summary: Bassist Michael Bisio recorded the drummerless SKM trio album Three with tenor saxophonist Stephen Gauci and pianist Kris Davis in 2008.
michael-bisio.why_it_matters: His bowed and plucked bass approaches sustain the open trio's free interplay.

evidence.claim: CAM Jazz's Soul Note catalog credits Michael Cochrane on piano with bassist Marcus McLaurine and drummer Alan Nelson on Song Of Change, listing original catalog 121251-2 and 1993.

The composer's sheet-music publisher gives the September 23-24, 1985 Elements recording with Cochrane on piano, Tom Harrell on trumpet, Bob Malach on tenor, Dennis Irwin on bass and Jimmy Madison on drums.
Second Floor Music identifies Cochrane's Proof Of The Pudding as another original composition recorded on the 1985 Elements quintet sessions, with contrasting A-minor and A-major sections.

michael-cochrane.limitations: Elements was recorded September 1985 but issued in 1986; Soul Note's current digital catalogue may show later reissue dates. Composer credits do not prove he solos on every track.
michael-cochrane.summary: Pianist Michael Cochrane led the 1985 Soul Note quintet Elements with Tom Harrell and returned in 1993 with the trio album Song of Change.
michael-cochrane.why_it_matters: Original Soul Note label inventory and the composer's own music publisher document two distinctive ensembles and dated original works.

evidence.claim: Jackson's biography dates his debut Clarity to 1977 and names Oliver Lake, David Murray and Leo Smith.
His official biography cites Oliver Lake recordings Holding Together (1976) and Life Dance of Is (1978).

michael-gregory-jackson.limitations: Official biography includes extensive broad collaborators; only specific projects cited.
michael-gregory-jackson.summary: Guitarist Michael Gregory Jackson played New York loft jazz and recorded Clarity in 1977 with Oliver Lake, David Murray and Leo Smith, crossing jazz and rock idioms.
michael-gregory-jackson.why_it_matters: Documents creative guitar practice across avant-garde jazz and other music.

evidence.claim: The Van Gelder original session discography lists Michael Hashim on alto sax in a 1991 quartet with organist Mike LeDonne, guitarist Peter Bernstein and drummer Kenny Washington.
The same session catalog attributes Smoke-Down, Our Miss Brooks and Rose Street Summer to Hashim's original Stash album A Blue Streak, catalog ST-CD-546.

BBC Music Magazine's contemporary review of Transatlantic Airs documents Hashim on soprano and alto saxophone beside pianist David Newton, drummer Clark Tracey and singer Tina May for the 33 Records release.

michael-hashim.limitations: The exact day of the 1991 Van Gelder session is not given in the archive and is not inferred. The 2012 review describes a recording on 33 Records but does not establish the original recording date.
michael-hashim.summary: Alto saxophonist Michael Hashim recorded A Blue Streak with Mike LeDonne and Peter Bernstein in 1991, then made Transatlantic Airs with a UK quartet.
michael-hashim.why_it_matters: The Van Gelder studio session index preserves precise original Stash personnel and title repertoire; a contemporary BBC Music Magazine review identifies his later London ensemble.

evidence.claim: His official biography lists Innocent Green with Gary Peacock and Billy Hart in 1996.
The discography lists Ellington Now with Oliver Hahn in 2019.

michael-hornstein.limitations: Artist website supplies session credits; avoid unverified instrumentation beyond alto sax.
michael-hornstein.summary: Munich alto saxophonist Michael Hornstein mixes jazz and electronic music. He recorded Innocent Green with Gary Peacock and Billy Hart and Ellington Now with Oliver Hahn.
michael-hornstein.why_it_matters: Links German jazz improvisation with modern production and electronic music.

evidence.claim: Turn It Up was recorded at Toronto's Revolution Recording in May and July 2022.
Ron Lopata co-wrote and produced Turn It Up with Kaeshammer.
Kaeshammer performed at the 2006, 2008 and 2010 Olympic Games.

michael-kaeshammer.limitations: Artist site promotes current releases; recording team and approximate dates from interview.
michael-kaeshammer.summary: Pianist and singer Michael Kaeshammer blends boogie-woogie, jazz and pop. He made the album Turn It Up with producer and bassist Ron Lopata after 2022 sessions.
michael-kaeshammer.why_it_matters: His self-directed music places boogie piano in contemporary song arrangements.

evidence.claim: Soul Note's Here At! credits Michael Marcus on tenor and baritone saxophones, saxello, stritch, manzello and B-flat clarinet.
The original album entry gives sessions at Sear Sound, New York, on September 7-8, 1993.
Soul Note lists Fred Hopkins, William Parker, Ted Daniel and Steve Swell among the Here At! participants.

michael-marcus.limitations: Here At! contains differing rhythm-section personnel; avoid implying every listed musician performed together on every track.
michael-marcus.summary: Multi-reed player Michael Marcus led the 1993 Soul Note recording Here At!, switching between tenor and baritone saxophones and rare low reeds.
michael-marcus.why_it_matters: Soul Note's original album credits specify the recording dates, multiple instruments and named players in an experimental ensemble.

evidence.claim: Clean Feed credits Michael Moore on alto saxophone and clarinet on Orquesta del Tiempo Perdido's Sepk.
The label calls Sepk the orchestra's third album and credits Jeroen Kimman with composing, mixing and producing all music.

michael-moore.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
michael-moore.summary: Reed player Michael Moore contributed alto saxophone and clarinet to Sepk, an eclectic Orquesta del Tiempo Perdido album composed by Jeroen Kimman.
michael-moore.why_it_matters: His saxophone and clarinet join a broad contemporary improvising orchestra.

evidence.claim: Niesemann taught oboe at Cologne's music university from 1993 to 2007.
His discography includes jazz with The Atmosphere Orchestra.
He was among the founding members of Concerto Koeln and joined Gardiner's orchestras as solo oboist in 1994.

michael-niesemann.limitations: University biography presents a broad crossover career; original jazz track credits not specified.
michael-niesemann.summary: Oboist and saxophonist Michael Niesemann recorded jazz with The Atmosphere Orchestra. He also played in Musica Antiqua Koeln and co-founded Concerto Koeln.
michael-niesemann.why_it_matters: His ensemble work links period-instrument performance with free improvisation.

evidence.claim: Hanns Eisler School appointed Schiefel professor of jazz voice in summer 2024.
The school says he experimented with electronic loop devices during his Berlin studies.

michael-schiefel.limitations: Institution page reflects its 2024 faculty appointment, not indefinite present tenure.
michael-schiefel.summary: German jazz vocalist Michael Schiefel explores loop devices and vocal electronics. He taught jazz voice in Weimar and was appointed at Berlin's Jazz Institute.
michael-schiefel.why_it_matters: Represents exploratory European jazz vocal practice.

evidence.claim: Art Canada Institute's Snow biography states he supported himself by playing nightly with Mike White Imperial Jazz Band from 1958 to 1962.
The Art Canada Institute biography places Michael Snow among the founders of the Canadian Creative Music Collective around 1974.
The Music Gallery's own founding history says its creative-music venue was established by CCMC in Toronto in 1976.

michael-snow.limitations: Art Canada traces CCMC to 1974, while the Music Gallery itself dates its venue founding to 1976; these are separate events, not conflicting dates of a single concert.
michael-snow.summary: Toronto pianist Michael Snow played with Mike White's Imperial Jazz Band in 1958-62 and helped form free-improvising collective CCMC in the 1970s.
michael-snow.why_it_matters: An art-history institute traces Snow's jazz piano career, while a music institution confirms his experimental collective's venue legacy.

evidence.claim: Weiss's official biography names his work with Johnny Griffin, Art Farmer and the Vanguard Jazz Orchestra.
His official biography states he won the 2000 BMI/Thelonious Monk Institute Composers Competition.

michael-weiss.limitations: Artist-level historical synopsis; specific session credits restricted to cited primary material.
michael-weiss.summary: American jazz pianist Michael Weiss played with Johnny Griffin and Art Farmer and won a major composition award in 2000.
michael-weiss.why_it_matters: Documents concrete genre, performance and recording contributions to a diverse jazz catalog.

evidence.claim: The Impulse! discography lists Michael White on violin, Edwin Kelly on piano, Ray Drummond on bass and Kenneth Nash on percussion on Pneuma.
Pneuma was recorded July 17-19, 1972 at The Village Recorder in Los Angeles and issued as Impulse! AS-9221.

michael-white.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
michael-white.summary: Violinist Michael White recorded Pneuma with Edwin Kelly, Ray Drummond and Kenneth Nash in Los Angeles in July 1972 for the Impulse! label.
michael-white.why_it_matters: White helped place violin at the center of exploratory spiritual jazz.

evidence.claim: The Chicago Plan credits Michael Zerang on drums, Steve Swell on trombone, Gebhard Ullmann on tenor saxophone and bass clarinet, and Fred Lonberg-Holm on cello and electronics.
The Chicago Plan was recorded on September 22, 2015 at Kingsize Sound Labs in Chicago; tracks 1, 3, 5 and 6 were written by Ullmann.

michael-zerang.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
michael-zerang.summary: Drummer Michael Zerang joined Steve Swell, Gebhard Ullmann and Fred Lonberg-Holm for The Chicago Plan, recorded in Chicago in September 2015.
michael-zerang.why_it_matters: His rhythmic responses anchor a collective quartet of reeds, trombone and cello.

evidence.claim: The A&M archives list Wings as Colombier's 1971 ten-part orchestral album, catalog SP 3503, featuring Freedom and Fear, Thalassa and Emmanuel.
A&M's historical artist account attributes the inception of Wings to Herb Alpert's commission of a jazz ensemble, symphony orchestra and soloists, with Paul Williams later supplying song lyrics.
The archive documents a separate 1977 A&M 1928 single of Emmanuel and Pourquoi Pas? as altered versions from the original Wings album.

michel-colombier.limitations: The A&M history is an independent archival catalog of original record credits rather than today's record-label site; Wings combines classical, pop and jazz ensembles, not a conventional jazz quartet.
michel-colombier.summary: French composer Michel Colombier wrote and orchestrated the 1971 A&M jazz-orchestral suite Wings and reworked Emmanuel for a 1977 single.
michel-colombier.why_it_matters: A&M historical catalog reproduces original release details, arrangements and the specifically altered later single, distinguishing composition from sideman performance.

evidence.claim: The Hot Club de Limoges radio archive says Gaudry studied piano and clarinet before double bass.
The station biography dates his professional debut with Michel Hausser in Lausanne to 1955.

michel-gaudry.limitations: Original jazz-radio biographical research; first-party station authored.
michel-gaudry.summary: French bassist Michel Gaudry studied piano and clarinet before turning to double bass and playing with Michel Hausser in Lausanne.
michel-gaudry.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: JazzProfiles' specialist discography lists 1970 Agartha on Saravah with Cullaz on bass and Lubat on drums.
It records Ad Lib in Paris on July 9-10, 1976, with Jenny-Clark on bass and Aldo Romano on drums and percussion.

michel-graillier.limitations: Specialist discography synthesizes documented releases; session credit limited to listed sources.
michel-graillier.summary: French pianist Michel Graillier recorded Agartha with Alby Cullaz and Bernard Lubat, then Ad Lib with Jean-Francois Jenny-Clark and Aldo Romano.
michel-graillier.why_it_matters: Preserves documented jazz recording or instrumental context for this named performer.

evidence.claim: The Miles Davis official album catalog dates Michel Legrand Legrand Jazz to 1958 and lists The Jitterbug Waltz, Django, Wild Man Blues and Round Midnight as the four tracks on which Davis plays trumpet.
The John Coltrane session discography indexes Michel Legrand orchestral sessions of June 25 1958 with Miles Davis, John Coltrane and Bill Evans, and specifies personnel exclusions by title.
The original Columbia discography records Legrand as the arranger and conductor for the June 25 1958 session, while some reissues combine material from other dates.

michel-legrand.limitations: The June 25 original session included Miles Davis but the release collects three groups on June 25, 27 and 30. Not every player is on every track; 1959 pressings may differ from the 1958 issue.
michel-legrand.summary: French arranger Michel Legrand directed the 1958 jazz orchestra album Legrand Jazz; Miles Davis played on four tracks, including Django.
michel-legrand.why_it_matters: The official Miles Davis discography establishes the original album and the four specific Davis titles; independent original session indexing fixes dates and players.

evidence.claim: Power of Three recorded live at Montreux in 1986
Album combines Petrucciani-Hall duo and trio featuring Wayne Shorter

michel-petrucciani.limitations: Source-specific music facts; not a complete discography.
michel-petrucciani.summary: French pianist Michel Petrucciani recorded 'Power of Three' at Montreux in 1986 with guitarist Jim Hall; saxophonist Wayne Shorter joined for trio pieces.
michel-petrucciani.why_it_matters: Post-bop lyricism in an unusually intimate Hall/Shorter chamber-style collaboration

evidence.claim: His official biography lists the Thelonious Monk Award for Composition.
The same biography credits a Gouden Kalf award for the score to Tiramisu.

michiel-borstlap.limitations: Biography is self-published; awards described there.
michiel-borstlap.summary: Dutch pianist and composer Michiel Borstlap won the Thelonious Monk Composition Award and scored the Dutch film Tiramisu.
michiel-borstlap.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: The musician's official site describes Michiel Braam as a Dutch jazz pianist, composer and bandleader who founded his large ensemble in 1986.
Braam states that Bik Bent Braam continued as a working big band through 2013 and performed his 26-piece composition The XYZ of Bik Bent Braam.
The project history calls Bik Bent Braam a 13-piece improvising orchestra that performed without a fixed setlist.

michiel-braam.limitations: The artist's 1986-2013 dates refer to the orchestra's active period, not the musician's whole performing career.
michiel-braam.summary: Dutch pianist-composer Michiel Braam founded Bik Bent Braam in 1986, developing a 13-piece improvising big band that ran until 2013.
michiel-braam.why_it_matters: His official ensemble history explains the unusual no-setlist live improvisation method and original composition catalogue.

evidence.claim: Change of Heart credits Mick Hutton on bass, Martin Speake on saxophone, Bobo Stenson on piano and Paul Motian on drums.
The eight-track album features Martin Speake compositions and was recorded April 2002 in Oslo.

mick-hutton.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mick-hutton.summary: Bassist Mick Hutton played on Martin Speake's Change of Heart with Bobo Stenson and Paul Motian, recorded at Rainbow Studio in Oslo in April 2002.
mick-hutton.why_it_matters: His acoustic playing anchors the spacious modern jazz quartet.

evidence.claim: Concord lists Mickey Bass among the personnel on Art Blakey's Vol. 2: Mission Eternal, recorded in 1973.
Concord lists Mickey Bass in the personnel of Art Blakey's 1972-73 recording collection Vol. 1: Child's Dance.
The Mission Eternal notes place the Blakey sessions alongside contributions from Woody Shaw and Cedar Walton.

mickey-bass.limitations: Both releases gather recordings with changing bassists and lineups; participation is not assigned to every track.
mickey-bass.summary: Bassist Mickey Bass participated in Art Blakey's early-1970s sessions later issued as Child's Dance and Mission Eternal with Woody Shaw and Cedar Walton.
mickey-bass.why_it_matters: Prestige reissue documents name Mickey Bass in the Blakey group across two sets of 1972-73 recordings.

evidence.claim: Indiana University's Mickey Tucker collection describes him as an American jazz pianist and organist with manuscripts and recordings preserved in its African American Music and Culture archive.
The Indiana archive lists a June 20, 1985 Mickey Tucker Quartet video performance at Newark Museum.
The Indiana University finding aid lists a 1994 Mickey Tucker concert recording from Montsalvat Jazz in Melbourne, Australia.

mickey-tucker.limitations: Archive entries establish that recordings, programs and compositions exist, not automatic endorsement of a particular performance's quality.
mickey-tucker.summary: Pianist and organist Mickey Tucker's career is preserved in Indiana University's archive of scores, performance recordings, and his Australian jazz concerts.
mickey-tucker.why_it_matters: The original creator papers and performance reels provide a rare primary historical documentation trail for an active jazz pianist.

evidence.claim: Trombonist Mike Barone's own biography says he formed a big band in 1964 that played at Donte's jazz club during 1966-69.
Mike Barone's official biography states that he supplied compositions and arrangements to the Johnny Carson Tonight Show Band from 1968 to 1992.
The official Mike Barone Big Band personnel page identifies Barone as its leader, composer and arranger.

mike-barone.limitations: Self-authored career estimates and large arrangement counts are not independent session ledgers; no exact track credits are inferred.
mike-barone.summary: Jazz trombonist and arranger Mike Barone formed a Los Angeles big band in 1964 and wrote extensive arrangements for Johnny Carson's Tonight Show band.
mike-barone.why_it_matters: The musician's original professional biography documents Los Angeles jazz orchestration and stage work.

evidence.claim: Block's official biography says he joined Yo-Yo Ma's Silk Road Ensemble in 2005.
His site identifies Biriba Union with Christylez Bacon and Patricia Ligia as one of his touring bands.

mike-block.limitations: Only claims recorded in the cited artist, label, institution or original archive are included; crossovers are not classified exclusively as jazz.
mike-block.summary: American cellist Mike Block combines classical music with folk and improvisation, performing with Silkroad and his own cross-cultural groups.
mike-block.why_it_matters: Documents specific recordings, ensembles or performance roles and their place in jazz or adjacent genres.

evidence.claim: The British Jazz Sound Archive catalogs Mike Carr Trio on BBC Jazz Scene dated December 4, 1966 with John McLaughlin and titles including The Sidewinder.

mike-carr.limitations: The archived 1966 quartet-style personnel list includes four names under a Trio heading; no unsupported instrument is assigned to the fourth musician.
mike-carr.summary: British jazz organist Mike Carr led BBC-recorded trios in 1966 with guitarist John McLaughlin and in 1983 with bassist Paul Morgan and drummer Spike Wells.
mike-carr.why_it_matters: The British Jazz Sound Archive catalog identifies exact broadcast sessions, dates, musicians and performed tunes.

evidence.claim: On his personal artist biography, Fahn describes his first leader album Stepping Out and explicitly identifies John Patitucci as bassist.

mike-fahn.limitations: Fahn's own website calls Stepping Out his first CD, while the contemporary record review prints the title Steppin' Out. The exact album title is retained as printed in the review; no session date inferred.
mike-fahn.summary: Valve trombonist Mike Fahn made Steppin' Out with John Patitucci and later led East and West Coast Quintets, produced by Mary Ann McSweeney.
mike-fahn.why_it_matters: The trombonist's first-person biography and the producer's own release list connect two specific leader projects and collaborators, corroborated by a contemporary original review.

evidence.claim: Hammond's artist biography says he joined the Milt Jackson Quartet in 1988.
It identifies Bout Time as his debut recording for the Criss Cross label in 1988.

mike-ledonne.limitations: Manufacturer artist biography; avoid post-1999 leadership claim present in source because its wording is inconsistent.
mike-ledonne.summary: American pianist and Hammond organist Mike LeDonne played with Roy Eldridge at Jimmy Ryan's and joined Milt Jackson's quartet in 1988. He recorded Bout Time.
mike-ledonne.why_it_matters: Links mainstream piano playing to the Hammond organ tradition.

evidence.claim: Longo's own biography says Cannonball Adderley hired him to play in his quartet.
Steinway says Dizzy Gillespie named Longo leader of the Gillespie Quintet from 1966 to 1975.
The Steinway profile says he also directed an 18-piece New York State of the Art Jazz Ensemble.

mike-longo.limitations: Artist estate bio and Steinway profile support separate facts; no invented recorded titles.
mike-longo.summary: Jazz pianist Mike Longo played in Cannonball Adderley's quartet and later directed Dizzy Gillespie's quintet from 1966 to 1975. His work included education and big bands.
mike-longo.why_it_matters: His own estate documents his move from Florida jazz clubs to Dizzy Gillespie and concert teaching.

Concord credits Mike Melvoin on piano and keyboards in the collective Ray Brown and Herb Ellis sextet personnel alongside Plas Johnson and Jake Hanna.
Concord lists Mike Melvoin among the pianists for Leroy Vinnegar's jazz quintet album Leroy Walks Again! alongside Victor Feldman.

mike-melvoin.limitations: The Ray Brown set combines two albums with different pianists; Melvoin replaced George Duke only for Hot Tracks, not the whole double set.
mike-melvoin.summary: Pianist and keyboardist Mike Melvoin recorded with Herb Ellis and Ray Brown on Hot Tracks and appeared on Leroy Vinnegar's Leroy Walks Again!.
mike-melvoin.why_it_matters: Two original Concord label descriptions identify a working pianist and differentiate particular instrumental session credits.

evidence.claim: ABC recorded Nock's solo piano album Touch in 1993.
ABC recorded Hearing in the same studio for its 2023 release.

mike-nock.limitations: Original broadcaster provides dates and instrumentation; no assumed sidemen.
mike-nock.summary: New Zealand pianist Mike Nock recorded the solo album Touch at ABC's Eugene Goossens Hall in 1993 and returned there for Hearing in 2023.
mike-nock.why_it_matters: His original solo sessions document decades of reflective jazz piano.

evidence.claim: The Canterbury discography identifies Mike Osborne as the alto saxophonist on Mike Westbrook's Love Songs, recorded in March 1970.

mike-osborne.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mike-osborne.summary: Alto saxophonist Mike Osborne recorded with the Mike Westbrook Concert Band on Love Songs in 1970 and the expanded Metropolis sessions in 1971.
mike-osborne.why_it_matters: His alto-saxophone work is a distinct thread through early British creative big-band jazz.

evidence.claim: Ipecac Recordings official biography says Mike Patton formed Fantomas in 1998 with Buzz Osborne, Trevor Dunn and Dave Lombardo.
The official Fantomas Bandcamp lists its debut Fantomas as released April 26 1999, with later Director Cut in 2001 and Suspended Animation in 2005.

mike-patton.limitations: Fantomas is an avant-garde rock/noise ensemble, not a claim of jazz improvisational personnel or a bebop leader discography.
mike-patton.summary: Singer Mike Patton formed experimental group Fantomas in 1998 with Buzz Osborne, Trevor Dunn and Dave Lombardo; its debut appeared in 1999.
mike-patton.why_it_matters: The original-label and band archives document a genre-crossing lineup without mislabeling metal or experimental rock as straight jazz.

evidence.claim: Reed's official site identifies Greg Ward, Tim Haldeman and Jason Roebke as members of People, Places and Things.
His artist biography says he served as AACM vice-chairperson from 2009 to 2011.

mike-reed.limitations: Only claims recorded in the cited artist, label, institution or original archive are included; crossovers are not classified exclusively as jazz.
mike-reed.summary: Chicago drummer Mike Reed leads the quartet People, Places and Things, reimagining the city's 1950s jazz repertoire with modern improvisers.
mike-reed.why_it_matters: Documents specific recordings, ensembles or performance roles and their place in jazz or adjacent genres.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Mike Richmond on bass and electric bass with Jack DeJohnette, John Abercrombie, Alex Foster and Warren Bernhardt on Untitled.
The ECM track list credits Richmond as a co-composer of Fantastic, with Foster, DeJohnette and Abercrombie, and dates original release to September 1976.

mike-richmond.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mike-richmond.summary: Bassist Mike Richmond played acoustic and electric bass on Jack DeJohnette's Directions album Untitled, originally issued by ECM in September 1976.
mike-richmond.why_it_matters: His bass helped underpin DeJohnette's early blend of open jazz and electric instrumentation.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Mike Stern on guitar for Something There alongside Michael Mantler, Carla Bley, Steve Swallow and Nick Mason.
Something There was recorded during February-July 1982 and first issued January 4, 1983, although ECM also lists a later 1987 reissue.

mike-stern.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mike-stern.summary: Guitarist Mike Stern recorded Michael Mantler's Something There in 1982 with Carla Bley, Steve Swallow and Nick Mason plus London orchestral strings.
mike-stern.why_it_matters: His guitar adds an incisive electric voice to experimental orchestral jazz.

evidence.claim: The Royal Academy of Music lists Walker as Professor of Jazz Guitar.
The Academy's biography lists his collaborations with Dave Holland and Peter Erskine.

mike-walker.limitations: Institution biography; no specific record sessions inferred.
mike-walker.summary: British guitarist Mike Walker teaches jazz guitar at the Royal Academy of Music and has performed with Dave Holland and Peter Erskine.
mike-walker.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: The Canterbury discography credits Westbrook on piano, Norma Winstone on vocals, Mike Osborne on alto sax and Chris Spedding on guitar for Love Songs.
Love Songs was recorded in 1970 at Tangerine Studios in London for Deram with Peter Eden as producer.

mike-westbrook.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
mike-westbrook.summary: Pianist-composer Mike Westbrook led a large British jazz ensemble for Love Songs in 1970, featuring Norma Winstone, Mike Osborne and Chris Spedding.
mike-westbrook.why_it_matters: His large-band writing connected British improvisation, modern jazz and song.

evidence.claim: San Diego Music Hall of Fame says Wofford played with Red Norvo and Chet Baker after moving to Los Angeles.

mike-wofford.limitations: Hall of Fame biography is retrospective, without a track-level recording session discography.
mike-wofford.summary: Pianist Mike Wofford worked with Red Norvo and Chet Baker in Los Angeles jazz groups. He later served as a film and television studio pianist for Oliver Nelson.
mike-wofford.why_it_matters: Documents the connection between jazz clubs, jazz orchestras and screen music.

evidence.claim: Mikko Innanen / Jaak Sooaar / Han Bennink are credited for Spring Odyssey.

mikko-innanen.summary: Finnish saxophonist Mikko Innanen recorded 'Spring Odyssey' with Jaak Sooaar and Han Bennink; he also led the 10+ ensemble on 'GROTTO' (2016).
mikko-innanen.why_it_matters: Finnish large-ensemble composing and free saxophone improvisation.

mildred-bailey.limitations: Museum copy offers a broad career account, not a verified earliest-ever claim about women touring or detailed discographical personnel.
mildred-bailey.summary: Swing vocalist Mildred Bailey performed with Paul Whiteman's orchestra and later co-led radio shows with vibraphonist Red Norvo, her husband.
mildred-bailey.why_it_matters: The Smithsonian National Postal Museum connects the exact singer, jazz orchestra and radio career.

milton-delugg.summary: Composer and bandleader Milton DeLugg wrote the song Orange Colored Sky, recorded by Nat King Cole, and scored music for television and films.
milton-delugg.why_it_matters: Situates swing-era songcraft amid television and pop production.

mimi-fox.why_it_matters: Connects modern jazz guitar playing and teaching with homage to Wes Montgomery.

monnette-sudler.limitations: The institutional memorial reports band associations and a city music initiative, not precise recording personnel for individual tracks.
monnette-sudler.summary: Philadelphia jazz guitarist Monnette Sudler belonged to the 1970s Sounds of Liberation collective and later founded the Philadelphia Guitar Summit.

motoharu-yoshizawa.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.

mulgrew-miller.limitations: This card refers to separate band memberships and a leader debut; session personnel of later Tony Williams albums are not inferred from the timeline.
mulgrew-miller.summary: Pianist Mulgrew Miller joined Art Blakey Jazz Messengers in 1983, recorded his 1985 leader debut Keys to the City and played with Tony Williams.
mulgrew-miller.why_it_matters: The artist maintained biography gives exact years for touring bands and original early Landmark recordings.

evidence.claim: The Prestige original catalog records Musa Kaleem on flute beside Coleman Hawkins, Tiny Grimes and Ray Bryant at Van Gelder Studio on February 28, 1958 for Blues Groove.
The Blue Note discography credits Kaleem on tenor saxophone and flute in Dizzy Reece's July 17, 1960 sextet with Stanley Turrentine and Duke Jordan, including Goose Dance and Comin' On.
Prestige's 1958 45 rpm catalog separately lists Tiny Grimes' Blues Wail Parts 1 and 2 with Kaleem on flute, from the February 28 recording.

musa-kaleem.limitations: Jazzdisco is an independently compiled specialist sessionography reproducing original label catalog data; the label masters themselves were not directly inspected. Prestige's 1958 release and 1970 reissue must not be confused.
musa-kaleem.summary: Multi-reed jazz player Musa Kaleem recorded flute with Coleman Hawkins and Tiny Grimes in 1958 and tenor saxophone with Dizzy Reece in 1960.
musa-kaleem.why_it_matters: Specialist archives reconstruct original Prestige and Blue Note matrices, session dates, instrument changes and original record titles.

evidence.claim: Myra Melford's 2022 Fire and Water Quintet album features Mary Halvorson, Tomeka Reid and Susie Ibarra.
The quintet credits include Mary Halvorson, Tomeka Reid and Susie Ibarra.

myra-melford.limitations: Research is source-specific; credits denote actual documented roles, not an exhaustive discography.
myra-melford.summary: Pianist Myra Melford's Fire and Water Quintet recorded 'For the Love of Fire and Water' (2022) with Mary Halvorson, Tomeka Reid and Susie Ibarra.
myra-melford.why_it_matters: Piano-composed avant-jazz shaped by guitar, cello, sax and percussion.

evidence.claim: Smithsonian Folkways identifies Nadi Qamar as a jazz pianist and says he designed the Mama-Likembi from a grouping of African thumb pianos.
Smithsonian credits Qamar with six original compositions on Mama Likembi and documents African, Asian and jazz influences in his own liner commentary.
Folkways' Likembi Song Book names Qamar as Spaulding Givens before conversion to Islam and describes the album's teaching material.

nadi-qamar.limitations: The instrument is sometimes called a thumb piano, but the original Mama-Likembi was designed for finger playing; names and jazz context require precision.
nadi-qamar.summary: Jazz pianist Nadi Qamar, formerly Spaulding Givens, designed the Mama-Likembi instrument and recorded original music and instructional works for Folkways.
nadi-qamar.why_it_matters: Smithsonian Folkways preserves the musician's original liner notes, instrument design and recordings distinct from conventional jazz piano.

evidence.claim: Najma's official biography dates her first UK release Qareeb to 1987 and describes its jazz-ghazal fusion.
Her biography says Pukar appeared in 1992 using Persian, Indian and African instrumentation.

najma-akhtar.limitations: Artist biography supports these broad credits; no track-by-track session personnel inferred.
najma-akhtar.summary: British vocalist Najma Akhtar blends Urdu ghazal with jazz phrasing and recorded crossover albums including Qareeb and Pukar.
najma-akhtar.why_it_matters: Documents a distinctive jazz crossover artist with artist-authored album or ensemble facts.

evidence.claim: Harrow describes Wild Women Don't Have the Blues as her 1961 Candid debut.
She identifies John Lewis as arranger and pianist for the 1963 Atlantic album You Never Know.

nancy-harrow.limitations: Autobiographical source; album personnel quoted only where specifically provided.
nancy-harrow.summary: Jazz vocalist and composer Nancy Harrow released Wild Women Don't Have the Blues on Candid and You Never Know on Atlantic, then wrote story-based jazz musicals.
nancy-harrow.why_it_matters: Connects classic jazz singing with authored musical storytelling.

evidence.claim: Live at Jazz Standard with Fred Hersch earned 2006 Grammy nomination
Glen Moore among her longtime jazz collaborators

nancy-king.limitations: Source-specific musical details; does not establish exhaustive discography.
nancy-king.summary: Scat-focused jazz vocalist Nancy King made the 2006 duo album 'Live at Jazz Standard' with pianist Fred Hersch; she also worked with Glen Moore.
nancy-king.why_it_matters: Inventive vocal improviser and widely admired Portland jazz-scene educator

evidence.claim: The Roxy film credits Brock on tenor sax, flute and lead vocals.
Zappa's Roxy performances were filmed in December 1973.
The official Zappa archive calls Brock a new member of the 1973 Halloween lineup.

napoleon-murphy-brock.limitations: The Roxy documentation focuses on one ensemble era; no wider-career claims inferred.
