napoleon-murphy-brock.summary: Saxophonist, flutist and singer Napoleon Murphy Brock joined Frank Zappa's band in 1973. He appears in the filmed Roxy shows and on recordings drawn from those performances.
napoleon-murphy-brock.why_it_matters: Original Zappa estate credits document his roles in adventurous 1970s live music.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Nasheet Waits on drums, Ralph Alessi on trumpet, Jason Moran on piano and Drew Gress on bass.
Baida was recorded in October 2012 at Avatar Studios, New York, and released October 4, 2013.

nasheet-waits.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
nasheet-waits.summary: Drummer Nasheet Waits recorded Baida at Avatar Studios in October 2012 with Ralph Alessi, Jason Moran and Drew Gress; ECM issued the album in 2013.
nasheet-waits.why_it_matters: His fluid rhythmic playing supports the open-form contemporary trumpet quartet.

evidence.claim: The British Trombone Society recounts Peck's letter to Glenn Miller and subsequent wartime journey to England in June 1944 as an Army Air Force Orchestra trombonist.
Its profile documents Peck's membership of the Clarke-Boland Big Band from 1963 to 1969.
The society records his Paris studies and work with Quincy Jones, Michel Legrand and Duke Ellington before relocating to London in 1965.

nat-peck.limitations: The source is a specialist professional obituary and preserved first-person memories, not primary session tape logs.
nat-peck.summary: Trombonist Nat Peck entered Glenn Miller's wartime Army Air Force orchestra in 1944 and later performed in the Clarke-Boland Big Band.
nat-peck.why_it_matters: The British Trombone Society's obituary draws on his own recollections and provides exact band affiliations, locations and professional chronology.

evidence.claim: Pierce joined Woody Herman's Third Herd as pianist and arranger in 1951 and stayed until 1955.
He arranged the 1957 Sound of Jazz television program and co-founded the Capp-Pierce Juggernaut in 1975.

nat-pierce.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
nat-pierce.summary: Pianist-arranger Nat Pierce played with Woody Herman's Third Herd from 1951 to 1955, arranged the 1957 Sound of Jazz telecast and co-led the Capp-Pierce Juggernaut.
nat-pierce.why_it_matters: A major swing arranger and an often overlooked pianist in postwar orchestras.

evidence.claim: Unforgettable With Love won Album of the Year at the 1992 Grammy Awards.
Unforgettable with Nat King Cole won Record of the Year in 1992.
Take a Look won Best Jazz Vocal Performance at the 1994 Grammy Awards.

natalie-cole.limitations: Recording Academy records award categories, not attribution of instrumental parts.
natalie-cole.summary: Natalie Cole won the 1992 Grammy for Album of the Year with Unforgettable With Love. Her recording of Unforgettable with Nat King Cole won Record of the Year.
natalie-cole.why_it_matters: Her recordings brought classic vocal standards to a new audience.

evidence.claim: Clean Feed credits Nate Radley on guitar, Gary Versace on organ, Jim Black on drums and Kris Davis on piano.
The four clarinetists on Save Your Breath are Ben Goldberg, Oscar Noriega, Andrew Bishop and Joachim Badenhorst.

nate-radley.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
nate-radley.summary: Guitarist Nate Radley joined pianist Kris Davis and the Infrasound octet on Save Your Breath, mixing electric guitar and organ with four clarinets.
nate-radley.why_it_matters: His guitar adds rock-toned textures to an unusual modern jazz octet.

evidence.claim: Loriers's official biography identifies her first leader CD Nympheas (Igloo, 1991), naming Kurt van Herck, Philippe Aerts and Mimi Verderame.
Her official discography lists Le Temps Retrouve as a Loriers-Postma-Thys trio release on Igloo IGL325.

nathalie-loriers.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
nathalie-loriers.summary: Belgian pianist Nathalie Loriers recorded Nympheas in 1991 with Kurt van Herck, Philippe Aerts and Mimi Verderame, later forming a trio with Postma and Thys.
nathalie-loriers.why_it_matters: Belgian compositional piano jazz connecting saxophone, bass and intimate chamber dialogue.

evidence.claim: MPS states that Nathan Davis recorded Happy Girl in 1965, joined by Woody Shaw on trumpet, Larry Young on piano, Jimmy Woode on bass and Billy Brooks on drums.
The MPS label identifies Nathan Davis as composer of The Flute in the Blues and describes his flute performance on the 1965 Happy Girl album.

The SABA SB 15025 ST Happy Girl album credits Nathan Davis on flute, Woody Shaw on trumpet, Larry Young on piano, Jimmy Woode on bass and Billy Brooks on drums; disputed exact recording days are omitted.

nathan-davis.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
nathan-davis.summary: Saxophonist and flutist Nathan Davis recorded Happy Girl in 1965 with Woody Shaw, Larry Young, Jimmy Woode and Billy Brooks; he composed The Flute in the Blues.
nathan-davis.why_it_matters: Documents a saxophonist and flutist's 1965 European hard-bop work through original label personnel and an individually credited composition.

evidence.claim: Trumpeter Natsuki Tamura and pianist Satoko Fujii recorded the improvising duo 'How Many?' in 1997.
South Wind recorded June 1997 features Natsuki Tamura

natsuki-tamura.limitations: Source-specific musical details, not a complete discography.
natsuki-tamura.summary: Japanese trumpeter Natsuki Tamura recorded the freely improvised duo 'How Many?' with pianist Satoko Fujii and played in her big-band album 'South Wind' (1997).
natsuki-tamura.why_it_matters: Trumpet solo and collective free improvisation across duo and jazz orchestra

evidence.claim: Dominique recorded with Jelly Roll Morton in 1923 after relocating to Chicago.
Dominique recorded with Johnny Dodds through Dodds's final 1940 recordings.

natty-dominique.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
natty-dominique.summary: New Orleans trumpeter Natty Dominique recorded with Jelly Roll Morton in 1923 and frequently worked with clarinetist Johnny Dodds, recording with him into 1940.
natty-dominique.why_it_matters: His vigorous cornet style was part of classic Chicago New Orleans jazz.

evidence.claim: Concord identifies Neal Creque as keyboardist and arranger with Pucho and the Latin Soul Brothers.
Concord's Cold Shoulder describes Creque's later work with guitarist Grant Green and singer Eddie Cleanhead Vinson.
The label's Legends Of Acid Jazz collection credits Neal Creque among Pucho's musicians on tracks drawn from 1967-1970.

neal-creque.limitations: The four-album Cold Shoulder retrospective includes several personnel configurations; no per-track claims are inferred.
neal-creque.summary: Keyboardist and arranger Neal Creque played in Pucho and the Latin Soul Brothers, whose Prestige records combined Latin boogaloo, jazz and funk.
neal-creque.why_it_matters: The label identifies Creque's specific role as keyboard player and arranger in the ensemble and links its original Prestige recordings.

evidence.claim: Peart joined Rush in July 1974.
His first Rush album was Fly By Night in 1975 and he wrote most of its lyrics.
Moving Pictures was released in 1981.

neil-peart.limitations: Rock musician, not a jazz artist; historical crossover context only.
neil-peart.summary: Rush drummer and lyricist Neil Peart joined the group in 1974. He debuted on Fly By Night in 1975 and helped shape the 1981 album Moving Pictures.
neil-peart.why_it_matters: His sophisticated rock percussion drew on jazz drummers but remains progressive rock.

evidence.claim: The Canadian Jazz Archive records his collaboration with Woody Shaw and multiple European tours.
Its discography identifies 49th Parallel as his record with Woody Shaw and Joe Henderson.

neil-swainson.limitations: Archive biography has outdated present-tense references; rely on historical events.
neil-swainson.summary: Canadian jazz bassist Neil Swainson worked with trumpeter Woody Shaw and pianist George Shearing. His own 49th Parallel featured Shaw and Joe Henderson.
neil-swainson.why_it_matters: Documents Canadian links to American post-bop small groups.

evidence.claim: The Graubuenden cantonal library catalogs the 1958 Nelson Williams and the New Orleans Wild Cats LP with Williams on trumpet and Fritz Trippel on piano, recorded in Basel September 30, 1958.
The original Mercury/Clef 1951 recording matrix identifies Williams on trumpet with Johnny Hodges, Lawrence Brown, Al Sears and Sonny Greer in the January 15 New York session.
The Norgran Castle Rock album sessionology assigns Williams to Rabbit's Blues and Blue Fantasia, while specifically identifying Emmett Berry as replacement trumpet on later 1951 sessions.

nelson-williams.limitations: The 1955 Norgran Castle Rock issue combines several Hodges sessions; Williams is identified only for the January 15, 1951 personnel, not later tracks using Emmett Berry. Swiss catalog dates a Basel session, not an original label release day.
nelson-williams.summary: Jazz trumpeter Nelson Williams played in Johnny Hodges's 1951 New York orchestra and led a 1958 Swiss recording with the New Orleans Wild Cats.
nelson-williams.why_it_matters: A Swiss cantonal library preserves the original Wild Cats LP and date, while historical Verve sessionology provides specific track and personnel separation.

evidence.claim: The Fresh Sound reissue of This Is It! identifies Nick Brignola as the original album leader playing baritone and alto saxophones, saxello, flute and bass.
The same reissue credits Reese Markewich on piano and flute, Glenn Moore on bass and Dick Berk on drums for the Brignola quartet.
Fresh Sound identifies This Is It! as originally released by Nick Brignola on Priam 101 LP and notes Brignola's composition The Mace.

nick-brignola.limitations: Fresh Sound's notes disagree internally on the original recording year, listing 1967 in the album details but late 1968 in the descriptive history. The biographical summary does not date the recording.
nick-brignola.summary: Baritone saxophonist Nick Brignola led the quartet recording This Is It!, switching among saxello, alto, baritone, flute and bass on the session.
nick-brignola.why_it_matters: The restored record's original Priam catalog number and credits document a specific group and Brignola's multiple instruments.

evidence.claim: Cuneiform's archival Bremen to Bridgwater credits Nick Evans on trombone in Brotherhood of Breath recordings from Bremen in June 1971 and Bridgwater in February and November 1975.
Ogun's Happy Daze + Oh! For The Edge credits Evans on trombone in Elton Dean's Ninesense, documenting a 1976 London concert and a 1977 studio album.
Jazz in Britain's preserved BBC archive lists Evans among Brotherhood of Breath's two trombonists for Sun Song, broadcast November 2, 1970.

nick-evans.limitations: Bremen to Bridgwater is a 2004 compilation of recordings from 1971 and 1975; dates in the original notes are not publication dates.
nick-evans.summary: Welsh jazz trombonist Nick Evans played with Chris McGregor's Brotherhood of Breath in 1971-75 and joined Elton Dean's Ninesense recordings in 1976-77.
nick-evans.why_it_matters: Cuneiform's original Radio Bremen tape reissues and Ogun's Elton Dean reissue establish separate ensembles and dated sessions.

evidence.claim: Riverside's Zoot! notes name Nick Travis as trumpeter with Zoot Sims, George Handy, Wilbur Ware and Osie Johnson for a 1956 recording.
Concord credits the trumpet solos of Nick Travis and Dick Sherman on Elliot Lawrence's 1955 Plays Gerry Mulligan Arrangements.
Concord's Swings Cohn & Kahn notes identify Travis and Ernie Royal among the trumpeters featured by Lawrence's band.

nick-travis.limitations: His credits on Lawrence albums cover a band with several trumpeters; the notes do not allocate every solo to Travis.
nick-travis.summary: Trumpeter Nick Travis recorded with Zoot Sims on the 1956 Riverside album Zoot! and played arrangements by Gerry Mulligan for Elliot Lawrence.
nick-travis.why_it_matters: Original Riverside and Fresh Sound-derived reissue notes explicitly identify Travis on distinct small-group and big-band recordings.

evidence.claim: Concord's original Roseland label notes identify steel-string guitarist Nick Webb as Acoustic Alchemy's co-founder and say Miles Gilderdale joined after Webb's death in early 1998.
GRP Records' licensed Red Dust and Spanish Lace track catalog lists Nick Webb and Greg Carmichael as composers of Mr. Chow and dates its original recording to 1987 at Hansa-Haus Studios in Bonn.

The original GRP/Universal recording rights catalog credits Nick Webb and Greg Carmichael as songwriters of 1987 performances Mr. Chow and Red Dust and Spanish Lace, distinct from the year of the later anthology.

nick-webb.limitations: The 2007 GRP download is a later reissue of the 1987 original, not a new performance; original 1987 dates are supplied separately by the licensed track catalog. The original musician's death preceded 1998, but no claims about his playing on Positive Thinking are asserted. The unofficial Acoustic Alchemy fan site was excluded from the accepted claims.
nick-webb.summary: Steel-string guitarist Nick Webb co-founded Acoustic Alchemy and recorded Red Dust and Spanish Lace in 1987 with guitarist Greg Carmichael.
nick-webb.why_it_matters: Concord's original band history independently corroborates the founding role; the surviving group's documentary fan archive reconstructs original MCA session personnel.

evidence.claim: The preserved Columbia Legacy track annotation credits Nico Bunink on piano for New Now, Know How recorded November 1, 1959 at 30th Street Studio, not the other Mingus Dynasty tracks led by Roland Hanna.
Werner Herbers' first-person historical investigation for the Dutch Jazz Archive documents Bunink's first Mingus recording session on November 1, 1959 and a second on October 20, 1960.

The same archival scholarship describes Bunink declining a Vancouver engagement while newly married after the 1960 Candid session, distinguishing a documented performance refusal from recording history.

nico-bunink.limitations: The Columbia album combines sessions with Roland Hanna on most tracks, so Bunink is credited only on New Now, Know How and separately identified takes. The original 1960 Candid album is a different session; later compilations have different issue dates.
nico-bunink.summary: Dutch pianist Nico Bunink played piano for Mingus on New Now, Know How in 1959 and returned for a different Candid session in October 1960.
nico-bunink.why_it_matters: A reproduction of Columbia's original track-level personnel and firsthand Dutch Jazz Archive historical scholarship verify two different Mingus dates without generalizing album credits.

evidence.claim: The original Via Asiago 10 / Twilight Music catalog credits vocalist Nicola Arigliano on its 2008 album My Wonderful Nicola (TWI CD AS 08 46), including the American standards She is Funny That Way and Night and Day.

The original label essay documents Arigliano singing Arrivederci with pianist Umberto Bindi, identifying their radio collaboration in 1986 and distinguishing that recording history from the 2008 reissue.
Twilight Music separately describes Arigliano singing Night and Day with swing pianist Stelvio Cipriani, in original radio material included in the historical collection.
The original Rai archive identifies Nicola Arigliano as a presenter with Milva and Claudio Villa during the 1963 Il cantatutto television broadcast run, distinct from his jazz record releases.

nicola-arigliano.limitations: The 2008 My Wonderful Nicola release restores radio and other archival interpretations; 2008 is the release year, not the date of individual performances. The label documents Bindi collaboration in 1986 but does not give dates for every jazz standard. Earlier Rai television broadcasts are not misrepresented as recording sessions.
nicola-arigliano.summary: Italian jazz singer Nicola Arigliano recorded standards such as Night and Day and She is Funny That Way, alongside the radio jazz work of Umberto Bindi.
nicola-arigliano.why_it_matters: The original Via Asiago 10 / Twilight Music album catalog personally credits original vocals on classic American jazz standards and supplies original radio arrangements.

evidence.claim: Clean Feed credits Mitchell with flute, alto flute and piccolo on Ain't Nothing But a Cyber Coup & You.
The album credits Marty Ehrlich on clarinets and alto sax, Keir GoGwilt on violin, and Jim Black on drums and percussion.

nicole-mitchell.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
nicole-mitchell.summary: Flutist Nicole Mitchell played on Mark Dresser Seven's Ain't Nothing But a Cyber Coup & You with Marty Ehrlich, Jim Black and an expanded horn-and-strings group.
nicole-mitchell.why_it_matters: Her multiple flutes broaden the colors of creative ensemble jazz.

evidence.claim: Warner Classics lists Kennedy Meets Gershwin among his releases.
Warner Classics describes SHHH! as a 2010 Kennedy Quintet release of mainly original compositions.

nigel-kennedy.limitations: Primarily classical; do not classify his complete discography as jazz.
nigel-kennedy.summary: British violinist Nigel Kennedy records classical concertos and jazz projects; his Kennedy Meets Gershwin release and SHHH! album show his improvising interests.
nigel-kennedy.why_it_matters: Shows a classical violinist branching into Gershwin and improvised music.

evidence.claim: Edition Records credits Nikki Iles on piano with Martin Speake, Duncan Hopkins and Anthony Michelli for Bloor Street in 2010.
The Bloor Street original credits identify Moonbeam, Unit Six and Salem House as Nikki Iles compositions.
Edition Records credits Iles as composer, conductor and arranger on NDR Bigband's Face to Face, recorded in Hamburg in 2021 and 2022.
In an original ECM interview, Norma Winstone identifies Nikki Iles as her regular pianist for British performances.

identity_resolution.method: Independent exact-person corroboration across a conservatoire profile, an original record-label release, and an artist interview published by a separate record label.
identity_resolution.note: The Royal Academy of Music profile identifies jazz pianist Nikki Iles through the Secret Quartet's Bloor Street and NDR Bigband work, consistent with Edition Records and ECM's testimony. MBID collision remains unresolved; no arbitrary MBID chosen. These authorities corroborate the person without asserting a database identifier match.

nikki-iles.limitations: Queue marks Nikki Iles ambiguous; exact identity is independently supported by the two Edition label releases and ECM's first-person Norma Winstone testimony, without assigning an MBID.
nikki-iles.summary: British pianist Nikki Iles wrote and played three pieces for the Secret Quartet's Bloor Street and later composed and arranged Face to Face for NDR Bigband.
nikki-iles.why_it_matters: Two original Edition Records releases establish exact compositions, instruments and a cross-format transition from a quartet to large-ensemble arranging.

evidence.claim: Cecilie Grundt's Live at Dokkhuset was recorded March 29, 2019 in Trondheim and released May 1, 2024.
The credited guest Nils-Olav Johansen plays guitar, banjo and vocals with Grundt on reeds, Oyvind Froberg Mathisen on trumpet and Havard Aufles on piano.

nils-olav-johansen.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
nils-olav-johansen.summary: Norwegian guitarist and vocalist Nils-Olav Johansen joined Cecilie Grundt Quintet at Dokkhuset in March 2019 on guitar, banjo and voice.
nils-olav-johansen.why_it_matters: A versatile Norwegian guitarist spanning modern ensemble jazz, banjo and vocal improvisation.

evidence.claim: The Black Ark dates to 1969 and credits Howard as composer
Recorded with Arthur Doyle, Muhammad Ali and Norris Jones/Sirone

noah-howard.limitations: Source-specific musical details; does not establish exhaustive discography.
noah-howard.summary: Free-jazz alto saxophonist Noah Howard led 'The Black Ark' (1969), a fiery ensemble with Arthur Doyle, Muhammad Ali and bassist Sirone.
noah-howard.why_it_matters: A leader of the 1960s American free-jazz second wave with visceral ensemble improvisation

evidence.claim: Sissle and Eubie Blake co-wrote Shuffle Along, staged on Broadway in 1921.
Lena Horne sang with Sissle's orchestra in the mid-1930s.

noble-sissle.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
noble-sissle.summary: Singer-bandleader Noble Sissle collaborated with Eubie Blake on the 1921 Broadway musical Shuffle Along and later led an orchestra that featured Lena Horne.
noble-sissle.why_it_matters: His stage and dance-band work opened doors for Black jazz entertainers.

evidence.claim: Norway's National Library preserves the original RCA 78 rpm issue Tango for to / Sonnavindvalsen, dated February 19, 1957, crediting Brockstedt as singer with Egil Monn-Iversen's orchestra.

The library catalogs Nora Brockstedt: 1956-1957 Pa svensk with Swedish songs including Tango for tva and Karleksbrev i sanden, and lists Normann's 2015 compilation separately from the historic performances.
The National Library's jazz seminar program singled out Brockstedt and Monica Zetterlund as vocalists bringing jazz inflection into Nordic popular song.

nora-brockstedt.limitations: The 2015 Normann issue gathers recordings labelled 1956-57; 2015 is the reissue date. Brockstedt's music also includes popular song and is not exclusively jazz.
nora-brockstedt.summary: Norwegian singer Nora Brockstedt recorded Tango for to for RCA in 1957 with Egil Monn-Iversen's orchestra and later released a Swedish-language repertoire.
nora-brockstedt.why_it_matters: The National Library of Norway archives a dated original RCA shellac release and distinctly catalogs a later Swedish-recordings collection.

evidence.claim: Blue Note confirms the original Come Away With Me was released February 26 2002 and the final original album was produced by Arif Mardin.
The label describes the early recordings made with producer Craig Street at Allaire Studios and notes that most of those sessions appeared first on the 2022 anniversary deluxe edition.

norah-jones.limitations: Blue Note explicitly says the crossover debut was not strictly a jazz album; the 2022 anniversary edition and previously unreleased Craig Street recordings are not 2002 original releases.
norah-jones.summary: Pianist and singer Norah Jones released the Blue Note debut Come Away With Me in February 2002; Arif Mardin produced the final original album.
norah-jones.why_it_matters: Blue Notes label archive reconstructs sessions and names the original versus twenty-year expanded retrospective versions.

evidence.claim: Ajazz credits Norbert Gottschalk with vocals beside Rolf Marx on guitar and German Klaiber on bass for Songs in the Key of Jazz, catalog A538.
Ajazz assigns Matthias Nadolny's tenor saxophone specifically to tracks 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7, rather than claiming he plays on the entire album.
Gottschalk's official discography distinguishes his 2011 Solo album, 2013 Stars and the 2022 Songs in the Key of Jazz trio project.

norbert-gottschalk.limitations: The Ajazz catalog lists copyright 2021 whereas the artist website identifies a 2022 CD: publication dating remains unresolved. Recordings of compositions by others do not imply Gottschalk wrote those songs.
norbert-gottschalk.summary: German jazz vocalist Norbert Gottschalk made the trio album Songs in the Key of Jazz with guitarist Rolf Marx and bassist German Klaiber.
norbert-gottschalk.why_it_matters: The original Ajazz label identifies player and track-specific tenor sax credits; the singer's discography independently documents earlier solo and duo releases.

evidence.claim: His official biography lists WDR Big Band productions in 1996.
His official biography states a jazz guitar teaching appointment at Mainz starting in 1997.

norbert-scholly.summary: German jazz guitarist Norbert Scholly worked with the WDR Big Band and began teaching jazz guitar at Mainz University in 1997.
norbert-scholly.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: The original Commodore 1521 disc Rockin' Chair / Pitchin' a Bit Short lists Norma Teagarden among the credited recording artists, with a 1944 recording year.
A separate 1944 Commodore 592 shellac artifact Big T Blues / Chinatown, My Chinatown again lists Norma with Jack Teagarden's Swingin' Gates and Max Kaminsky.
Smithsonian's original Jazz Oral History archive preserves three Norma Teagarden DAT cassettes dated February 19-22, 1993.

norma-teagarden.limitations: The Smithsonian discs list her as a recording artist without a track-specific piano-solo annotation; the 1993 oral history is an interview, not a music recording. No precise 1944 session days stated.
norma-teagarden.summary: Pianist Norma Teagarden appeared on two 1944 Jack Teagarden and His Swingin' Gates Commodore discs and later recorded a jazz oral history for Smithsonian.
norma-teagarden.why_it_matters: Smithsonian retains separate original Commodore shellac objects with exact side titles, plus dated original historical interview recordings.

evidence.claim: ECM states that Winstone wrote new words for film music by composers including Morricone and Nino Rota on Descansado.
The album was recorded at ArteSuono Studio in Udine in March 2017 with pianist Glauco Venier, reed player Klaus Gesing, percussionist Helge Norbakken and cellist Mario Brunello.

norma-winstone.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
norma-winstone.summary: British jazz vocalist Norma Winstone recorded Descansado in March 2017 with Klaus Gesing, Glauco Venier and guests Norbakken and Brunello.
norma-winstone.why_it_matters: Vocal improvisation meets movie themes and newly written lyrics in a chamber-jazz setting.

evidence.claim: The International Archives for the Jazz Organ identifies Brown on organ for the Cadet Raising the Roof LP, catalog LPS-775, with saxophonists Artee Payne and Thomas Purvis and drummer Curtis Prince.
The same organ archive dates Raising the Roof to a July 1966 Chicago session and identifies the group's 1967 Cadet Mellow Yellow LP as catalog LPS-788.
The archive separately documents Brown as organist in a Chicago April 1966 session with alto saxophonists Sonny Stitt and Bunky Green and drummer Maurice White.

odell-brown.limitations: The jazz organ archive is a historical specialist reconstruction rather than a direct Chess master ledger; Cadet release dates are separate from recording dates, and the lineup may vary between releases.
odell-brown.summary: Organist Odell Brown formed the Organ-Izers and recorded the 1966 Cadet LP Raising the Roof and the 1967 follow-up Mellow Yellow.
odell-brown.why_it_matters: The specialist International Archives for the Jazz Organ reproduces original Cadet catalog numbers, recording years and organ-group instrumental personnel.

evidence.claim: Talmor co-led the Lee Konitz Nonet, Konitz-Talmor String Project and Konitz-Talmor Big Band.
Back to the Land features bassist Chris Tordini and drummer Eric McPherson.
His Double Concerto premiered in Porto in February 2010 with Jason Moran and Dan Weiss.

ohad-talmor.limitations: Artist autobiography details groups, not individual release personnel beyond stated ensembles.
ohad-talmor.summary: Tenor saxophonist Ohad Talmor co-led three projects with Lee Konitz. His Back to the Land group explores newly discovered Ornette Coleman material.
ohad-talmor.why_it_matters: His projects link modern jazz improvisation to orchestral composition.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Temiz on percussion for Dona Nostra, recorded at Oslo's Rainbow Studio in March 1993 and released on March 1, 1994.
Temiz shares composition credit on Fort Cherry, Arrows and Ahayu-Da alongside Don Cherry, Lennart Aberg, Bobo Stenson, Anders Jormin and Anders Kjellberg.

okay-temiz.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
okay-temiz.summary: Turkish percussionist Okay Temiz played on Don Cherry's Dona Nostra, recorded in Oslo in March 1993 with Bobo Stenson and Lennart Aberg.
okay-temiz.why_it_matters: His percussion and co-improvisation link Turkish rhythmic practice with European free jazz.

evidence.claim: The artist's December Songs page credits Olga Konkova on piano and Jens Thoresen on guitar, production and recording.
The album documentation dates the Losen Records release to 2017 and lists Konkova as arranger on Away in Manger, Du Gronne Glitrende Tre and other tracks.

olga-konkova.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
olga-konkova.summary: Russian-born Norwegian jazz pianist Olga Konkova recorded the piano-guitar duo December Songs with Jens Thoresen, originally issued in 2017.
olga-konkova.why_it_matters: Small-scale Scandinavian jazz arranging reframes Christmas standards as intimate duo music.

evidence.claim: The official Fly Now credits list Trummer on vocals, piano, Rhodes, Hammond and Wurly, with Kurt Rosenwinkel on guitar on tracks 3, 6 and 10.
The release is dated 2014; studio sessions took place in Brooklyn in July 2013 and Berlin in November 2013; all music and lyrics are credited to Trummer.

olivia-trummer.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
olivia-trummer.summary: German pianist and vocalist Olivia Trummer recorded Fly Now in New York and Berlin in 2013 with bassist Matt Penman and guest Kurt Rosenwinkel.
olivia-trummer.why_it_matters: A contemporary pianist mixing her own songs with modern jazz harmony and varied keyboards.

evidence.claim: QANTAR was released April 15, 2018 and credits Omer Avital on bass and compositions with pianist Eden Ladin and drummer Ofri Nehemya.
The album credits Alexander Levin on tenor saxophone and Asaf Yuria on soprano and tenor saxophone, and the project notes date the band's founding to 2016.

omer-avital.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
omer-avital.summary: Israeli bassist Omer Avital formed Qantar in 2016 and released its self-titled quintet album in 2018 with two saxophones, piano and drums.
omer-avital.why_it_matters: Brooklyn jazz ensemble connects improvising horns and Avital's Middle Eastern-rooted compositions.

evidence.claim: Simeon recorded with Jelly Roll Morton in 1926 and 1928, including Black Bottom Stomp.
Simeon joined Earl Hines's big band in 1931 and stayed for six years.

omer-simeon.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
omer-simeon.summary: Clarinetist Omer Simeon recorded with Jelly Roll Morton in 1926 and 1928, then played in Earl Hines's big band and Wilbur DeParis's New Orleans ensemble.
omer-simeon.why_it_matters: His fluid clarinet linked classic New Orleans recordings with big-band swing.

evidence.claim: The November 3, 2025 release PAPOLEO explicitly credits Orlando Poleo with quitipla and congas as a featured performer.
Its composition is credited to Paoli Mejias; Gabriel Chakarji arranged the track and plays piano and electric keyboard.

orlando-poleo.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
orlando-poleo.summary: Venezuelan conga player Orlando Poleo performs on Paoli Mejias's 2025 PAPOLEO, adding quitipla and congas to the Latin-jazz arrangement.
orlando-poleo.why_it_matters: Connects Afro-Venezuelan percussion techniques with contemporary Afro-Caribbean jazz.

evidence.claim: Smoke Sessions describes Evans leading the quartet with Vicente Archer on bass, Bill Stewart on drums and Immanuel Wilkins on alto saxophone on The Magic of Now.
Smoke Sessions identifies The Captain Black Big Band's Presence as a live recording at Chris' Jazz Cafe and South Kitchen and Jazz Parlor in Philadelphia.
Jazz at Lincoln Center lists Evans as pianist in a March 2025 quartet with Robert Hurst and Jeff Tain Watts, with guest vocalist Lisa Fischer.

identity_resolution.method: Independent identity triangulation between original record-label discographies, an original jazz concert presenter, and a university jazz-program event.
identity_resolution.note: All three independently identify the same Philadelphia jazz pianist Orrin Evans: Smoke Sessions as a recording bandleader, Jazz at Lincoln Center as a performing pianist, and Temple University as the pianist, composer and Imani Records founder. The ambiguous queue MBID collision remains unresolved; no arbitrary MBID chosen or assigned.

orrin-evans.limitations: Queue classifies this name as ambiguous. Distinct original institutional authorities identify the same Philadelphia pianist; reciprocal MBID remains unresolved and no arbitrary MBID is asserted.
orrin-evans.summary: Jazz pianist Orrin Evans recorded The Magic of Now with Vicente Archer, Bill Stewart and Immanuel Wilkins and led the Captain Black Big Band.
orrin-evans.why_it_matters: Original Smoke Sessions releases document separate small-group and big-band recordings; three independent institutions establish exact identity.

evidence.claim: MPS identifies Oscar Klein on trumpet in the reunited Tremble Kids group on The Tremble Kids Are Back, released in 1972, and describes his solo on Collier's Clambake.
MPS credits Klein as the trumpet and guitar player in Fatty George's 1978 Chicago Jazz Band sextet, alongside drummer Charly Antolini.
MPS documents Klein's muted and open trumpet on Big Butter and Egg Man in the Tremble Kids' Midnight Session, whose release entry gives March 12, 1973.

oscar-klein.limitations: MPS album release years do not guarantee the precise recording dates. Klein's guitar playing on Fatty '78 must not be generalized to every track.
oscar-klein.summary: Austrian trumpeter Oscar Klein played in the Tremble Kids revival on MPS and appeared with clarinetist Fatty George and singer Miriam Klein.
oscar-klein.why_it_matters: Three distinct original MPS releases provide exact ensemble roles, instrumental solos and the boundaries of separate sessions.

evidence.claim: Jaco Pastorius's official archive credits Othello Molineaux and Leroy Williams on steel drums on the self-titled album, released by Epic in 1976.
The Jaco Pastorius Epic discography assigns Molineaux and Leroy Williams to steel drums on Opus Pocus, with Wayne Shorter on soprano sax and Herbie Hancock on keys.
Pastorius's Word of Mouth recording (August 1980, issued 1981) credits Molineaux and Leroy Williams with steel drums on Liberty City.

othello-molineaux.limitations: Specific original session and track credits; not a complete discography.
othello-molineaux.summary: Steel-pan player Othello Molineaux recorded Opus Pocus on Jaco Pastorius' 1976 solo debut and Liberty City on Word of Mouth, issued in 1981.
othello-molineaux.why_it_matters: Credited steel-pan performances introduce Caribbean timbres within Pastorius's electric jazz ensemble music.

evidence.claim: Ground-Zero discography includes Consume Red (1997)
Otomo led Ground-Zero through the 1990s

otomo-yoshihide.limitations: Source-specific musical details, not a complete discography.
otomo-yoshihide.summary: Japanese guitarist Otomo Yoshihide led Ground-Zero's 'Consume Red' (1997), building collective noise improvisation around sampled traditional Korean music.
otomo-yoshihide.why_it_matters: Cut-up turntables and radical ensemble improvisation with international experimental music

evidence.claim: Liebert's official biography dates the first Luna Negra band to 1989.
His biography says Marita: Shadows and Storms was reissued as Nouveau Flamenco by Higher Octave.

ottmar-liebert.limitations: Official site offers multiple historical bio revisions; selects the 2022 history.
ottmar-liebert.summary: German-born guitarist Ottmar Liebert founded Luna Negra in 1989 and released Nouveau Flamenco after a self-produced Santa Fe recording.
ottmar-liebert.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: Hardwick left Duke Ellington's orchestra in 1928 and traveled to Europe.
Hardwick returned to Ellington in 1932, played there until 1946 and co-composed Sophisticated Lady.

otto-hardwick.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
otto-hardwick.summary: Alto saxophonist Otto Hardwick was an early Duke Ellington colleague, left the orchestra in 1928, returned in 1932 and stayed until 1946.
otto-hardwick.why_it_matters: His lyrical alto helped establish early Ellington reed-section identity.

evidence.claim: GLOW was recorded March 1-3, 2010 at Deutschlandfunk Kammermusiksaal and released February 17, 2011.
The GLOW credits include harpist Kathrin Pechlof, bassist Robert Landfermann, drummer Jonas Burgwinkel and saxophonists Sebastian Gille and Niels Klein.

pablo-held.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
pablo-held.summary: German pianist Pablo Held expanded his trio into a ten-piece ensemble for GLOW, recording the sessions in March 2010 for a February 2011 release.
pablo-held.why_it_matters: Cologne compositional jazz blends intricate ensemble voicings with collective improvisation.

evidence.claim: Milner's official biography says he became keyboardist for Tom Jones after working with Jack Bruce.
The official site identifies him as a member of Jawbone and co-founder of Ronnie Scott's Blues Explosion.

paddy-milner.limitations: Official artist account, no session-level credits claimed.
paddy-milner.summary: British pianist and songwriter Paddy Milner plays blues and New Orleans piano, performing with Tom Jones and the group Jawbone.
paddy-milner.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: The University of Colorado Glenn Miller Collections' Jubilee 227 catalog lists the September 1947 concert and credits Page Cavanaugh on piano and vocals, Al Viola on guitar and vocals, and Lloyd Pratt on string bass and vocals.
The Smithsonian National Museum of American History catalogs a Page Cavanaugh Trio Armed Forces Radio Service disc featuring Baby All the Time, How Cute Can You Be, Man With a Horn and Yesterdays.

Scott Yanow's AllMusic biography reports that Cavanaugh met guitarist Al Viola and bassist Lloyd Pratt during military service, and that their swing trio became popular in the second half of the 1940s.

page-cavanaugh.limitations: The Colorado URL serves a verified, accessible archival PDF despite lacking a PDF extension. Smithsonian's object page timed out and AllMusic's direct page returned 403; its biographical passage was independently visible in indexed search results. Smithsonian track details were retained from the earlier research draft, not newly reopened.
page-cavanaugh.summary: Pianist and singer Page Cavanaugh led a swing trio with guitarist Al Viola and bassist Lloyd Pratt, heard on 1947 Armed Forces Radio concerts.
page-cavanaugh.why_it_matters: The University of Colorado's AFRS Jubilee catalog documents the 1947 concert personnel; Smithsonian preserves a radio disc with named repertoire, while Scott Yanow's AllMusic biography describes the trio's military origins.

evidence.claim: Royal Albert Hall lists Faith with Guy Barker Jazz Orchestra at the 5 September 2014 Proms.
The performance used a 42-piece jazz orchestra and fresh arrangements of her albums.

paloma-faith.limitations: Primarily soul and pop; one big-band concert does not make her a jazz specialist.
paloma-faith.summary: British soul and pop singer Paloma Faith performed in the 2014 BBC Proms with Guy Barker's Jazz Orchestra and the Urban Voices Collective, using orchestral arrangements.
paloma-faith.why_it_matters: A verified example of pop vocals crossing into orchestral big-band work.

evidence.claim: Paolo Conte's official biography says he played vibraphone in local Asti jazz groups as a young musician.
The artist's official biography identifies Azzurro, sung by Adriano Celentano, among Conte's compositions from the 1960s.
The official biography dates the album Paris Milonga to 1981 and the double album Aguaplano to 1987.

paolo-conte.limitations: Conte's mature career encompasses Italian songwriting and theatre, beyond strict jazz; the official PDF's page screenshot was blocked by a challenge, though extracted text was accessible.
paolo-conte.summary: Italian songwriter Paolo Conte first played jazz vibraphone in Asti, wrote Azzurro for Adriano Celentano and later recorded Paris Milonga and Aguaplano.
paolo-conte.why_it_matters: Conte's official artist biography documents his early jazz playing, writing for other singers and dated recordings under his own name.

evidence.claim: Smithsonian Folkways documents Celestin's Original Tuxedo Orchestra, first recordings in 1925 and postwar weekly radio broadcasts.
Original Arhoolie track credits identify Celestin singing and playing trumpet on Panama with trombonist Bill Mathews and clarinetist Alphonse Picou.
Smithsonian credits Celestin's French-language Eh, La Bas in the same band and identifies the full sextet.

papa-celestin.limitations: The 1996 Arhoolie release date is a reissue; the radio performances are from the early 1950s.
papa-celestin.summary: New Orleans trumpeter and singer Papa Celestin led the Tuxedo Jazz Band, first recorded in 1925 and returned to nationally broadcast performances after World War II.
papa-celestin.why_it_matters: Smithsonian's Arhoolie archive preserves original band recordings and identifies individual trumpeter-vocalist and collaborator credits.

evidence.claim: The Canadian Jazz Archive says LaBarbera toured for seven years with the Buddy Rich band.
It records a 2000 Juno for his album Deep in a Dream.

pat-labarbera.limitations: Archive contains some dated career descriptions; historical events chosen.
pat-labarbera.summary: Saxophonist Pat LaBarbera toured with Buddy Rich's band before moving to Toronto in 1974. He later worked with Elvin Jones and won a Juno for Deep in a Dream.
pat-labarbera.why_it_matters: Bridges American big-band touring and Toronto's jazz scene.

evidence.claim: Pat Martino recorded 'El Hombre' in May 1967 with organist Trudy Pitts and Latin percussionists.
The session features organist Trudy Pitts and Latin percussionists.

pat-martino.limitations: Research is source-specific; credits denote actual documented roles, not an exhaustive discography.
pat-martino.summary: Guitarist Pat Martino's leader debut 'El Hombre' (1967) featured Trudy Pitts on organ and Latin percussion, an early soul-jazz guitar statement.
pat-martino.why_it_matters: Groove-driven soul-jazz guitar with Latin rhythmic color.

evidence.claim: Moraz formed Refugee with Lee Jackson and Brian Davison and recorded an album in 1974.
He joined Yes in 1974 and remained until 1976.
Moraz and drummer Greg Alban released The M.A.P. Project in 2015.

patrick-moraz.limitations: Artist page includes self-reported reminiscences; avoided disputed birth location.
patrick-moraz.summary: Swiss keyboardist Patrick Moraz formed the group Refugee and recorded its 1974 album before joining Yes. His later work included the Moody Blues and the Moraz Alban Project.
patrick-moraz.why_it_matters: Moraz's jazz-trained keyboard style moves between progressive rock and improvisation.

evidence.claim: Bown toured Europe as pianist in Quincy Jones's big band in 1959 for Free and Easy.
Bown worked on recordings with Gene Ammons and accompanied Dinah Washington.

patti-bown.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
patti-bown.summary: Seattle pianist Patti Bown joined Quincy Jones's 1959 European big-band tour for Free and Easy; she also recorded with Gene Ammons and accompanied Dinah Washington.
patti-bown.why_it_matters: A significant woman pianist whose jazz work crossed big bands and vocal sessions.

evidence.claim: New Orleans drummer Paul Barbarin wrote 'Bourbon Street Parade', which he recorded for Atlantic in January 1955.
The foundation describes Barbarin's Atlantic January 7 1955 recording and ensemble.

paul-barbarin.limitations: Research is source-specific; credits denote actual documented roles, not an exhaustive discography.
paul-barbarin.summary: Drummer Paul Barbarin wrote New Orleans standard 'Bourbon Street Parade'; his Atlantic recording of January 1955 pairs parade rhythm with jazz improvisation.
paul-barbarin.why_it_matters: New Orleans parade drums meeting collective jazz lines.

evidence.claim: Bridging credits Dunmall and Simon Picard on tenor saxophones, Gethin Liddington on trumpet and Paul Rutherford on trombone.
Clean Feed says the octet recorded Bridging live at Jazz em Agosto, a festival of the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation.

paul-dunmall.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
paul-dunmall.summary: Saxophonist Paul Dunmall led an octet on Bridging, recorded live at the Jazz em Agosto festival with Keith Tippett, Paul Rutherford and other improvisers.
paul-dunmall.why_it_matters: His writing connects post-bop forms with extended free improvisations.

evidence.claim: Route 66's Creole Gal reissue notes identify Gayten's 1947 De Luxe single True and his jazz-influenced blues piano style.
The El Toro Ain't Nothing Happenin' collection documents performances by Gayten and Annie Laurie together on I'll Never Be Free and I Ain't Gotta Let You In.
The same reissue's original label history identifies Gayten's production work with Clarence Frogman Henry, Larry Darnell and Bobby Charles.

paul-gayten.limitations: These are R&B and blues recordings with jazz influences; the available album history does not establish Gayten as pianist on every assembled track.
paul-gayten.summary: New Orleans pianist and bandleader Paul Gayten recorded the 1947 De Luxe hit True, led Annie Laurie's band and produced later Chess-associated R&B singles.
paul-gayten.why_it_matters: Original Route 66 and El Toro retrospective label notes preserve named singles and his combined roles as pianist, bandleader and producer.

evidence.claim: Hanmer formed Unofficial Language with drummer Ian Herman and bassist Peter Sklair and the trio recorded Primal Steps in 1994.
Unofficial Language made its second album Move Moves in 1996, according to Hanmer's career archive.
Sheer Sound released Hanmer's first leader album Trains to Taung in 1997 with Denis Lalouette and Louis Mhlanga among his collaborators.

paul-hanmer.limitations: The artist biography gives dates for original recordings; later digital store dates must not be mistaken for those sessions.
paul-hanmer.summary: South African pianist Paul Hanmer recorded two Unofficial Language trio albums in 1994 and 1996 and led Trains to Taung in 1997.
paul-hanmer.why_it_matters: The musician's own documented ensemble history ties original recording years, personnel and his leader debut.

evidence.claim: Blue Note describes his R&B session work in the 1970s and 1980s.
Its biography states he gained an Atlantic solo recording deal in 1986.

paul-jackson-jr.limitations: The label page does not establish exact guitar parts on individual songs.
paul-jackson-jr.summary: Los Angeles guitarist Paul Jackson Jr. recorded in R&B sessions for artists including the Temptations and Luther Vandross before launching a solo career on Atlantic.
paul-jackson-jr.why_it_matters: Connects jazz guitar with soul studio recording and crossover instrumentals.

evidence.claim: Lytton plays percussion and live electronics while Wachsmann plays violin, viola and live electronics.
Some Other Season was recorded October 1997 at Hardstudios, Winterthur, and released January 11, 1999.

paul-lytton.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
paul-lytton.summary: Percussionist Paul Lytton recorded Some Other Season with violinist Philipp Wachsmann in Winterthur in October 1997, and ECM issued the duo in 1999.
paul-lytton.why_it_matters: Percussion and live processing intersect in his European improvised duos.

evidence.claim: Clean Feed credits Paul Rutherford and Malcolm Griffiths on trombones for the Paul Dunmall Octet release Bridging.
The Bridging octet also includes Keith Tippett on piano, Paul Rogers on bass and Tony Levin on drums; it was recorded live at Jazz em Agosto.

paul-rutherford.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
paul-rutherford.summary: Trombonist Paul Rutherford joined Paul Dunmall's Bridging octet with Keith Tippett, Gethin Liddington and Tony Levin for a live Jazz em Agosto recording.
paul-rutherford.why_it_matters: His trombone helped define British free jazz across large and small ensembles.

evidence.claim: Concord's Daydream credits explicitly list Paul Smith on piano among Karrin Allyson's accompanying musicians.
Concord also credits Smith on piano for Karrin Allyson's Sweet Home Cookin'.
The 1979 Montreux Digital III anthology includes Paul Smith among the contributing Pablo-label musicians.

paul-smith.limitations: Compilation credits from Montreux cover multiple bands, so they do not pinpoint Smith's specific stage set.
paul-smith.summary: Jazz pianist Paul Smith accompanied Karrin Allyson on multiple Concord albums including Daydream and Sweet Home Cookin' and worked at Montreux.
paul-smith.why_it_matters: Multiple original Concord release credits identify Smith's instrument and separate recording contexts for vocal accompaniment.

evidence.claim: Smithsonian's original Bluebird artifact lists Kelly and the Four Modernaires as vocalists on I Know Why with Glenn Miller and His Orchestra.
A second Bluebird artifact in Smithsonian's Harry Warren Papers credits Kelly with Ray Eberle, Tex Beneke and the Modernaires for It Happened in Sun Valley.
The paired Bluebird recording credits Kelly and Ernie Caceres in the vocals for The Kiss Polka; a separate damaged commercial disc is also preserved.

paula-kelly.limitations: Original Bluebird catalog artifacts do not provide precise session days. These are recorded singer credits, not songwriting credits; the Smithsonian archive should not be used to assign Kelly to the other disc side.
paula-kelly.summary: Big-band singer Paula Kelly sang on Glenn Miller's Bluebird records I Know Why, It Happened in Sun Valley and The Kiss Polka with the Modernaires.
paula-kelly.why_it_matters: The Smithsonian's Harry Warren Papers preserve separate original Bluebird recording artifacts and name Kelly individually rather than inferring her voice from group membership.

evidence.claim: The artist says he founded the South Quartet in 2013 and later developed it into his eXtensions project.
His site dates the founding of electroacoustic duo Dark Fader with Roald Baudoux to 2009.

peer-baierlein.limitations: Only claims recorded in the cited artist, label, institution or original archive are included; crossovers are not classified exclusively as jazz.
peer-baierlein.summary: German trumpeter and composer Peer Baierlein leads the South Quartet and writes scores for theater, chamber groups and electroacoustic duo Dark Fader.
peer-baierlein.why_it_matters: Documents specific recordings, ensembles or performance roles and their place in jazz or adjacent genres.

evidence.claim: CSUN University Library identifies Peggy Gilbert as a jazz saxophonist who organized all-female ensembles from the 1930s.
The library says Gilbert founded her Dixie Belles group at age 69 and that it toured across the US between 1974 and 1996.
CSUN reports that its Peggy Gilbert Collection preserves scrapbooks, scores, flyers, clippings and her Sex or Sax memoir notebook.

peggy-gilbert.limitations: The archive describes US touring dates but does not verify the lineups of every concert by the Dixie Belles.
peggy-gilbert.summary: Jazz saxophonist Peggy Gilbert formed all-women bands in the 1930s and later led the Dixie Belles, which toured US jazz events from 1974 to 1996.
peggy-gilbert.why_it_matters: California State University Northridge holds original scrapbooks, scores and programs documenting her bands and musicians' union work.

evidence.claim: Her official biography says she played with salsa bands Azteca and Supercombo in San Francisco.
The biography records collaborations with Lee Konitz, Gerry Mulligan and Emily Remler.

peggy-stern.limitations: Artist biography supports these broad credits; no track-by-track session personnel inferred.
peggy-stern.summary: American jazz pianist Peggy Stern combines improvised jazz with Latin grooves and played in San Francisco salsa bands.
peggy-stern.why_it_matters: Documents a distinctive jazz crossover artist with artist-authored album or ensemble facts.

evidence.claim: Adams recorded with Paul Chambers and John Coltrane in 1955.
Adams began working with Donald Byrd in 1958 and later co-led a band with him.

pepper-adams.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
pepper-adams.summary: Baritone saxophonist Pepper Adams worked with Kenny Burrell and Paul Chambers in 1955, moved to New York in 1956 and began extensive recording with Donald Byrd in 1958.
pepper-adams.why_it_matters: He brought agile hard-bop lines to the usually weighty baritone saxophone.

evidence.claim: The artist archive dates Velodromer to May 6, 2005 and credits solo piano and production to Per Henrik Wallin.
The studio recordings were made May 12, 2004 and January 16, 2005 by Ingemar Johansson; all works but track three are attributed to Wallin.

per-henrik-wallin.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
per-henrik-wallin.summary: Swedish free-jazz pianist Per Henrik Wallin recorded his final solo album Velodromer across two sessions in 2004 and 2005.
per-henrik-wallin.why_it_matters: An uncompromising Swedish improviser joining original forms with playful free-piano phrasing.

evidence.claim: Zanussi Five's debut album was released February 12, 2005 and credits Per Zanussi on double bass and production.
The three saxophonists are Eirik Hegdal, Kjetil Moster and Rolf-Erik Nystrom; the drummer is Per Oddvar Johansen, credited as Per Oddvar Johan on the release.

per-zanussi.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
per-zanussi.summary: Norwegian bassist Per Zanussi led the three-saxophone quintet Zanussi Five, whose self-titled debut appeared in February 2005.
per-zanussi.why_it_matters: A distinct Norwegian free-jazz ensemble with arranged themes and multiple saxophone voices.

evidence.claim: The National Endowment for the Arts names Percy Heath its 2002 Jazz Master and documents his main instrument as bass.
Its Jazz Masters biography puts Heath in Dizzy Gillespie sextet from 1950 to 1952 and dates the Modern Jazz Quartet beginning to 1952, with Milt Jackson, John Lewis and Kenny Clarke.
The NEA selected discography lists the Heath Brothers Marchin On! on Strata-East in 1976 and Modern Jazz Quartet Celebration on Atlantic in 1992.

percy-heath.limitations: MJQ membership is a long-running career credit, not proof that every album has the same drummer; the NEA list labels 1952-55 a range, not one session date.
percy-heath.summary: Bassist Percy Heath joined Dizzy Gillespie in 1950 and became a founding member of the Modern Jazz Quartet in 1952 with John Lewis and Milt Jackson.
percy-heath.why_it_matters: The federal NEA Jazz Masters biography distinguishes his MJQ tenure from the later Heath Brothers ensemble and provides dated records.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Percy Jones on bass alongside Shankar on 10-string double violin, Caroline on vocals and tamboura, and Steve Vai on guitar.
The Epidemics was recorded February 1985 at Stickwork Studios, New York, and first released January 1, 1986.

percy-jones.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
percy-jones.summary: Bassist Percy Jones joined Shankar and Caroline on The Epidemics, a 1985 studio session featuring 10-string double violin and electronic textures.
percy-jones.why_it_matters: His electric-bass sound connects progressive fusion with experimental studio jazz.

evidence.claim: Como signed to RCA Victor in 1943.
His 1945 hit 'Til the End of Time adapted Chopin's Polonaise in A-flat.
Catch a Falling Star earned the first Grammy for Best Male Vocalist in 1958.

perry-como.limitations: Hall of Fame institutional profile; primarily popular music, not a pure-jazz card.
perry-como.summary: Crooner Perry Como recorded for RCA Victor after signing in 1943. He scored a 1945 hit with 'Til the End of Time and won a Grammy for Catch a Falling Star.
perry-como.why_it_matters: His big-band era singing became a prominent pop standard, adjacent to vocal jazz.

evidence.claim: Smithsonian Folkways' Keyhole Blues track credits Pete Briggs on tuba in Louis Armstrong's Hot Seven with Johnny Dodds, Johnny St. Cyr, Lillian Hardin Armstrong and Baby Dodds.
Jazz Education Network's original instructional notes identify Briggs on tuba for Potato Head Blues, recorded in 1927 and originally issued as Okeh 8503.
The same educational source identifies the cornet, clarinet, trombone, piano, banjo and drum performers surrounding Briggs on Potato Head Blues and analyzes the instrumental solos separately.

pete-briggs.limitations: Smithsonian's anthology years 1950 and 2011 are reissue years. Its broad West End Blues anthology personnel mix may span different Hot Five/Seven groups, so no Pete Briggs credit is inferred for that track.
pete-briggs.summary: Jazz tubist Pete Briggs played with Louis Armstrong's Hot Seven on the 1927 recordings Potato Head Blues and Keyhole Blues, supporting its early rhythm section.
pete-briggs.why_it_matters: Smithsonian original recording performer credits and Jazz Education Network's score notes establish track-specific tuba contributions and distinguish 1927 sessions from later anthology issue dates.

evidence.claim: Candoli played with the bands of Woody Herman and Stan Kenton.
He worked in Los Angeles television and film studios, including the Tonight Show band.
He formed a band with brother Conte and performed with it intermittently.

pete-candoli.limitations: Institutional archival overview; exact individual soundtrack credits not asserted.
pete-candoli.summary: Lead trumpeter Pete Candoli played in the Woody Herman and Stan Kenton big bands and worked in Los Angeles television and recording studios. He also led bands with brother Conte.
pete-candoli.why_it_matters: A high-register big-band specialist became a versatile screen and studio musician.

evidence.claim: Pianist Pete Jolly joined Shorty Rogers's West Coast jazz quintet in 1954.
The 1955 RCA album Jolly Jumps In featured Shelly Manne and Curtis Counce.

pete-jolly.limitations: Research is source-specific; credits denote actual documented roles, not an exhaustive discography.
pete-jolly.summary: West Coast pianist Pete Jolly joined Shorty Rogers's quintet in 1954 and recorded 'Jolly Jumps In' for RCA in 1955 with Shelly Manne and Curtis Counce.
pete-jolly.why_it_matters: West Coast piano, accordion and session-era small-group swing.

evidence.claim: Basra recorded May 19 1965 at Van Gelder studio
On Pete La Roca's 'Basra' (1965), Joe Henderson played tenor sax, Steve Kuhn piano and Steve Swallow bass.

pete-la-roca.limitations: Source-specific musical details; does not establish exhaustive discography.
pete-la-roca.summary: Drummer Pete La Roca led 'Basra' (Blue Note, 1965) with Joe Henderson, Steve Kuhn and Steve Swallow, exploring modal colors inside hard bop.
pete-la-roca.why_it_matters: Rhythmic post-bop experiment on a widely studied 1965 quartet session

evidence.claim: The Museum of Canadian Music catalogs Peter Appleyard's 1990 Concord jazz album Barbados Heat with eight tracks including Take the A Train, Nuages and Caravan.
The museum's Barbados Cool catalog identifies Appleyard on vibes with Bucky Pizzarelli on guitar, Major Holley on bass, Butch Miles on drums and Rick Wilkins on tenor sax.
Barbados Cool's original Concord track list includes Tangerine, Air Mail Special, Passion Flower and Cherokee in a ten-piece program.

peter-appleyard.limitations: The museum's stylistic comparisons are reviewers' opinions; dates refer to catalogued releases, not necessarily recording sessions.
peter-appleyard.summary: Vibraphonist Peter Appleyard led the 1990 Concord album Barbados Heat and the 1991 follow-up Barbados Cool with Bucky Pizzarelli and Butch Miles.
peter-appleyard.why_it_matters: The Museum of Canadian Music preserves two separately catalogued original Concord releases with specific repertoires and musicians.

evidence.claim: Criss Cross Jazz 1237 lists Peter Beets on piano, Larry Grenadier on bass and Willie Jones III on drums for New York Trio - Page Two, recorded in Brooklyn on December 16, 2002.
The Criss Cross original album page gives May 8, 2003 availability and credits For Simon, It Has Happened and In A Hazy Mood to Peter Beets, but Paradox to Sonny Rollins.

peter-beets.limitations: Specific source-reviewed session and personnel credits, not a complete discography.
peter-beets.summary: Dutch pianist Peter Beets recorded New York Trio - Page Two in Brooklyn on Dec. 16, 2002 with bassist Larry Grenadier and drummer Willie Jones III; released in 2003.
peter-beets.why_it_matters: Original Criss Cross documentation gives the precise piano-trio lineup and distinguishes Beets's compositions from Rollins and Jamal standards.

evidence.claim: Peter White official timeline records signing with Columbia Sony in 1995 and his fifth solo album Caravan of Dreams in 1996.
The same artist timeline says White joined the Guitars and Saxes touring project with Kirk Whalum, Marc Antoine and Rick Braun in 1996.

peter-white.limitations: Artist tour chronology dates the 1996 tour as a group event, not a claim of all four players recording together on Caravan of Dreams.
peter-white.summary: British smooth-jazz guitarist Peter White released Caravan of Dreams in 1996 after work with Al Stewart and toured with Guitars and Saxes.
peter-white.why_it_matters: Artist chronological autobiography documents original solo releases and concert collaborators across early smooth-jazz crossover years.

evidence.claim: Cohran remained in Chicago when Sun Ra relocated his Arkestra in 1961.
He helped establish the AACM in 1965 with Steve McCall, Muhal Richard Abrams and Jodie Christian.
He developed the Frankiphone, a modified electric thumb piano.

phil-cohran.limitations: AACM's institutional tribute gives the broad chronology; record dates excluded.
phil-cohran.summary: Trumpeter Phil Cohran worked with Sun Ra in Chicago and helped found the AACM in 1965. His Artistic Heritage Ensemble and Frankiphone pursued African-rooted sounds.
phil-cohran.why_it_matters: He helped connect independent Chicago jazz education with new ensembles and instruments.

evidence.claim: NAMM's oral-history archive says Harris began his career as a drummer around Bing Crosby and Paul Whiteman.
The archive says he began his Jack Benny Show bandleader role in 1936.

phil-harris.limitations: Comedic acting and animation are distinct from jazz recordings.
phil-harris.summary: Drummer, bandleader and singer Phil Harris led radio orchestras and played on The Jack Benny Show from 1936, later voicing Baloo in Disney's Jungle Book.
phil-harris.why_it_matters: Connects radio-era dance bands with popular entertainment.

evidence.claim: JazzInBelgium dates Catherine's joining Ponty's quintet to 1971.
The biography lists September Man among his mid-1970s leader albums.

philip-catherine.limitations: Research is source-specific; credits denote actual documented roles, not an exhaustive discography.
philip-catherine.summary: Belgian guitarist Philip Catherine joined Jean-Luc Ponty's quintet in 1971 and released 'September Man' in 1974, crossing swing and fusion.
philip-catherine.why_it_matters: European guitar phrasing across swing, jazz and fusion styles.

evidence.claim: Igloo's compilation notes identify Back to the Old World (IGL162, 2002) as Aerts's second leader album.
Its quartet personnel are Aerts on bass, Bert Joris on trumpet and flugelhorn, John Ruocco on tenor saxophone and clarinet, and Tony Levin on drums.

philippe-aerts.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
philippe-aerts.summary: Belgian bassist Philippe Aerts led the quartet recording Back to the Old World in 2002 with Bert Joris, John Ruocco and drummer Tony Levin.
philippe-aerts.why_it_matters: His unhurried bass leadership places Belgian jazz dialogue above virtuoso display.

evidence.claim: Ayler Records credits Deschepper and Noel Akchote on electric guitars, with recording on May 22-23, 2024 at Das Institut, Zurich.
Deschepper composed Miniature and Toy Train; the duo also plays pieces by Paul Motian, Ornette Coleman, Steve Swallow and Henri Texier.

philippe-deschepper.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
philippe-deschepper.summary: French electric guitarist Philippe Deschepper recorded MMXXIV AD in Zurich in May 2024 with fellow improvising guitarist Noel Akchote.
philippe-deschepper.why_it_matters: Electric guitar duet reinterprets jazz composers through collective free improvisation.

evidence.claim: The BnF authority identifies Cavalli as a Swiss jazz guitarist and popular orchestra leader.
BnF cites Feeling + finesse = jazz as a recording with Cavalli on electric guitar and Stephane Grappelli on violin.

pierre-cavalli.limitations: National Library authority metadata supports limited scope only.
pierre-cavalli.summary: Swiss jazz guitarist Pierre Cavalli led popular-music orchestras and recorded guitar with violinist Stephane Grappelli.
pierre-cavalli.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: Miles Davis official credits Michelot as bass in 1957
Recorded Ascenseur pour l'echafaud soundtrack

pierre-michelot.limitations: Specific sourced music facts, not a comprehensive discography.
pierre-michelot.summary: French bassist Pierre Michelot played on Miles Davis's improvised 'Ascenseur pour l'echafaud' film score (Paris, December 1957) with Kenny Clarke.
pierre-michelot.why_it_matters: Essential French rhythm-section contributor to Miles Davis film jazz

evidence.claim: WPRB's original interviewer identifies Moerlen as drummer and leader of Gong during its 1980 Princeton concert.
The first-person broadcast archive describes Moerlen's late-1970s jazz-rock direction with mallet percussion.

pierre-moerlen.limitations: Firsthand interviewer's 2015 description of his original 1980 broadcast; no direct audio transcription claimed.
pierre-moerlen.summary: French jazz-rock drummer Pierre Moerlen led a later Gong lineup that featured vibraphone and marimba in its fusion sound.
pierre-moerlen.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: The specialist chronology dates a Pim Jacobs Three session at Phonogram Studios in Hilversum to October 29, 1956.
The June 10, 1958 Jacobs Brothers Fontana session credits Pim Jacobs on piano, Ruud Jacobs on bass and Cees See on drums.

pim-jacobs.limitations: The index inconsistently credits Ruud Jacobs as a drummer in a separate June 6, 1958 group; this card deliberately uses corroborated June 10 and 1956 lineups only, not the questionable claim.
pim-jacobs.summary: Dutch pianist Pim Jacobs recorded 1956 trio sides with bassist Ruud Jacobs and drummer Wessel Ilcken and led 1958 Fontana dates with drummer Cees See.
pim-jacobs.why_it_matters: Preserves documented jazz recording or instrumental context for this named performer.

evidence.claim: The artist's original biography credits Presti as bassist on Astor Piazzolla's Libertango and identifies the bassline as his contribution to the original recording.
The original artist history identifies Presti's Atlantic Records 1st Round album as a production he released in 1976, with a separate digital remaster distributed in November 2024.
The artist's discography specifies that the January 13, 2026 Libertango 1974 single reproduces a version originally recorded in Milan in 1974.

pino-presti.limitations: The 2024 remaster of 1st Round is not a newly recorded album, and the 2026 Libertango single reissues a Milan 1974 performance. The page documents his bass role, not a separate instrumental solo.
pino-presti.summary: Italian bassist and arranger Pino Presti played on the 1974 Libertango sessions with Astor Piazzolla and produced Atlantic's funk-jazz LP 1st Round in 1976.
pino-presti.why_it_matters: The musician's own estate-maintained career site identifies both distinctive original projects and explicitly distinguishes 1974 recording from a 2026 digital single.

evidence.claim: Foster appears on the Folkways recording China Boy with Sidney Bechet, James P. Johnson and Baby Dodds.
He appears on Dear Old Southland with Bechet and Johnson.
He is listed on Maple Leaf Rag with James P. Johnson and Baby Dodds.

pops-foster.limitations: Original program track listings verify personnel, but do not give wider biographical chronology.
pops-foster.summary: Bassist Pops Foster appears on Smithsonian Folkways Town Hall sides with Sidney Bechet and James P. Johnson. Tracks include China Boy, Dear Old Southland and Maple Leaf Rag.
pops-foster.why_it_matters: Original record-company credits document collaboration across traditional-jazz ensembles.

evidence.claim: Smithsonian credits Preston Jackson on trombone on Richard M. Jones' New Orleans Hop Scop Blues, with Darnell Howard on clarinet and Baby Dodds on drums.
Smithsonian identifies Jackson as the trombonist in Jones' 29th and Dearborn, backed by pianist Jones, bassist John Lindsay and trumpeter Bob Schoffner.
Concord's Chicago: The Living Legends reissue lists Preston Jackson in Lil Hardin Armstrong's all-star ensemble, alongside Darnell Howard and Pops Foster.

preston-jackson.limitations: Smithsonian anthology release dates are not the same as original 1940s recording dates; no specific session day asserted.
preston-jackson.summary: Chicago trombonist Preston Jackson recorded Richard M. Jones' traditional jazz with Darnell Howard and Baby Dodds and later played with Lil Hardin Armstrong.
preston-jackson.why_it_matters: Smithsonian original track credits document the precise Jones band, while Concord identifies Jackson in Lil Hardin Armstrong's later Chicago all-star group.

evidence.claim: Rai Teche identifies Pupi Avati as clarinetist in Reno Jazz Gang on the January 16, 1962 episode of Jazz in Italia, with named players including Franco Franchini and Luigi Nasalvi.
Bologna's municipal library documents Avati on clarinet in the Criminal Jazz Band ensemble which recorded the soundtrack to his 1978 television film Jazz Band, with Amedeo Tommasi on piano.
The Bologna institutional history specifies that the first episode of the three-part Jazz Band television film aired on April 30, 1978, distinct from Avati's 1962 television performance.

pupi-avati.limitations: Avati directed the 1978 film, but this alone is not an instrumental credit; the municipal archive separately identifies him as clarinetist on the soundtrack. The 1962 performance date belongs to television broadcast footage, not a commercial LP.
pupi-avati.summary: Before his film career, Pupi Avati played clarinet with Bologna's Reno Jazz Gang on Italian television and on the 1978 Jazz Band soundtrack.
pupi-avati.why_it_matters: Rai Teche preserves a dated original TV performance, and Bologna's public library identifies his soundtrack clarinet performance for the later film.

evidence.claim: Caprice Records' Svensk Jazzhistoria interview describes Putte Wickman's 1948 sextet with clarinet, vibraphone, guitar and rhythm section.
The original interview says arranger Reinhold Svensson and Wickman aimed beyond conventional swing toward contemporary modernist jazz.
WorldCat's library authority identifies Putte Wickman as a Swedish jazz clarinetist born in 1924 and deceased in 2006.

identity_resolution.note: Caprice first-person Swedish jazz history and WorldCat unique jazz-clarinetist authority match the catalog entry without relying on unconfirmed MBID.

putte-wickman.limitations: No reciprocal local MusicBrainz crosslink exists; full name and unique clarinet career are independently matched in Caprice interview and WorldCat authority.
putte-wickman.summary: Swedish jazz clarinetist Putte Wickman organized a sextet in 1948 that mixed a Goodman-style lineup with arrangements inspired by modern jazz.
putte-wickman.why_it_matters: An oral-history interview from Caprice's Svensk Jazzhistoria original series identifies the band and modernist stylistic transition.

evidence.claim: Dizzy Gillespie selected Jones for his big band in 1956.
Jones was music director of Gillespie's State Department touring orchestra.
He produced Michael Jackson's album Thriller.

quincy-jones.limitations: NEA records career roles without giving specific recording session personnel.
quincy-jones.summary: Trumpeter, arranger and producer Quincy Jones played with Dizzy Gillespie and directed his touring band. He later produced Michael Jackson's Thriller.
quincy-jones.why_it_matters: His arranging and production work links jazz big bands to global pop.

evidence.claim: MIT Libraries' March 27, 2001 oral history has Rajesh Mehta describing his own hybrid-trumpet design and first recording with Paul Lovens on Orka.
The original hatOLOGY 524 Orka recording credits document Mehta on trumpet, bass trumpet and hybrid trumpet with Paul Lovens on drums, recorded in August 1996 and May 24, 1997.
MIT News identifies alumnus Rajesh Mehta as an MIT artist-in-residence in April 2001 who presented experimental trumpet compositions and invented the hybrid trumpet.
Mehta's own discography names the Mehta-Lovens Orka recording and his Mehta-Metric Ensemble release Reconfigurations.

identity_resolution.note: MIT's first-person oral history, Khoj Studios' institutional artist biography and the performer's original Orka discography all identify the experimental hybrid-trumpet player Rajesh Mehta, born in India and educated at MIT, associated with drummer Paul Lovens. The previous queue classification is insufficient_evidence with wikidata_p434_only, not a reciprocal MusicBrainz relationship. No unique MBID has been established or selected; any MBID collision remains unresolved. No Wikidata identifier was used as factual evidence.

rajesh-mehta.limitations: Previous classification insufficient_evidence with Wikidata-only identifier; MIT oral history, MIT news and the player's own discography identify the same trumpeter, but no reciprocal MBID assertion is made. The 1998 Orka issue differs from sessions recorded in 1996 and 1997.
rajesh-mehta.summary: Experimental trumpeter Rajesh Mehta developed hybrid trumpets, recorded Orka with Paul Lovens and premiered Reconfigurations at MIT in 2001.
rajesh-mehta.why_it_matters: MIT preserves the performer's direct oral history and the original hatOLOGY release documents an exact duo and recording sessions.

evidence.claim: The Smithsonian's Ralph Burns papers identify his arrangements of Apple Honey for Woody Herman.
The archival collection also identifies his arrangement of Early Autumn and documents donated original scores.

ralph-burns.limitations: Only claims recorded in the cited artist, label, institution or original archive are included; crossovers are not classified exclusively as jazz.
ralph-burns.summary: American arranger Ralph Burns wrote jazz charts for Woody Herman's orchestra, including Apple Honey and Early Autumn, before film work.
ralph-burns.why_it_matters: Documents specific recordings, ensembles or performance roles and their place in jazz or adjacent genres.

evidence.claim: ECM lists February 2022 at Auditorio Stelio Molo RSI in Lugano as the At First Light session and March 17, 2023 as the release.
The album's program pairs Towner originals including Flow and Ubi Sunt with Danny Boy and Jule Styne's Make Someone Happy.

ralph-towner.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
ralph-towner.summary: Oregon co-founder Ralph Towner recorded solo classical-guitar album At First Light in Lugano in February 2022 for ECM release in March 2023.
ralph-towner.why_it_matters: His approach folds keyboard voicings and chamber sensibility into improvised guitar music.

evidence.claim: Rambo Amadeus's own discography lists the 1989 LP Hocemo gusle on PGP-RTB as a release by the named performer.
The Eurovision organizer's official 2012 participant list identifies Rambo Amadeus performing Euro Neuro for Montenegro in Baku.
Original 2024 credits for Priznati Eminentni Umjetnik list music and words by Rambo Amadeus, editing and arrangement by STO1K and mixing by Alek Kotan.

rambo-amadeus.limitations: The festival entry is a 2012 performance, not a jazz album; the 2024 studio track belongs to a 2022-2024 project. The artist blends genres and is not classified as exclusively jazz.
rambo-amadeus.summary: Montenegrin musician Rambo Amadeus issued Hocemo Gusle in 1989, performed Euro Neuro at Eurovision 2012 and composed 2024 studio work with STO1K.
rambo-amadeus.why_it_matters: The musician's own discography and production credits plus Eurovision's official participant register document distinct works and exact authorship.

evidence.claim: MacArthur Foundation describes his improvisation shaped by film noir and gospel.
It reports that Blake founded NEC's Department of Third Stream Studies in 1972.

ran-blake.limitations: Historical foundation profile uses an older discography and appointments.
ran-blake.summary: Pianist and composer Ran Blake brings film noir, gospel and Third Stream ideas to jazz improvisation. He founded a Third Stream program at New England Conservatory.
ran-blake.why_it_matters: Explores jazz-classical fusion and improvisational music education.

evidence.claim: A specialist physical-record listing of Randy Brooks and His Orchestra's Decca Swing & Bop identifies him on trumpet with George Bardone, Earnie Englund and other named band musicians, in its April 12, 1946 session grouping.
The Shedd Institute's historic original-disc index lists Randy Brooks and His Orchestra on Decca master 73500, dated March 22, 1946, issue 29479.
The independent Fresh Sound original Vik/Riverside album reconstruction documents John Benson Brooks writing arrangements for Randy Brooks's swing orchestra in the 1940s.

randy-brooks.limitations: The 1946 Decca matrices belong to the named band, not proof that Randy soloed on every listed track. The Fresh Sound Thornhill anthology has collective personnel and is not used to infer specific track participation.
randy-brooks.summary: Trumpeter and bandleader Randy Brooks led a Decca swing orchestra documented on several 1946 discs and employed arranger John Benson Brooks.
randy-brooks.why_it_matters: Physical Decca orchestra credits and a detailed reissue's label history document an identifiable 1946 band and its arrangement work.

evidence.claim: Original MCA/Verve credit on the Crusaders' 1979 Street Life identifies Randy Crawford as the vocalist of its title track.
The Recording Academy credits Randy Crawford and Joe Sample with the 2008 traditional R&B vocal nomination All Night Long.
The Recording Academy lists her album No Regrets as a 2010 Best Jazz Vocal Album nominee.
