randy-crawford.limitations: Her Grammy entries describe nominations, not award victories; the original Street Life year is not a CD reissue year.
randy-crawford.summary: Singer Randy Crawford performed the Crusaders' 1979 Street Life and later recorded All Night Long with Joe Sample and No Regrets.
randy-crawford.why_it_matters: An original MCA/Verve recording credit and the Recording Academy establish two independent performance projects.

evidence.claim: Concord's original Randy Jackson Music Club label biography names his first session assignment with jazz violinist Jean-Luc Ponty and its 2008 Stax/Concord album.
Concord's Tom Coster artist interview identifies Randy Jackson as bassist in Coster's early solo ensemble, alongside Joaquin Lievano and Steve Smith.
Concord's original Ivory Expeditions release notes credit Randy Jackson as a member of Tom Coster's ensemble on T.C. (1981) and Ivory Expeditions (1983).

randy-jackson.limitations: This is the American Idol judge and session bassist, not a namesake rock singer. Concord's 2008 Music Club is not categorized as a straight-ahead jazz album.
randy-jackson.summary: Bassist Randy Jackson played on Jean-Luc Ponty sessions and Tom Coster's early solo albums before producing Randy Jackson's Music Club Vol. 1.
randy-jackson.why_it_matters: Two original Concord artist profiles and a project album page corroborate roles as bassist, producer and band member.

evidence.claim: Library of Congress film copyright finding aid catalogs Ray Anthony and His Orchestra in the Columbia Pictures Thrills of Music series in 1947.
Library of Congress stock-arrangements catalog identifies Thunderbird and Harlem Nocturne as Ray Anthony Capitol recordings represented by 1953 printed arrangements.

ray-anthony.limitations: The printed arrangements were published in 1953, which is not asserted to be the session date. A separate Billy May finding aid was inaccessible and its 1953-1954 rights claim was excluded.
ray-anthony.summary: Trumpeter Ray Anthony led an orchestra filmed in 1947 and recorded Thunderbird and Harlem Nocturne for Capitol, as documented by Library of Congress archives.
ray-anthony.why_it_matters: Two separately accessible Library of Congress archives document his 1947 orchestra film and contemporary printed arrangements linked to Capitol recordings.

evidence.claim: His 1962 Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music reached number one on the Billboard 200.
Genius Loves Company won Album of the Year at the 2005 Grammys.
Here We Go Again with Norah Jones won Record of the Year in 2005.

ray-charles.limitations: Grammy evidence supports specific collaborations and award categories; not instrument credits.
ray-charles.summary: Ray Charles crossed jazz, gospel and R&B in his singing and piano work. Genius Loves Company paired him with Norah Jones, B.B. King and Gladys Knight.
ray-charles.why_it_matters: His recordings demonstrate dialogue across jazz, soul, country and pop.

evidence.claim: Conniff played trombone with Bunny Berigan's Orchestra and Bob Crosby's Bobcats.
Mitch Miller hired him as a Columbia arranger in 1954.
Somewhere My Love won a 1967 Grammy for Pop Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals.

ray-conniff.limitations: Blue Note retrospective identifies career; Grammy details verified institutionally.
ray-conniff.summary: Arranger Ray Conniff played trombone with Bunny Berigan and Bob Crosby before creating wordless vocal-orchestral recordings for Columbia in the 1950s.
ray-conniff.why_it_matters: His arranging practices transformed swing-band experience into orchestral pop.

evidence.claim: Ray Foxley's own biography from the June 14, 1947 Jazz at Birmingham Town Hall original concert program identifies his early piano training and initial study of Cow-Cow Boogie.
The historical concert archive identifies Foxley performing with the Original Levee Ramblers and playing Deadman Blues on the BBC Jazz Club recording.
A photographed Jeton 1003301 physical LP catalog records Ray Foxley playing solo Steinway piano on Prof. Foxley's Sporting House Music, direct-to-disc sessions March 21 and 22, 1979.

ray-foxley.limitations: The artist autobiography is preserved as a reproduction of original 1947 program notes. The Jeton LP cover labels sessions March 21-22, 1979 and should not be confused with a 1951 Riverside recording.
ray-foxley.summary: British ragtime pianist Ray Foxley wrote his own 1947 Birmingham concert biography and recorded solo piano on a 1979 Jeton direct-to-disc LP.
ray-foxley.why_it_matters: A contemporary artist-authored concert program and a collector's original physical LP documentation confirm two separate, personally attributable performances.

evidence.claim: Ray Lema's official discography lists Riddles with pianist Laurent de Wilde in 2016 and Wheels with de Wilde in May 2021.
His biography dates the Franco Luambo tribute concert in Kinshasa to 2019 and the album Nzimbu to 2015.

ray-lema.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
ray-lema.summary: Congolese pianist Ray Lema recorded the 2016 two-piano album Riddles with Laurent de Wilde and returned to Kinshasa for a Franco Luambo tribute in 2019.
ray-lema.why_it_matters: Transforms Congolese rhythmic language into modern jazz piano and cross-cultural composition.

evidence.claim: Nance played with Earl Hines in 1937-38 and Horace Henderson in 1939-40 before joining Ellington.
He played the trumpet solo on Ellington's original Take the A Train and violin on Black, Brown and Beige.

ray-nance.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
ray-nance.summary: Trumpeter and violinist Ray Nance joined Duke Ellington after work with Earl Hines and Horace Henderson; he soloed on the original Take the A Train.
ray-nance.why_it_matters: He brought distinct plunger trumpet, violin and singing voices to Ellington's orchestra.

evidence.claim: Concord's Presenting Red Mitchell credits Mitchell's own quartet with James Clay, Lorraine Geller and Billy Higgins.
Concord's Red Norvo Trio notes identify the 1954 trio as Norvo on vibraphone, Jimmy Raney on guitar and Red Mitchell on bass.
Concord's The Seance liner notes identify Mitchell as bassist with Hampton Hawes and Donald Bailey on music recorded in 1966.

red-mitchell.limitations: The Norvo trio source concerns its 1954 recordings; the Mitchell quartet's personnel should not be projected onto other sessions.
red-mitchell.summary: Bassist Red Mitchell led a West Coast quartet with James Clay, Lorraine Geller and Billy Higgins and played in Red Norvo's guitar-vibes-bass trio.
red-mitchell.why_it_matters: Original-label reissue notes document Mitchell both as an album leader and as a central member of a pioneering chamber-jazz trio.

evidence.claim: Rodney was on the road with Jerry Wald at age fifteen.
He played with Charlie Parker's quintet in his early twenties.
He returned to jazz performing in Europe in 1972 and the United States in 1979.

red-rodney.limitations: Retrospective label liner material; sideman dates may vary across biographies.
red-rodney.summary: Trumpeter Red Rodney played in dance bands before joining Charlie Parker's quintet. The label Concord documents his return to jazz in the 1970s and later small-group releases.
red-rodney.why_it_matters: The label's reissue history connects early bebop playing with the trumpeter's revival.

evidence.claim: MacArthur Foundation awarded ragtime pianist and composer Reginald R. Robinson a fellowship on September 28, 2004.
MacArthur lists The Strongman (1993), Sounds in Silhouette (1994), Euphonic Sounds (1998) and Man Out of Time among Robinson's albums.
The Foundation states that Robinson discovered and recorded a previously unknown Scott Joplin fragment from Fisk University's archive.

reginald-robinson.limitations: The Foundation identifies Robinson primarily as a ragtime composer, not a free-jazz improviser; the historical relation to jazz is contextual.
reginald-robinson.summary: Ragtime pianist Reginald R. Robinson recorded The Strongman and Euphonic Sounds for Delmark and won a 2004 MacArthur fellowship for his compositions.
reginald-robinson.why_it_matters: The MacArthur Foundation's fellowship record documents original albums, an archival Joplin discovery, and work on early jazz's ragtime roots.

evidence.claim: Schott's artist biography identifies Winterschladen as an NDR Big Band member since 1995.
Schott names his earlier work in Trance Groove, Nighthawks and the Klaus Koenig Orchestra.

reiner-winterschladen.limitations: Publisher profile; no inferred recording dates.
reiner-winterschladen.summary: German trumpeter Reiner Winterschladen joined the NDR Big Band in 1995 after work in jazz, rock and funk groups.
reiner-winterschladen.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: The Los Angeles Times' June 2003 eyewitness concert review records Renee Olstead performing At Last, Cry Me a River and Sentimental Journey at Pasadena Jazz Institute.
Warner's original phonographic credit for What a Difference a Day Makes identifies Olstead on vocals, Alan Broadbent on piano and David Foster as producer.
The 143 Records/Warner Bros album Renee Olstead is cataloged as a 2004 recording with Hollywood and Los Angeles studios.

renee-olstead.limitations: The artist also works in pop and television; no claim is made that all recordings are jazz.
renee-olstead.summary: Vocalist Renee Olstead sang jazz standards at the Pasadena Jazz Institute in 2003 and recorded with pianist Alan Broadbent on Warner.
renee-olstead.why_it_matters: A witnessed period performance and Warner's original recording-credit metadata document specific musicianship.

evidence.claim: Blue Note biography dates Renee Rosnes's own recordings from 1990.
Pianist Renee Rosnes became music director of ARTEMIS, whose Blue Note debut appeared in 2020.

renee-rosnes.limitations: Research is source-specific; credits denote actual documented roles, not an exhaustive discography.
renee-rosnes.summary: Pianist Renee Rosnes recorded as a Blue Note leader from 1990 and became music director of ARTEMIS, whose debut Blue Note album arrived in 2020.
renee-rosnes.why_it_matters: Contemporary piano leadership and compositions for ARTEMIS ensemble.

evidence.claim: UNF archive identifies his Matteson-Phillips Tubajazz Consort recordings.
UNF says he taught jazz improvisation at North Texas and joined its faculty in 1986.

rich-matteson.limitations: University memorial account is retrospective; avoid claimed rankings of instrumentalists.
rich-matteson.summary: Jazz euphonium and tuba player Rich Matteson co-led the Matteson-Phillips Tubajazz Consort and taught improvisation at North Texas and the University of North Florida.
rich-matteson.why_it_matters: Documents an uncommon jazz solo instrument and influential teaching work.

evidence.claim: Official bio identifies Bona as bassist, vocalist and multi-instrumentalist
Performed and recorded with Pat Metheny and Herbie Hancock among others

richard-bona.limitations: Source-specific musical details; does not establish exhaustive discography.
richard-bona.summary: Cameroonian bassist and vocalist Richard Bona folds African melody into jazz and Afropop; his collaborations include Pat Metheny and Herbie Hancock.
richard-bona.why_it_matters: African vocal phrasing and bass groove brought into modern crossover jazz

evidence.claim: Richard Carpenter wrote and arranged Prelude and played piano on the track alongside clarinetist Jim Kanter and Earle Dumler on English horn.
On Yesterday Once More, the original credit lists Carpenter as co-writer with John Bettis, arranger and keyboard player.
Karen's Theme is credited as written by Richard Carpenter, with Richard on piano and Earle Dumler on English horn.

richard-carpenter.limitations: Richard Carpenter's official catalog has inconsistent 1997/1998 issue dating; no exact year is claimed. Original pop arranging is not automatically called jazz.
richard-carpenter.summary: Richard Carpenter played piano on Prelude and wrote and arranged Karen's Theme for his own instrumental solo album.
richard-carpenter.why_it_matters: The artist's original album credits distinguish his piano, keyboard, composition and arrangement roles by track.

evidence.claim: Richard Elliot official biography identifies Trolltown as his 1986 solo debut and lists Summer Madness among his 2016 releases.
Original Heads Up Summer Madness 2016 liner notes identify Rick Braun as producer and recording engineer at Brauntosoarus Studio.

richard-elliot.limitations: The 2016 liner notes are tied to Summer Madness; the Rick Braun production credit does not generalize to prior Elliot albums.
richard-elliot.summary: Smooth-jazz saxophonist Richard Elliot began his solo discography with Trolltown in 1986 and recorded Summer Madness for Heads Up in 2016.
richard-elliot.why_it_matters: Artist history and original Heads Up tech notes document solo chronology and named producer rather than inferred collaborators.

evidence.claim: Long touring partnership with vocalist Eddie Jefferson through 1979
Cole also recorded Side by Side with Phil Woods

richie-cole.limitations: Source-specific music facts; not a complete discography.

silje-nergaard.summary: Norwegian vocalist Silje Nergaard joined Espen Berg Trio on the Paul Simon song I'd Do It For Your Love, released in March 2022.
silje-nergaard.why_it_matters: Nordic jazz singer collaborating on acoustic piano trio reinterpretations.

evidence.claim: The Swedish Performing Arts Agency history identifies the Brehm Bal Palais band, recordings Seven Eleven and Things Ain't What They Used to Be (1952) and Blues for a Broken Bass (1954).
Bear Family's original Lill-Babs album notes say Brehm engaged the singer in early 1954 and ended his touring orchestra in 1958.
Povel Ramel's historical society identifies Brehm on bass in the 1941 Embassy sextet and with Ramel's radio work in 1946-1951.

simon-brehm.limitations: Dates concern different endeavors: 1952 label founding, 1954 touring and 1958 end of his touring orchestra; these are not asserted as recording years.
simon-brehm.summary: Swedish jazz bassist Simon Brehm led a Bal Palais dance band, started the Karusell label in 1952 and recruited singer Lill-Babs for a 1954 tour.
simon-brehm.why_it_matters: Swedish national music history, the original Bear Family reissue and Povel Ramel's society identify separate work.

evidence.claim: D'Sound's official history names Eriksrud as a founding vocalist with Jonny Sjo and Kim Ofstad in 1993.
The band says she rejoined the founders on the 2022 single Flashback and later recordings.

simone-eriksrud.limitations: Official band history, not an independent solo discography.
simone-eriksrud.summary: Norwegian singer Simone Eriksrud co-founded D'Sound in 1993, singing on its jazz-soul debut Spice of Life and later returning to the group.
simone-eriksrud.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: Clean Feed lists Sirone on double bass alongside Charles Gayle on tenor saxophone and Gerald Cleaver on drums for Shout.
The label notes that Sirone had previously worked on Gayle recordings Spirits Before, Homeless and Always Born.

sirone.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
sirone.summary: Bassist Sirone joined Charles Gayle and Gerald Cleaver for the studio trio release Shout, pairing exploratory tenor saxophone with agile acoustic rhythm.
sirone.why_it_matters: His acoustic bass helps link early American free jazz with later trio experiments.

evidence.claim: Dicionario Cravo Albin states Sivuca joined Miriam Makeba's backing group as guitarist in 1965 and subsequently directed that ensemble.

sivuca.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
sivuca.summary: Brazilian accordionist Sivuca worked with Miriam Makeba as guitarist and bandleader and recorded a 1984 accordion duo with Chiquinho do Acordeom.
sivuca.why_it_matters: Brazilian accordion jazz reaches across choro, forro and international popular music.

evidence.claim: Concord Prestige album notes identify Skeeter Best among Etta Jones Don't Go to Strangers personnel alongside Frank Wess, Richard Wyands, George Duvivier and Roy Haynes.
Fresh Sound original Coral album reissue Stepping Into Swing Society names Skeeter Best as guitarist among Mercer Ellington 1958 New York orchestra personnel.
Fresh Sound Lucky Thompson Meets Oscar Pettiford original-album reissue credits Skeeter Best on guitar with Lucky Thompson, Hank Jones and Oscar Pettiford.

skeeter-best.limitations: Mercer Ellington sessions have different guitarists on different dates; credits are limited to the tracks specifically featuring Best.
skeeter-best.summary: Guitarist Skeeter Best recorded with Etta Jones on the 1960 Prestige album Don't Go to Strangers and in Mercer Ellington's 1958 orchestra.
skeeter-best.why_it_matters: Original Prestige and Coral reissue notes credit Best in two different identifiable New York jazz and vocal sessions.

evidence.claim: Carnegie Hall's official institutional history identifies Skitch Henderson as founder of the New York Pops, resident from 1983.
A Carnegie Hall primary concert record credits Henderson as conductor of the New York Pops in a 1991 program including My Funny Valentine.
In a National Endowment for the Arts oral history, drummer Sherrie Maricle recalls Henderson recruiting her to the New York Pops in 1990.

skitch-henderson.limitations: His orchestral and popular-music repertoire should not be generalized as entirely jazz.
skitch-henderson.summary: Pianist-conductor Skitch Henderson founded the New York Pops in 1983 and conducted a Carnegie Hall program featuring My Funny Valentine.
skitch-henderson.why_it_matters: Carnegie Hall's performance database and the NEA's direct interview corroborate the orchestra's history.

evidence.claim: Young served as lead trumpeter and soloist in Jimmie Lunceford's band from 1939 to 1942.
Young helped found the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis Orchestra in 1966 and played in The Tonight Show orchestra.

snooky-young.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
snooky-young.summary: Trumpeter Snooky Young played lead with Jimmie Lunceford in 1939-42, helped found the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis Orchestra in 1966 and joined The Tonight Show band.
snooky-young.why_it_matters: A leading big-band brass player with a distinctive cup-mute sound.

evidence.claim: Fresh Sound's original Urania Accent on Trombone reissue credits Sol Yaged on clarinet alongside Jack Teagarden, Ruby Braff and Lucky Thompson, recorded in New York in October 1954.
Library of Congress Gottlieb collection lists Sol Solomon Yaged in a photograph with Doc Pomus, John Levy, Rex Stewart and Uffe Bode at New York's Pied Piper circa September 1947.

sol-yaged.limitations: The 1947 Gottlieb photo documents presence with jazz colleagues, not a recorded performance. The 1954 session date is distinct from the Fresh Sound reissue date.
sol-yaged.summary: Clarinetist Sol Yaged played a 1954 Jack Teagarden session and appeared at New York's Pied Piper in 1947 with Rex Stewart and Doc Pomus.
sol-yaged.why_it_matters: A restored original Urania session ledger and a Library of Congress contemporary performance-scene photograph document separate musical contexts.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Solveig Slettahjell with vocals on Statements alongside reciters Sidsel Endresen and Miki N'Doye.
Statements was recorded in 2003-2004 at Bugge's Room and first released September 5, 2005.

solveig-slettahjell.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
solveig-slettahjell.summary: Norwegian vocalist Solveig Slettahjell contributed to Jon Balke's Batagraf album Statements, made during 2003-04 and released by ECM in 2005.
solveig-slettahjell.why_it_matters: Her voice joins Balke's percussion and speech-driven experimental jazz.

evidence.claim: The original Argo LP-669 session inventory credits Sonny Brown on drums with Roland Kirk, Ira Sullivan, William Burton and Donald Garrett at a Chicago date on June 7, 1960.
Resonance Records' original tape-restoration release credits drummer Sonny Brown with Rahsaan Roland Kirk at the Village Gate in New York on November 26-27, 1963.
Resonance's archival album documentation distinguishes the November 1963 live tapes from its first issue as Vibrations in the Village in December 2025.

sonny-brown.limitations: Introducing Roland Kirk was recorded June 1960 and issued in 1960; Resonance's 2025 CD is a first archival release of November 1963 concert tapes, not a new 2025 performance.
sonny-brown.summary: Drummer Sonny Brown joined Roland Kirk on the 1960 Argo Introducing Roland Kirk session and at the Village Gate concert tapes recorded in 1963.
sonny-brown.why_it_matters: The original Argo matrix-based discography and Resonance's archival tape release document two separately recorded Kirk ensembles featuring Brown.

evidence.claim: Hunger's official music page lists the album Monday's Ghost.
The same official discography lists Molecules and Halluzinationen.

sophie-hunger.limitations: Official discography supports titles; label affiliation independently displayed at Two Gentlemen.
sophie-hunger.summary: Swiss songwriter Sophie Hunger released albums including Monday's Ghost and Molecules and records for the Two Gentlemen label.
sophie-hunger.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: Milman's official biography identifies Make Someone Happy as a JUNO Award-winning album.
Her official biography credits Chris Potter, Randy Brecker and Larry Grenadier on In The Moonlight.

sophie-milman.limitations: Artist-level historical synopsis; specific session credits restricted to cited primary material.
sophie-milman.summary: Russian-born Canadian jazz singer Sophie Milman combines classic standards with contemporary jazz arrangements and international influences.
sophie-milman.why_it_matters: Documents concrete genre, performance and recording contributions to a diverse jazz catalog.

evidence.claim: Powell was hired by CBS New York in 1943 as the first Black musician at a national network.
He worked in Ray Bloch's CBS orchestra from 1947 to 1972.
He recorded with Red Norvo, Erroll Garner, Charlie Parker and Billie Holiday.

specs-powell.limitations: Union account makes a specific CBS hiring claim; use its precise wording.
specs-powell.summary: Drummer Specs Powell became the first Black staff musician at a US national network when CBS hired him in 1943. He played in the Ed Sullivan orchestra from 1947 to 1972.
specs-powell.why_it_matters: His career illustrates the movement of jazz musicians into network radio and television orchestras.

evidence.claim: The Blue Note Records biography identifies Stan Levey as drummer with the Charlie Parker Quintet in 1945 and with Parker and Dizzy Gillespie that year.
Blue Note records that Stan Kenton hired Levey and saxophonist Richie Kamuca in Philadelphia in 1952.
The same label biography states that after Kenton dissolved the band in 1954, Levey played with the Lighthouse All-Stars and retired to professional photography in 1973.

stan-levey.limitations: A 1945 band affiliation is not proof of personnel for every recorded Parker side; later studio work is not attributed to a single year.
stan-levey.summary: Bebop drummer Stan Levey worked with Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker in 1945, then joined Stan Kenton orchestra in 1952.
stan-levey.why_it_matters: The original Blue Note label artist profile identifies a 1945 Parker-Gillespie group and the later West Coast jazz role in Kenton and Lighthouse.

evidence.claim: The UK National Jazz Archive identifies Tracey as Ronnie Scott's house pianist from 1960 and names his support of American visitors including Ben Webster and Sonny Rollins.
The Tracey family album archive identifies the 1965 Under Milk Wood quartet as Stan Tracey on piano, Bobby Wellins on tenor sax, Jeff Clyne on bass and Jackie Dougan on drums.

stan-tracey.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
stan-tracey.summary: British pianist Stan Tracey led the 1965 Under Milk Wood quartet with Bobby Wellins, Jeff Clyne and drummer Jackie Dougan after backing guests at Ronnie Scott's.
stan-tracey.why_it_matters: His original jazz suite and club work helped establish a distinct British modern-jazz voice.

evidence.claim: ECM lists Stanley Cowell on piano, Stanley Clarke on bass and Jimmy Hopps on drums for Illusion Suite.
Illusion Suite was recorded in November 1972 at Sound Ideas Studio in New York and first released November 28, 1973.

stanley-cowell.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
stanley-cowell.summary: Pianist Stanley Cowell recorded Illusion Suite with Stanley Clarke and Jimmy Hopps in New York in November 1972; its original release followed in 1973.
stanley-cowell.why_it_matters: Cowell's compositions join harmonic exploration to a modernist trio language.

evidence.claim: Mainz University's jazz faculty biography says Steffen Weber studied jazz and popular music at Mannheim from 1995 to 1999.
Mainz University says he was an SWR Big Band member from 2008 to early 2012 and joined the HR Big Band in 2012.
Origin Records' original artist profile lists Weber on Chamber 3's Transatlantic (OA2 22153) and Grassroots (OA2 22115).

steffen-weber.limitations: His listed work with major guests refers to performances in the HR Big Band, not necessarily recordings under his name.
steffen-weber.summary: German saxophonist Steffen Weber co-founded L14,16, played in the SWR Big Band from 2008 to 2012 and joined the Frankfurt Radio Big Band in 2012.
steffen-weber.why_it_matters: The Mainz university and independent Origin Records profile preserve specific ensemble, employment and teaching credits.

evidence.claim: Micus records and layers traditional instruments himself, sometimes building choral vocals by overdubbing.
His 2024 ECM album To the Rising Moon features the Colombian tiple.
ECM's Snow lists duduk, Bavarian zither and charango among his instruments.

stephan-micus.limitations: ECM categorizes his work beyond standard jazz; avoid claiming traditional performances.
stephan-micus.summary: Multi-instrumentalist Stephan Micus studies instruments worldwide and overdubs them in solo compositions. His 2024 album To the Rising Moon featured Colombian tiples.
stephan-micus.why_it_matters: His ECM catalog explores the sound of non-Western acoustic instruments in new combinations.

evidence.claim: Jazz Lives' original record analysis identifies Sterling Bose on trumpet with Johnny Mercer, Jack Teagarden, Fulton McGrath, Dick McDonough and Hank Wayland in Victor Young's August 24, 1934 session of The Bathtub Ran Over Again.
The Syncopated Times' original historical investigation identifies Bose as a member of the Original Crescent City Jazzers and as a later player with Jean Goldkette.
The original historical article traces Bose recordings and orchestral work between 1930 and 1936 with Pollack, Teagarden, Haymes and Ray Noble.

sterling-bose.limitations: The Library of Congress Joe Haymes finding aid could not be directly inspected. The 1934 session is documented by a specialist's listening and record-history investigation, not by an original Decca session ledger.
sterling-bose.summary: Cornetist Sterling Bose played in Joe Haymes's big band and performed with the Original Crescent City Jazzers before later swing-orchestra work.
sterling-bose.why_it_matters: Specialist investigations of original early swing recordings document Bose's dated trumpet work and his orchestral affiliations.

evidence.claim: Clean Feed lists Steve Beresford on electronics and Simon H. Fell on bass for Positions & Descriptions, Composition No. 75.
The ensemble credits also include Tim Berne on alto saxophone, Rhodri Davies on harp, Philip Thomas on piano and Mark Sanders on drums.

steve-beresford.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
steve-beresford.summary: Improviser Steve Beresford supplied electronics to Simon H. Fell's large-ensemble work Positions & Descriptions alongside Tim Berne and Rhodri Davies.
steve-beresford.why_it_matters: His electronics help merge electroacoustic sound with ensemble improvisation.

evidence.claim: Tulane's Music Rising archival research identifies bassist Steve Brown as a New Orleans musician who recorded with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings in Chicago in 1922.
Tulane dates Brown's electrically recorded slap-bass work with Jean Goldkette's Orchestra to January 1927 and places him with Paul Whiteman in 1927-1928.
Concord's New Orleans Rhythm Kings original-label reissue includes Steve Brown among the musicians across recordings made in August 1922, March 1923 and July 1923.
A specialist study published by Cambridge University Press documents Brown's slap-bass approach and his experience recording the Goldkette orchestra for Victor.

steve-brown.limitations: Concord's three-session compilation names Brown in a collective roster but does not allocate him to every track; the 1927 Goldkette recording work is independently documented by Tulane and historical scholarship.
steve-brown.summary: New Orleans bassist Steve Brown recorded with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings in 1922 and made influential slap-bass sides with Jean Goldkette in 1927.
steve-brown.why_it_matters: Tulane's original Gulf South music research establishes the artist's two recording eras, while Concord preserves the original NORK label-session grouping.

evidence.claim: Zaum original Bandcamp liner notes identify Steve Harris on drums on the October 31, 2007 Live in Brighton concert with Cathy Stevens, Geoff Hearn, Udo Dzierzanowski, Karen Wimhurst, J'm Black and Adrian Newton.
Zaum release notes state Live in Brighton appeared via Amazon Records in 2008 and was remastered from the original concert tapes in November 2018.
The ensemble's Eye of the Sea archival release directly credits Steve Harris on drums and Jan Kopinski on tenor sax for their late-2007 duet concert; the digital release was November 8, 2018.

steve-harris.limitations: Live in Brighton was performed October 31, 2007, originally released in 2008 and digitally remastered in 2018; the 2018 Eye of the Sea issue likewise preserves a 2007 concert, not a 2018 performance.
steve-harris.summary: English drummer Steve Harris founded the improvising group Zaum, recorded a 2007 Brighton concert and played a late duet with saxophonist Jan Kopinski.
steve-harris.why_it_matters: The original ensemble recordings identify two separate performances and directly credit Harris on drums, with first-hand notes explaining later digital reissues.

evidence.claim: Pianist Steve Kuhn briefly joined John Coltrane's quartet in 1960.
ECM 2012 Wisteria lineup included Steve Swallow and Joey Baron.

steve-kuhn.limitations: Research is source-specific; credits denote actual documented roles, not an exhaustive discography.
steve-kuhn.summary: Pianist Steve Kuhn played in John Coltrane's quartet in 1960; his ECM trio album 'Wisteria' (2012) united Steve Swallow and Joey Baron.
steve-kuhn.why_it_matters: Lyrical piano language connected to modal modern jazz.

evidence.claim: Lukather played guitar and bass during Thriller sessions.
Toto's 1978 debut credits him on guitar and vocals.
His solo album Lukather included Eddie Van Halen and Jan Hammer.

steve-lukather.limitations: The official site contains a section flagged as content suggestion; corroborate controversial specifics in original album credits.
steve-lukather.summary: Guitarist Steve Lukather co-founded Toto and played on Michael Jackson's Thriller. His solo album Lukather features guest musicians including Eddie Van Halen and Jan Hammer.
steve-lukather.why_it_matters: His playing crosses jazz-influenced pop sessions and instrumental guitar collaborations.

evidence.claim: Points of View credits Steve Nelson on vibraphone and marimba with Dave Holland, Robin Eubanks, Steve Wilson and Billy Kilson.
ECM dates the Points of View recording to September 1997 at Avatar Studios in New York and the original release to April 4, 1998.

steve-nelson.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
steve-nelson.summary: Vibraphonist Steve Nelson recorded Dave Holland Quintet's Points of View in September 1997, alternating vibes and marimba in the new band.
steve-nelson.why_it_matters: Nelson's mallet harmonies give Holland's interlocking quintet music unusual color.

evidence.claim: ECM credits Steve Rodby on bass guitar, acoustic bass and bass drum on Pat Metheny Group's First Circle.
First Circle was recorded in February 1984 at Power Station, New York, and originally released October 1, 1984.

steve-rodby.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
steve-rodby.summary: Bassist Steve Rodby recorded First Circle with the Pat Metheny Group at New York's Power Station in February 1984 alongside Lyle Mays.
steve-rodby.why_it_matters: His acoustic and electric low end supported a landmark blend of modern jazz and global rhythmic ideas.

evidence.claim: Avant Pop credits Steve Turre and Frank Lacy on trombones in Lester Bowie's Brass Fantasy, recorded March 1986 in Ludwigsburg.

steve-turre.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
steve-turre.summary: Trombonist Steve Turre recorded Avant Pop with Lester Bowie's Brass Fantasy at Tonstudio Bauer in March 1986 and contributed two compositions.
steve-turre.why_it_matters: His trombone writing and performance connect the brass band's avant-garde arrangements to popular song.

evidence.claim: In a 2014 firsthand interview Williamson says clarinet was his first school instrument and saxophone followed at sixteen.

steve-williamson.limitations: Claims taken from direct artist interview; not biographical speculation.
steve-williamson.summary: British saxophonist Steve Williamson began on clarinet, took up saxophone at sixteen and drew early inspiration from jazz-funk records.
steve-williamson.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: The Association of Composers of Serbia identifies Stjepko Gut in the Trumpet & Rhythm Unit and Markovic-Gut Sextet during the late 1970s and early 1980s.
The composer's association dates Gut's teaching at the University of Music and Performing Arts Graz from 1985 and lists his 1995 Steve Gut & Mr. Clark Terry album.
Tom Lord's specialist original jazz session index independently lists Stjepko 'Steve' Gut on trumpet and flugelhorn with recordings from 1979 to 2007.

stjepko-gut.limitations: The association's account of the 1999 festival appearance is not extrapolated into a claim that he led all the other trumpeters.
stjepko-gut.summary: Serbian trumpeter Stjepko Gut played in the Markovic-Gut Sextet, taught jazz in Graz from 1985 and appeared at the 1999 Trumpet Summit.
stjepko-gut.why_it_matters: The Serbian Composers' Association's musician biography and specialist discographic session index independently support his work.

evidence.claim: Sofia Philharmonic's performer biography says Yankulov spent seven years in the Bulgarian National Radio Big Band and graduated from the Pancho Vladigerov academy.
Stoyan Yankulov's own biography names jazz collaborations with Milcho Leviev and Ivo Papazov and his drumming on tupan.
Bulgarian News Agency's September 2026 interview identifies his concerts with GloBalkan and the Vladigerov Brothers.

stoyan-yankulov.limitations: Formerly insufficient_evidence: the full name and stage name Stundzhi match across first-party profiles; no birthplace assertion is made.
stoyan-yankulov.summary: Bulgarian drummer Stoyan Yankulov spent seven years in the national radio big band and combined jazz drumming with Bulgarian folk percussion.
stoyan-yankulov.why_it_matters: Sofia Philharmonic's original performer profile and the artist's primary biography document separate ensemble and training details.

evidence.claim: Sony's licensed Apple Music credits identify Stuart Zender as bass guitarist and songwriter on Jamiroquai's Virtual Insanity, originally released in 1996.
Licensed track personnel for Travelling Without Moving identify Zender on bass guitar and among the songwriters; the track is dated August 28, 1996.

stuart-zender.limitations: Both credits refer to Jamiroquai's 1996 music; later remastered editions are not new performance dates. Album-wide membership has not been used to infer other track participation.
stuart-zender.summary: Bassist Stuart Zender performed and co-wrote Jamiroquai's 1996 tracks Virtual Insanity and Travelling Without Moving, before the 2016 remasters.
stuart-zender.why_it_matters: Licensed track-level rights and musician metadata document an actual bass performance and composition credit for two named recordings.

evidence.claim: ECM's Trance release credits Sue Evans on percussion with Steve Kuhn, Steve Swallow and Jack DeJohnette in November 1974 New York sessions, originally released February 1975.
A collector's transcription of original CTI Good King Bad jacket credits identifies Sue Evans on percussion in the George Benson personnel.
The original CTI 1976 sleeve and 1982 Cast Your Fate to the Wind reissue notes reproduced by a physical-record seller name Sue Evans and differentiate 1975 recording sessions from later issue years.

sue-evans.limitations: Good King Bad was recorded in July and December 1975 and issued in 1976; a later 1982 release is a reissue. The CTI original cover credit does not establish Evans on every specific track.
sue-evans.summary: Percussionist Sue Evans recorded Steve Kuhn's Trance in November 1974 and played on George Benson's CTI album Good King Bad in 1975.
sue-evans.why_it_matters: ECM's own session notes and reproduced original CTI physical-record credits document her on two independently recorded jazz projects.

evidence.claim: ESP-Disk session discography lists Sunny Murray drums, Jacques Coursil trumpet, Byard Lancaster and Jack Graham alto sax and Alan Silva bass in NYC January 1966.
The JazzProfiles research discography places the self-titled Sunny Murray album on ESP 1032 in 1966 and distinguishes later reissues.

sunny-murray.limitations: A January 1966 recording session differs from later 1992 and 2005 reissues; the album does not prove his appearance on every related ESP compilation.
sunny-murray.summary: Free-jazz drummer Sunny Murray led a January 1966 New York ESP-Disk session with Alan Silva, Jacques Coursil and Byard Lancaster.
sunny-murray.why_it_matters: The original ESP-Disk session log documents personnel and dating for one avant-garde drum-led recording.

evidence.claim: ECM's April credits list vocalist Susanne Abbuehl, pianist Wolfert Brederode, clarinetist Christof May and drummer Samuel Rohrer, recorded in November 2000.
ECM states that April was originally released on October 1, 2001 and includes pieces connected with Carla Bley and E. E. Cummings.
ECM credits Compass to Abbuehl's voice alongside Wolfert Brederode, Lucas Niggli, Christof May and Michel Portal, with original release in 2006.

susanne-abbuehl.limitations: ECM's 2019 Touchstones edition of Compass is a reissue, not its 2006 original release; the album was recorded in 2003 and 2004.
susanne-abbuehl.summary: Swiss-Dutch jazz vocalist Susanne Abbuehl recorded April for ECM in 2000 and later made Compass with pianist Wolfert Brederode and drummer Lucas Niggli.
susanne-abbuehl.why_it_matters: ECM gives precise recorded-vs-reissued dates, instrumentation and the singer's approach to poetry and improvisation.

evidence.claim: Alt's official album page dates Royalty for Real to February 16, 2024 and says it was recorded at EastSide Sound in New York.
The New York quartet is Alt on saxophone with James Hurt on keys, bassist Gerald Cannon and drummer Willie Jones III; the project is dedicated to Roy Hargrove.

susanne-alt.limitations: Specific source-reviewed music claims; not a comprehensive discography.
susanne-alt.summary: German-born Amsterdam saxophonist Susanne Alt recorded Royalty for Real in New York with James Hurt, Gerald Cannon and Willie Jones III.
susanne-alt.why_it_matters: Modern saxophone-led jazz reconnecting acoustic grooves with Roy Hargrove's repertoire.

evidence.claim: The Norwegian encyclopedic institute credits him with forming a trio in 1967 with bassist Bjoernar Andresen.
Its authored entry lists the trio album Plastic Sun (1970) and his work as painter and graphic artist.

svein-finnerud.limitations: Institutional original biographical entry; personnel spelling transliterated.
svein-finnerud.summary: Norwegian pianist and visual artist Svein Finnerud formed a free-jazz trio in 1967 and issued Plastic Sun in 1970.
svein-finnerud.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: The institutional biography dates Herstad's trio album Dig to 1993.
It credits him with composing Suite for Simmons for Sildajazz in 2005.

svein-olav-herstad.summary: Norwegian jazz pianist Svein Olav Herstad led piano trios and wrote Suite for Simmons for the 2005 Sildajazz festival.
svein-olav-herstad.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: His official biography names Piaia as his first album in 1993.

sylvain-luc.limitations: Artist biography; album credits not independently rechecked.
sylvain-luc.summary: French guitarist Sylvain Luc released Piaia in 1993 and later recorded duo albums with Louis Winsberg and Bireli Lagrene.
sylvain-luc.why_it_matters: Documents this musician's distinctive role in jazz and related music.

evidence.claim: Blue Note's Tarus Mateen biography identifies his New York relocation in 1988 and subsequent appointment in Betty Carter's band.

Blue Note's 2013 tour announcement bills Mateen with Jason Moran's Bandwagon at SFJAZZ on May 4 and 5.

tarus-mateen.limitations: The trio album Ten dates from 2010; the later 2024 vinyl release is a reissue.
tarus-mateen.summary: Bassist Tarus Mateen worked in Betty Carter's band and formed Jason Moran's Bandwagon trio with drummer Nasheet Waits on Facing Left and Ten.
tarus-mateen.why_it_matters: Original Blue Note biographies, album credits and a tour announcement document distinct professional activities.

evidence.claim: The specialist Ted Curson session discography places his Paris quartet at Studio Acousti August 1 1964 with Bill Barron, Herb Bushler and Dick Berk.
JazzDisco catalog identifies the original Tears for Dolphy as Fontana 688 310 ZL issued in 1965, with reissues on Freedom and Arista.

ted-curson.limitations: The session was recorded in 1964 but original Fontana issue is cataloged 1965; later Freedom/Arista issues are reissues.
ted-curson.summary: Trumpeter Ted Curson recorded Tears for Dolphy in Paris on August 1 1964 with Bill Barron, Herb Bushler and drummer Dick Berk.
ted-curson.why_it_matters: Session matrix and original 1965 Fontana issue document a precise transatlantic small-group album.

evidence.claim: The National Portrait Gallery identifies Ted Heath as a trombonist who worked with Jack Hylton, Bert Ambrose and Geraldo before leading his own orchestra.
